title: Book of Moses 1:33–38
speaker: Joseph Smith
office: First Elder of the Church
venue: Revelation (Visions of Moses), later canonized in the Pearl of Great Price

quotes.excerpt: And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose; and by the Son I created them, which is mine Only Begotten. … And as one earth shall pass away, and the heavens thereof even so shall another come; and there is no end to my works, neither to my words.
quotes.note: A single divine speaker creates all the worlds — though the restored clause names a second divine agent in the act of creation, “by the Son I created them.” He is the originator of the series, not a member of it.

notes: Retagged in v2: MANY-WORLDS, not INFINITE-CHAIN. Plurality of worlds is not succession of Gods. This text is context for later chain teachings rather than evidence of them — and the interpretive move by which Pratt and Young later recruit it is itself the datum, logged on those entries.

title: Discourse, 30 January 1842
speaker: Joseph Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: Joseph Smith's home, Nauvoo, Illinois (evening)

quotes.excerpt: the God & father of our Lord Jesus Christ was once the same as the Son or Holy Ghost but having redeemed a world became the eternal God of that world he had a son Jesus Christ who redeemed this earth the same as his father had a world which made them equal & the Holy Ghost would do the same in his turn & so would all the Saints who inherited a Celestial glory so their would be Gods many & Lords many
quotes.note: Father-referent and explicit: the Father was once as the Son is, redeemed a world of His own, and stands in a repeating series ("Gods many & Lords many"). Backward regress and forward progression are stated in one breath, with the Christological analogy already doing the argumentative work it will do again in the King Follett Discourse. Two corrections. The reading is JSP's “but having,” with its editorial note “TEXT: Possibly ‘bothaving [both having]’”; the conjectural “both having” would make the Son and Holy Ghost the subjects, where “but having” makes the Father the sole subject. And BACKWARD-EXPLICIT is dropped: that the Father had a Father follows here only by Christological symmetry, not by statement, while FATHER-BECAME-GOD (“having redeemed a world became the eternal God of that world”) is stated outright.

notes: Added in v2. This discourse predates the Sermon in the Grove by nearly two and a half years and is quoted in Joseph Smith Papers footnote 18 to the Bullock report of the King Follett Discourse (https://www.josephsmithpapers.org/paper-summary/discourse-7-april-1844-as-reported-by-thomas-bullock/3), which is where this entry was found. The earlier claim that it revises the working position that the Sermon in the Grove is Joseph Smith's only unambiguous Father-referent BACKWARD-EXPLICIT statement is withdrawn along with that tag: the 1842 text says the Father “was once the same as the Son or Holy Ghost,” from which a Father of the Father follows only by inference. Rated C: JSP's source note names Wilford Woodruff as the scribe and its historical introduction records that he was away from Nauvoo on 30 January and likely worked from someone else's notes (see witnesses). The wording above follows the JSP document transcript of Discourse, 30 January 1842.

witnesses.scribe: Wilford Woodruff
witnesses.note: Copied into Woodruff's 'Book of Revelations' ca. 30 Jan. 1842. JSP: Woodruff's journal indicates he was away from Nauvoo on 30 January and he 'likely used someone else's notes of the sermon when he recorded it.' Only extant account apart from Willard Richards's brief note in JS's journal.

title: Book of Abraham 3:18–26; 4:1
speaker: Joseph Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: Published in Times and Seasons, Nauvoo; later canonized in the Pearl of Great Price

quotes.excerpt: if there be two spirits, and one shall be more intelligent than the other … have no beginning; they existed before, they shall have no end, they shall exist after, for they are gnolaum, or eternal.
quotes.note: Eternal, uncreated intelligences — no beginning means no begetting.

quotes.excerpt: And then the Lord said: Let us go down. And they went down at the beginning, and they, that is the Gods, organized and formed the heavens and the earth.
quotes.note: Context rather than evidence: plural organizing Gods, with no statement of how those Gods came to be. Locus: Abraham 4:1, at https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/scriptures/pgp/abr/4 — the entry's URL serves only chapter 3.

notes: The TRIPARTITE tag is dropped in v2. Abraham 3 asserts eternal intelligences and plural organizing Gods; it never articulates intelligence → spirit → body staging. Note too that "intelligences" and "spirits" are used interchangeably across 3:22–23, which cuts against reading a stage distinction into the chapter at all. The three-stage model is B. H. Roberts's later synthesis — filed separately.

title: Doctrine and Covenants 132:19–20, 63
speaker: Joseph Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: Revelation recorded at Nauvoo; first published 1852; canonized 1876

quotes.excerpt: ...which glory shall be a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever. Then shall they be gods, because they have no end... then shall they be above all, because all things are subject unto them.
quotes.note: Promises deification and continuing "seeds" without naming either the mechanism or the object. Nothing here says spirit children.

quotes.excerpt: …and for their exaltation in the eternal worlds, that they may bear the souls of men; for herein is the work of my Father continued, that he may be glorified.
quotes.note: On the full text the mortality-only reading is not the plainest one: the verse expressly frames the bearing as being “for their exaltation in the eternal worlds.”

notes: Downgraded in v2 from FORWARD-EXPLICIT to FORWARD-EUPHEMISM. This is deliberate and contestable: the explicit spirit-procreation reading is supplied by later interpreters — Pratt, the 1909 First Presidency, Ballard — not by the verse. Holding the canon itself to the strict standard is what makes the euphemism/explicit boundary load-bearing, and that boundary is where the whole taper story lives. The dependency is preserved: the explicit teachings that cite this text carry the explicitness themselves, and the citation links show it.

title: King Follett Discourse
speaker: Joseph Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: General Conference, Nauvoo

witnesses.scribe: Thomas Bullock
witnesses.note: Contemporaneous longhand; the base text for the standard versification.

witnesses.scribe: William Clayton
witnesses.note: Contemporaneous longhand; sole witness to the "all Gods" wording.

witnesses.scribe: Willard Richards
witnesses.note: Highly abbreviated notes in Joseph Smith's own journal. Records the deification injunction ('you have got to learn how to make you[r]selves Gods Kings. Prie[s]ts.— &— by going from a small to g[r]eat capacity'), but with no comparison-class clause — no 'as all Gods has done' and no 'same as all have done'.

witnesses.scribe: Wilford Woodruff
witnesses.note: Journal account. Records the deification injunction ('you have got to learn how to make yourselves God, king and priest, by going from a small capacity to a great capacity'), but with no comparison-class clause.

quotes.excerpt: Going to tell you how God came to be God. We have imagined that God was God from all eternity... to know that we may converse with him as one man with another & that he was once as one of us and was on a planet as Jesus was in the flesh
quotes.note: Referent is unambiguously the Father — "the Father of us all" — but the Father's mortality is established by analogy to Christ. The Christological analogy is the engine of the discourse, and Snow later runs the same engine. Retagged for the Father axis: “was once as we are now” is the mortal experience; “is an exalted man” is the attainment. Text corrected in v2: the previous excerpt (“was once as we are now… dwelt on an earth”) was the amalgamated Times and Seasons / TPJS / 1971 Ensign reading and appears in none of the four witnesses. This is Clayton. Bullock reads “God himself the father of us all dwelt on a Earth same as J C himself did” and, at this point, “he was God from the begin of all Eternity”; Richards has “refute the Idea that God was God from all eternity.”

quotes.excerpt: you have got to learn how to be a god yourself... to be priests & Kings as all Gods has done— by going from a small degree to another from exaltation to ex[altation] (Clayton) / you have got to learn how to be a God yourself & be a K[ing] & God Priest to God same as all have done (Bullock)
quotes.note: Verification resolved, and it matters. Of the four accounts, only Clayton attests "as all Gods has done"; Bullock has the weaker "same as all have done" with no "Gods"; Richards and Woodruff record the deification injunction but attach no comparison clause to it at all. The familiar amalgam reading "the same as all Gods have done before you" therefore rests on a single witness, and smooths away a real divergence. Weight the INFINITE-CHAIN tag on this quote accordingly.

quotes.excerpt: The mind of man— the intelligent part is coequal with God himself... God never did have power to create the spirit of man at all. He could not create himself— Intelligence exists upon a selfexis[t]ent principle— is a spirit from age to age & no creation about it.
quotes.note: The strongest support in the corpus for organization over begetting, and in direct tension with the viviparous statements of 1909.

notes: Amalgamated texts — the 1855 History draft, Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, and the April 1971 Ensign — are citations of these four witnesses, not independent originals, and are filed as such. Honest accounting on the backward direction: the King Follett Discourse teaches that the Father was mortal. The had-a-Father inference arrives ten weeks later in the Sermon in the Grove.

title: Nauvoo Expositor: “a plurality of Gods above the God of this universe”
speaker: The proprietors of the Nauvoo Expositor
office: Dissenting former members of the Church at Nauvoo
venue: Nauvoo Expositor, June 7, 1844, p. 2 col. 3 (“Resolutions”)

witnesses.scribe: Gordon A. Madsen, Sustaining the Law: Joseph Smith's Legal Encounters, 434 and nn. 30–38
witnesses.note: Quotes the charge in full with column-level citations to the issue.

quotes.excerpt: introduced false and damnable doctrines into the Church, such as a plurality of Gods above the God of this universe, and his liability to fall with all his creations; the plurality of wives, for time and eternity; the doctrine of unconditional sealing up to eternal life, against all crimes; except that of shedding innocent blood…
quotes.note: The full charge, including the clause that usually goes missing. Two things the standard ellipsis hides. First, the regress charge is bundled into one sentence with polygamy and unconditional sealing, so it is an item in a bill of particulars rather than a free-standing theological complaint. Second, “and his liability to fall with all his creations” is a distinct and independently striking claim — that God could fall — which no other source in this dataset touches, and it is preserved here deliberately. As a hostile witness this is evidence about what was audible in Nauvoo, not about what Joseph Smith taught.

notes: Verified verbatim against Gordon A. Madsen's quotation with column-level citation in Sustaining the Law: Joseph Smith's Legal Encounters, 434 (nn. 30–38 cite Nauvoo Expositor, June 7, 1844, p. 2, cols. 3–4). The Internet Archive item carries an OCR text layer (Nauvoo_Expositor_1844_djvu.txt); its OCR of the Resolutions column is heavily corrupt but corroborates every word of the excerpt, and the wording here follows Madsen's column-level quotation. The excerpt begins mid-sentence: the original reads “inasmuch as they have introduced…,” so the opening verb here is the paper's own word and not a smoothing. Chronology is what gives this entry its value. It appears two months after the King Follett Discourse (kfd-1844) and nine days before the Sermon in the Grove (sermon-grove-1844) — so before Joseph Smith's most explicit surviving statement of the Father's Father, hostile insiders already understood “a plurality of Gods above the God of this universe” to be what was being taught in Nauvoo. The paper was destroyed by order of the Nauvoo city council the following week; a single issue exists.

title: Sermon in the Grove
speaker: Joseph Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: East grove near the temple, Nauvoo

witnesses.scribe: Thomas Bullock
witnesses.note: Primary contemporaneous report.

witnesses.scribe: George Laub
witnesses.note: Reminiscent copy in Laub's journal, not a contemporaneous report.

quotes.excerpt: if J. C was the Son of God & John disc[overe]d. that God the Fa[the]r. of J. C had a fa[the]r. you may suppose that he had a Fa[the]r. also— where was there ever a Son with[ou]t. a Fa[the]r.— when ever did a tree or any thing spring into existence with[ou]t. a progenitor
quotes.note: Unambiguously Father-referent, and exegetical rather than visionary: the claim is derived from a reading of Revelation 1:6 ("God and his Father"), not asserted from revelation. The epistemic register matters for how later sources handle it.

notes: The clearest Father-referent backward-explicit statement in Joseph Smith's corpus, though no longer the earliest — see the 30 January 1842 discourse. Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith 370–73 is an amalgamated citation of these witnesses. Every later correlated BACKWARD-EXPLICIT text traces to this sermon, which is why collapsing citations leaves the backward-explicit column empty after 1844.

title: Brigham Young at the Nauvoo conference: “when they have progressed through millions of worlds, it is eternity still before them”
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, presiding over the Church
venue: Discourse on baptism for the dead, morning session of the April 1845 general conference, Nauvoo (Thomas Bullock booklet #3, Church History Library, CR 100 318; conference section, catalog items 23–30, the passage at item 24)

witnesses.scribe: Nauvoo, Illinois, April 6–8, 1845 manuscript minutes (Thomas Bullock, five written leaves)
witnesses.note: The preferred witness for the conference as a whole, and it does not preserve this discourse: it records only that "the morning was spent in teaching on the baptism for the dead by President Young, which will be hereafter reported in full." The promised full report is not in the record. The same minutes close by noting that George D. Watt "has taken down the speeches delivered on this occasion, and they will appear from time to time as circumstances will allow" — no such published report of this discourse has been located, which leaves the Bullock booklet as the only witness to the sentence quoted here.

quotes.excerpt: The Lord leads his people a little at a time, and when a man receives a little he shall continue to receive more, until he obtains to the fulness of the Godhead. When they have progressed through millions of worlds, it is eternity still before them.
quotes.note: Read carefully, this is a claim about beings who have already arrived: a man keeps receiving until he obtains the fulness of the Godhead, and even after progressing through millions of worlds eternity still lies ahead. Attaining the fulness of the Godhead is therefore not the terminus of progression, which is the substance of the divine-progression affirmation — but it is asserted of exalted men rather than of the Father, and Young does not here take the further step of naming God as the subject. Hence the ambiguous referent and the review flag: the tag records a real claim about progression after godhood, not a statement that the Father is still learning. MANY-WORLDS for "millions of worlds." Transcription conventions of the source apply: Bullock's abbreviations are expanded by the transcriber and uncertain readings are bracketed; this sentence carries no brackets and is a direct reading.

notes: Quoted from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/early-restoration/1845/1845-04-conference-record-nauvoo-conference.md, which transcribes both Church History Library witnesses to this conference directly from the catalog page images; the transcription of the Bullock booklet was collated word for word against the scans in a heavyweight pass that corrected several real misreadings elsewhere in the booklet and left one phrase openly bracketed as still-uncertain shorthand. The sentence quoted here sits in Bullock's notes on Young's baptism-for-the-dead discourse of April 6, 1845 (booklet item 24). Hearsay C, and the grade should be taken seriously rather than as a formality: this is one scribe's abbreviated summary of a spoken discourse, not a verbatim report — the vault file grades the whole record "fragmentary" precisely because both witnesses summarise rather than preserve — and Young never reviewed it. Do not treat the wording as his sentence construction; treat it as reliable evidence of the claim, not of the phrasing. Placement in the timeline: April 1845 is ten months after the King Follett Discourse and nine months after Joseph Smith's death, at the first general conference over which Young presided as head of the Church. The endless-progression claim is therefore attested in his teaching from the very start of his presidency, twelve years before Woodruff's 1857 statement (woodruff-progression-1857) and twenty-two years before Young's own "the God that I serve is progressing eternally" (young-progressing-eternally-1867).

title: Eliza R. Snow, “My Father in Heaven” (now the hymn “O My Father”)
speaker: Eliza R. Snow
office: Secretary, Female Relief Society of Nauvoo
venue: Poem published in Times and Seasons as “My Father in Heaven”; hymn in continuous use since

quotes.excerpt: In the heav'ns are parents single? No, the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there.
quotes.note: Affirms a Mother in Heaven and premortal parentage; states no generative mechanism.

notes: Tightened in v2 to HEAVENLY-MOTHER only — the spirit-birth tag was retrojection. The hymn has anchored Heavenly Mother in lived worship for 180 years while leaving the mechanism unstated, which makes it the template for the later euphemism strategy. Verify inclusion and numbering in the current hymnal rollout (Hymns — For Home and Church, 2024–), which supersedes the 1985 hymnal's no. 292.

title: Orson Pratt on the trail: how the first God was formed
speaker: Orson Pratt, as recorded by Wilford Woodruff
office: Apostle
venue: Wilford Woodruff pioneer-trail journal, 26 June 1847, quoted at length in William V. Smith, The King Follett Sermon: A Biography, 117–18

quotes.excerpt: One of the most important items if true was presented by Professor Pratt… It was upon the subject of the original formation of the first God; we all admitted in the first place that which we believed to be an important truth ie the eternal duration of matter spirit, intelligence in some form or other we also agreed in the opinion that neither God nor man always had from all eternity the same formation that they now have but did exhist in some form… then the question arose how did God recieve his present formation the answer given by Professor Pratt was something in the following language.
quotes.note: The question as Woodruff frames it is “the original formation of the first God” — a first God is presupposed, which is the exact negation of the chain. Untagged: the available category set has no tag for a terminating chain, and INFINITE-CHAIN would state the opposite of what the passage says. Woodruff's spellings are preserved.

quotes.excerpt: An eternity was filled as it were with particules of intelligences who had their agency, two of these particles in the process of time might have joined their interest together exchanged ideas & found by persueing this course that they gained double strength to what one particle of intelligence would have & afterwards were joined by other particles & continued untill they organized a combination or body though through a long process & as they had power over other intelligences in consequence of their combination, organization & strength and in process of time this being—or God seeing the advantage of such an organization desired company or a companion and having some experience got to work & organized other beings by prevailing on intelligences to come together… it was found to be the most expeditious & best way to recieve there formations or bodies either spiritual or temporal [was] through the womb.
quotes.note: An emergentist account of godhood: intelligences coalesce into ever-larger organizations until one attains sufficient power to organize others. The tail of it — bodies “either spiritual or temporal” received “through the womb” — is the viviparous mechanism Pratt would systematize in The Seer six years later. The bracketed [was] is W. V. Smith's editorial supply.

notes: Woodruff's own diary entry for the day, recording a conversation he took part in while walking with Orson Pratt and Albert Carrington on the pioneer trail. Hearsay D rather than C: the record is contemporaneous, but Woodruff is reconstructing from memory and says so — “the answer given by Professor Pratt was something in the following language.” Pratt offered these ideas as speculation for discussion, not as doctrine, and presenting the passage as his settled position misreads the setting entirely. The contrast that makes this entry worth having: the same Orson Pratt publishes the opposite six years later in The Seer, insisting there could be no first world in the succession and no first Father in the genealogy (see pratt-seer). Counter-cult compilations file the two texts in opposite sections of the same list without noticing they are one man changing his mind between 1847 and 1853, which is also the interval in which he moved from trail speculation to a printed apostolic system. Text verified verbatim against W. V. Smith's block quotation of the diary; Smith's endnote 26 (p. 145) sources it to the Journal of Wilford Woodruff, June 26, 1847, and to Kenney, Wilford Woodruff's Journal, 3:217, which is the date and reference carried here (the Kenney edition itself has not been consulted).

title: John Taylor in Bullock's minutes: “he cant create a world,” and the God above who “as been all his days engaged in public enterprize”
speaker: John Taylor
office: Apostle, Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference in the Bowery, Great Salt Lake City, October 6–7, 1849 (Historian's Office general Church minutes, 1839–1877, "General Conference proceedings, Salt Lake City," CR 100 318, Box 2 fd 15, 11 leaves, recorded by Thomas Bullock)

witnesses.scribe: Thomas Bullock fair copy, "Minutes of the General Conference, held Great Salt Lake City, Oct. 6 & 7, 1849" (8 leaves)
witnesses.note: Bullock's own later copy, carrying the note "See following for original minutes with more detail" and pointing back to the 11-leaf original quoted here. It compresses the discourses and does not preserve these sentences.

witnesses.scribe: Millennial Star 12, no. 8 (April 15, 1850): 122–124
witnesses.note: The editorial summary in which this conference reached the Saints abroad. It corroborates the manuscript on business and personnel throughout and contradicts it nowhere, but it omits both passages quoted here entirely — it records only that "Elders Erastus Snow and John Taylor spoke on the same subject" of tithing. A useful measure of how much doctrinal content the circulated summaries dropped.

quotes.excerpt: we are a nucleus [?] pertaining to our Chil[dren] & Chil. Chil. worlds without end - if we are got to be K. & P. we are to be rulers - & if they dont no how to rule they will be in a poor place - they will be same as Napoleon at Elba - he an Emperor & no one to rule over
quotes.note: Endless posterity with no mechanism attached — children and children's children "worlds without end" — which is the euphemism, not the explicit claim. Two precision notes. "Worlds without end" here is the liturgical idiom for endlessness attached to posterity, not an assertion of plural worlds, so MANY-WORLDS is withheld on the reasoning used at penrose-endless-increase-1911-q1. And the Napoleon-at-Elba figure is doing real work: Taylor's argument is that a king needs subjects, which makes posterity the answer to what an exalted man's kingdom is made of — the same equation Brigham Young states outright in Journal of Discourses 11:262. Spoken in the October 6 morning session, the day before q2 and q3. Bracketed "[?]" marks an uncertain reading and bracketed expansions are the transcriber's; both are preserved.

quotes.excerpt: if a man cant pay his tithing support his family & go to the nations to preach - he cant create a world
quotes.note: World-creation as the assumed destiny of the faithful, and the mode of assertion is what makes it evidence: it is the minor premise of an a fortiori argument about tithing, not a doctrine being taught. Taylor expects a Bowery congregation in 1849 to grant without explanation that they are in training to create worlds. Tagged FORWARD-EXPLICIT on the world-making half of the category definition (cf. pratt-key-theology-1855-q3), and flagged for review because the begetting half of the eternal-increase proposition is entirely absent — no offspring, no spirit children, no mechanism anywhere in the discourse.

quotes.excerpt: we are not under the Levitical Economy but under the P. of an Et[erna]l. life - Melchisedek was a K. & P. to the most hi[gh] God, & distributed as he thot. fit & we av. P. houses &c to build. that [people] who are most enterprize are thot. most of by nations - it has a tendency to exalt that nation - we av. temples to build that shall be more magnificent than any on the Earth & Princes shall come to Zion to learn wisdom - the God that sits above as been all his days engaged in public enterprize as he wod. not av. been there
quotes.note: Attainment language without mortality, which by the Father-status precedent takes FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone: God occupies the station he occupies because of what he has done with his days, and "he would not have been there" otherwise. Referent must stay ambiguous — Taylor says "the God that sits above," and the surrounding sentences name Jehovah — but the claim itself is unambiguous, and it is unusually blunt for 1849. Deliberately not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION: "all his days engaged in public enterprize" is an account of how the station was reached, not a claim that God still advances, and collapsing the two is the exact conflation this dataset exists to prevent. Note the rhetorical direction, too. The theology is subordinate to a civic argument — build temples, outstrip the nations, be the most enterprising people on earth — which is why the divine career is invoked as a precedent for public works rather than expounded for its own sake.

notes: Quoted from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/early-restoration/1849/1849-10-conference-record-great-salt-lake-city-conference.md, whose spine is a direct transcription of the original 11-leaf Church History Library minutes read leaf by leaf from the catalog delivery API at 2x–5x magnification, with document order reconstructed from session headings, Bullock's ink leaf numbering, and sentence continuity across breaks. Bracketed expansions, "[?]" for uncertain readings, "[struck: …]" for cancellations and "^" for interlineations are the transcriber's conventions and are preserved in the excerpts. Hearsay B rather than C: these are contemporaneous notes taken by the trained clerk of conference in his own minute-hand, with no shorthand-to-print editing layer of the Journal of Discourses kind between the speaker and the page — but they are compressed at speed, they carry word-level uncertainty throughout, and Taylor never reviewed them, so the wording must not be treated as his sentence construction. Dating: q2 and q3 are from the October 7 afternoon session (delivery-order leaf 7), q1 from the October 6 morning session (leaf 11); the entry is dated to the day of the substantive passages. Why the entry is worth having. It catches the doctrine in its least self-conscious register — not in a sermon on the nature of God but inside a fundraising talk about the Perpetual Emigrating Fund and tithing, where world-creation and a God who earned his station are assumed as common ground by an apostle who does not pause to defend either. It also documents what the circulated record lost: the Millennial Star summary that carried this conference to the Saints in Britain preserves the votes and the mission calls and drops both sentences.

title: Brigham Young: “They shall reign over kingdoms, and have power to be Gods”
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Sermon delivered in the Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City, April 7, 1852, during the April general conference (Journal of Discourses 6:314–322)

witnesses.scribe: Journal of Discourses 6:314–322 (BYU ContentDM page images)
witnesses.note: The scan against which the vault text was collated across all nine printed pages at final review, restoring the British spellings a prior ingestion had Americanised (favour, endeavours, neighbour, colour, honour, Saviour, waggon).

quotes.excerpt: The Lord must and will have a company of Saints who will follow him to the cross, if it be necessary; and these he will crown. They are the ones who will wear a celestial crown and have dominion, rule, and government. These are they who will receive honour of the Father, with glory, exaltation, and eternal lives. They shall reign over kingdoms, and have power to be Gods, even the sons of God. Those other classes will take different stations and possess inferior glories, according to their works in the flesh. That class who will altogether serve the world and disregard the cause of truth will become servants to the sons of God and be in servitude throughout eternity.
quotes.note: Godhood with dominion, stated plainly, and still only a euphemism on the increase axis: "eternal lives" and "kingdoms" with no offspring, no spirit children, no worlds created, and no mechanism of any kind. What the passage adds to the bare formula is a rival answer to the question the formula usually answers by implication — who fills an exalted man's kingdom. Here it is the damned: those who served the world "become servants to the sons of God and be in servitude throughout eternity." Set that against Young's own answer in Journal of Discourses 11:262 — the kingdoms an exalted man rules "are his own progeny" (quoted at lee-true-concept-of-god-1969-q4) — and the two accounts of the population of a celestial kingdom do not obviously fit together. Recorded because the dataset's forward axis usually assumes the progeny answer.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1852/1852-04-young-the-lord-at-the-head-of-his-kingdom.md, whose final-review pass collated the complete discourse against the BYU ContentDM page scan of Journal of Discourses volume 6, pp. 314–322, and confirmed the printed header, place and date. Hearsay C: Pitman shorthand report, published without the speaker's review, and printed seven years after delivery in a later volume of the Journal of Discourses than its date would suggest. Lean by design. The discourse is about self-discipline, settling disputes out of court, and the theology curriculum of the Elders — "Every Elder should become a profound theologian" — and the exaltation material is a single closing paragraph. It is filed because the phrase "power to be Gods, even the sons of God" is the sort of sentence routinely cited as evidence for eternal increase or for a chain of Gods, and it supports neither: no succession backward, no offspring forward. It is the same speaker who, two days later at the same conference, states both explicitly (young-adam-god-1852). The pairing is the point — two general conference sermons, forty-eight hours apart, one of which says everything and one of which says the formula.

title: Brigham Young's first public Adam–God discourse: “begotten by his Father in heaven … and so on in succession”
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Sermon delivered in the Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City, April 9, 1852, during the April general conference (Journal of Discourses 1:46–53)

witnesses.scribe: Journal of Discourses 1:46–53 (BYU ContentDM page images)
witnesses.note: The scan against which the vault text was collated page by page at final review, which recovered six archaic spellings a prior pass had silently modernised ("centre," "fulness," "vail," "marvellous" ×2, "for ever," "vallies"). BYU's item pages currently fail to render client-side, which is why the archive.org page-anchored scan is used as the entry URL.

quotes.excerpt: That is a small portion of the duty required of you in order to obtain crowns of glory, immortality, and eternal lives. … Preach the simple, unadorned truth; work out your salvation with diligence, and do that which will guarantee you a warranted deed, an undeniable title to eternal lives.
quotes.note: "Eternal lives" twice, the D&C 132 term of art for eternal increase, with no mechanism attached either time. Recorded because of where it sits: the same discourse states the generative mechanism explicitly a few pages later (q2), so the euphemism and the explicit claim are not successive stages of the tradition here but two registers available to one speaker in one sitting.

quotes.excerpt: Our Father in Heaven begat all the spirits that ever were, or ever will be, upon this earth; and they were born spirits in the eternal world. Then the Lord by His power and wisdom organized the mortal tabernacle of man. We were made first spiritual, and afterwards temporal.
quotes.note: Begetting and birth, in those words, and set against organisation rather than alongside it — the spirits were begotten and born; the mortal tabernacle was organized. That contrast inside one sentence is what makes the viviparous tag secure without any physiology being supplied; the "spirit element in their veins" account belongs to Young's later sermons (young-celestial-bodies-1876) and to Pratt. Note also that the staging is two-stage, not three: no intelligences appear, so TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK does not apply.

quotes.excerpt: When our father Adam came into the garden of Eden, he came into it with a celestial body, and brought Eve, one of his wives, with him. He helped to make and organize this world. He is Michael, the Archangel, the Ancient of Days! about whom holy men have written and spoken—He is our Father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do.
quotes.note: The Adam–God identification, and it is recorded untagged because an identification is not a claim on any of the axes. It is here because it is the premise that makes q4 a backward-direction statement at all: if Adam is "our Father and our God," then Adam's Father in heaven is a God above the God we worship. The printed Journal of Discourses italicises "celestial body," "one of his wives," "He is our Father and our God, and the only God with whom" and "we"; the vault carries the emphasis as markdown asterisks and it is stripped here, with no words changed.

quotes.excerpt: And who is the Father? He is the first of the human family; and when he took a tabernacle, it was begotten by his Father in heaven, after the same manner as the tabernacles of Cain, Abel, and the rest of the sons and daughters of Adam and Eve; from the fruits of the earth, the first earthly tabernacles were originated by the Father, and so on in succession.
quotes.note: The earliest public form of the argument that reaches its famous shape two years later in the grandfather sentence (young-adam-god-chain-1854-q2). BACKWARD-EXPLICIT is earned on Young's own terms: the being he has just identified as "our Father and our God" was himself begotten by "his Father in heaven." INFINITE-CHAIN rests entirely on the closing clause "and so on in succession," and the review flag is there because the clause's antecedent is genuinely unsettled in the printed text — read one way it extends the begetting relation up a line of Fathers, read another it continues only the account of how the first earthly tabernacles came to be originated. Handling caution, the same one that attaches to the 1854 discourse: this is not a free-standing cosmological thesis. The whole passage is an argument about the paternity of Jesus, aimed at the claim that Christ was begotten by the Holy Ghost, and the ancestral premise is doing Adam–God work. Emphasis on "his Father" is italic in the print and is not reproduced here.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1852/1852-04-young-self-government-mysteries-recreation.md, whose final-review pass collated the complete body against the BYU ContentDM page scan of Journal of Discourses volume 1, pp. 46–53, and verified the printed header ("A Sermon Delivered by President Brigham Young, in the Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City, April 9, 1852"). Hearsay C: a Pitman shorthand report, edited for publication, which Young did not review. Filed original with no citation edges — Young quotes no dataset text here. Context the timeline reader needs. This is the discourse in which the Adam–God teaching was first stated publicly, delivered at general conference to a congregation Young had just called on to surrender their livestock for Church debts, and framed by him as a sequence of separate short sermons ("This will answer for one sermon") with the Deity material announced as "my next sermon … to both Saint and sinner." The printed title the Journal of Discourses gives it names the doctrine outright: "Adam, Our Father and Our God." Read it as the origin point of a line the dataset follows forward — the grandfather argument of 1854 (young-adam-god-chain-1854), the succession language of 1859 (by-chain), the relayed Joseph Smith saying of 1862 (young-father-mother-1862) — and, at the far end, Spencer W. Kimball's 1976 repudiation of the Adam–God teaching (kimball-1976). Anyone citing q4 as regress evidence has to carry the Adam–God frame with it.

title: Orson Pratt, “Celestial Marriage” — generation, Gods themselves, and worlds without number
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Apostle, Quorum of the Twelve
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 1:53–66)

witnesses.scribe: No reporter credited on the printed page
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 1:53–66. The speaker did not review the text before publication.

quotes.excerpt: If we were to reason from analogy—if we admit analogical reasoning in the question, what would we say? We should say, that our spirits were formed by generation, the same as the body or tabernacle of flesh and bones. But what says revelation upon the subject? We will see whether revelation and analogy will agree.
quotes.note: The mechanism, and its epistemic status. Pratt reaches viviparous spirit birth by analogy from the mortal body — the same anatomical argument Erastus Snow runs in 1885 and the First Presidency ratifies in 1909 — but he explicitly marks it as analogy and then turns to test it against revelation. Quoting the conclusion without the “if we were to reason from analogy” frame overstates what he claimed here.

quotes.excerpt: …when male and female are restored from the fall, by virtue of the everlasting and eternal covenant of marriage, they will continue to increase and multiply to all ages of eternity, to raise up beings after their own order, and in their own likeness and image, germs of intelligence, that are destined, in their times and seasons, to become not only sons of God, but Gods themselves.
quotes.note: Forward-explicit at full strength: exalted couples produce offspring (“beings after their own order… germs of intelligence”) and those offspring are destined to become Gods. The generative mechanism is not restated in this sentence — it is supplied by q1 earlier in the same discourse — so the viviparous tag is left on q1 rather than duplicated here.

quotes.excerpt: This accounts for the many worlds we heard Elder Grant speaking about yesterday afternoon. The peopling of worlds, or an endless increase, even of one family, would require an endless increase of worlds; and if one family were to be united in the eternal covenant of marriage, to fulfil that great commandment, to multiply his species, and propagate them, and if there be no end to the increase of his posterity, it would call for an endless increase of new worlds. And if one family calls for this, what would innumerable millions of families call for? They would call for as many worlds as have already been discovered by the telescope; yea, the number must be multiplied to infinity in order that there may be room for the inheritance of the sons and daughters of the Gods.
quotes.note: The cosmological consequence: infinite worlds are deduced as the housing requirement of infinite offspring. The infinity here is arithmetical and forward-facing — worlds needed downstream — not a series of predecessors. INFINITE-CHAIN is deliberately withheld.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1852/1852-08-pratt-o-celestial-marriage.md, whose complete text was collated against the BYU JoD volume 1 page scan, pp. 53–66, with print spellings preserved instance by instance (“fulfil,” “endeavour,” “practising”) — the “fulfil” in q3 is the print's, not a typo. Watt-era shorthand report with no reporter credited on the page and no speaker review, hence C. This is the first public discourse on plural marriage published in the Journal of Discourses, which is why the eternal-increase argument is doing polemical work rather than sitting as devotional aside. The reason it belongs in this collection is conflation trap #3 in its purest form: Pratt runs the chain forward to infinity three separate ways — offspring, godhood, worlds — and never once runs it backward. A reader primed for “infinite regression of Gods” supplies the backward half unaided. Pratt here asserts infinite progression, not infinite regression.

title: Parley P. Pratt: “He did not create their intelligence at all”
speaker: Parley P. Pratt
office: Apostle, Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Address delivered in the Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City, April 10, 1853, at the April general conference (Journal of Discourses 1:256–263)

witnesses.scribe: Journal of Discourses 1:256–263 (BYU ContentDM page images)
witnesses.note: The scan against which the complete address was collated page by page at final review; the printed header reads "HEIRSHIP AND PRIESTHOOD. AN ADDRESS DELIVERED BY ELDER PARLEY P. PRATT, IN THE TABERNACLE, GREAT SALT LAKE CITY, APRIL 10, 1853."

quotes.excerpt: In organizing and peopling the worlds, it was found necessary to place among the inhabitants some superior intelligences, who were capacitated to teach, to rule, and preside among other intelligences.
quotes.note: Plural worlds organized and peopled, taken as given rather than argued. No succession of Gods is claimed here or anywhere in the address; the plurality is of worlds under one God, which is exactly the boundary the category draws.

quotes.excerpt: We learn from the writings of Abraham and others, and from modern revelation, that the intelligences that now inhabit these tabernacles of earth were living, active intelligences in yonder world, while the particles of matter which now compose our outward bodies were yet mingled with their native element; that then our embodied spirits lived, moved, conversed, and exercised an agency.
quotes.note: Recorded untagged as the control on TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK, and it is the reason this entry exists in the form it does. The staging Pratt describes is two-stage — premortal existence, then a mortal tabernacle — and "intelligences" and "embodied spirits" name the same premortal beings inside a single sentence. There is no intelligence-becomes-spirit-child transition anywhere in the address, so the three-stage model is simply absent, and tagging it would be the retrojection the category's own definition forbids. Note also the source Pratt names for the doctrine: "the writings of Abraham," i.e. Abraham 3 (see citesId) — the passage most often read as tripartite and here read as nothing of the kind.

quotes.excerpt: It may be inquired, why God made one unequal to another, or inferior in intellect or capacity. To which I reply, that He did not create their intelligence at all. It never was created, being an inherent attribute of the eternal element called spirit, which element composes each individual spirit, and which element exists in an infinitude of degrees in the scale of intellect, in all the varieties manifested in the eternal God, and thence to the lowest agent, which acts by its own will.
quotes.note: The uncreated-intelligence position, from an apostle, in general conference, nine years after King Follett said the same thing ("God never did have power to create the spirit of man at all," kfd-1844-q3) and fifty-six years before the 1909 First Presidency statement made begetting the official account (fp-1909). The stance follows the kfd-1844-q3 precedent exactly: SPIRIT-BIRTH-ADOPTION at "denies" records the organized-and-uncreated position against the begetting proposition. Two observations kept out of the tags on purpose. First, Pratt makes intelligence an inherent attribute of the eternal element "spirit" rather than a prior stage of being — which is a positive metaphysics against the tripartite model, not merely a silence about it. Second, he places "the eternal God" and "the lowest agent" on one continuous scale of intellect: an ontological-continuity claim that asserts nothing whatever about how God came to occupy the top of the scale, and must not be read as one. Compare sill-same-species-1969-q1, the same formulation 116 years later.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1853/1853-04-10-pratt-pp-heirship-and-priesthood.md, freshly re-ingested and collated page by page against the BYU ContentDM images of Journal of Discourses volume 1, pp. 256–263, with no body changes required. Hearsay C: George D. Watt's Pitman shorthand report, published without the speaker's review. Correction to the screening pass that surfaced this address: it was flagged as tripartite, and it is the opposite. Pratt's whole point is that intelligence was never created and is not a stage — it is an attribute of the eternal spirit-element — which makes the address one of the strongest nineteenth-century statements of the organization-over-begetting position and a useful check on reading the three-stage model back into the 1850s. The doctrinal material sits inside an address whose subject is lineage and priesthood heirship, and whose argument is that the election of Abraham rests on pre-existent differences of intelligence; the racial and lineal reasoning of that argument is not this dataset's axis and is not summarised here, but a reader going to the source should expect it.

title: Orson Hyde: God, our heavenly Father, was perhaps once a child
speaker: Orson Hyde
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 1:121–130, at 1:123)

witnesses.scribe: George D. Watt (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of the printed Journal of Discourses 1:121–130. No reporter is credited on the printed page; the Watt attribution comes from LaJean Purcell Carruth's Church History Library research on the underlying shorthand, not from the JoD itself.

witnesses.scribe: LaJean Purcell Carruth transcription (CR 100 912, item cr-100-912-0629)
witnesses.note: Scholarly re-transcription of Watt's original shorthand for this discourse, catalogued at the Church History Library. Not yet collated against the printed text for this passage.

quotes.excerpt: Remember that God, our heavenly Father, was perhaps once a child, and mortal like we ourselves, and rose step by step in the scale of progress, in the school of advancement; has moved forward and overcome, until He has arrived at the point where He now is: “Is this really possible?” Why, my dear friends, how would you like to be governed by a ruler who had not been through all the vicissitudes of life that are common to mortals? If he had not suffered, how could he sympathise with the distress of others? If he himself had not endured the same, how could he sympathise and be touched with the feelings of our infirmities?
quotes.note: Two things must travel with this quote. First the hedge: “perhaps.” Hyde does not assert the Father's mortality flatly — he proposes it, nine years after King Follett, as something to remember rather than something revealed, and the chain length is left entirely unspecified. Second the motive: the claim is doing theodicy, not theogony. The warrant is a ruler's fitness to sympathize (Hebrews 4:15 in the background), and Hyde argues *from* the desirability of a sympathizing God *to* His past mortality. Nothing here says the Father had a Father, so no chain tag.

quotes.excerpt: Hence, our heavenly Father ascended to a throne of power; He has passed through scenes of tribulation, as the Saints in all ages have, and are still passing through; and having overcome, and ascended His throne, He can look down upon those who are following in the same track, and can realize the nature of their infirmities, troubles, and difficulties, like the aged father who looks upon his race, upon the smallest child… So with our heavenly Father; when He sees we are going astray, He stretches forth His chastening hand, at the same time He realizes the difficulties with which we have to contend, because he has felt the same; but having overcome, He goes no more out.
quotes.note: The same claim restated without the hedge — the mortality is now assumed and the conditional “perhaps” has dropped away inside a single discourse. Deliberately not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION: “He goes no more out” is Revelation 3:12 pillar imagery about permanence of place (the sermon's announced subject is “a pillar in the temple of God”), not a claim about whether God still increases in knowledge. Reading it as a denial of ongoing progression is retrojection.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1853/1853-10-hyde-the-man-to-lead-gods-people.md, whose body was collated page-by-page against the BYU ContentDM scan of Journal of Discourses 1:121–130 (that Final Review also restored the print's British “Saviour” throughout and removed an invented byline a prior pass had prepended). Contemporaneous report in Pitman shorthand, not reviewed by the speaker before publication — hence C. The pulpit research report places the passage at 1:123; that page-level location was not independently confirmed against the page image for this entry, so the venue carries only the verified 1:121–130 range. Value to the collection: this is the hedged, motivated form of the backward claim — an apostle in 1853 offering the Father's past mortality as a pastoral inference about divine sympathy, a full register below the flat assertions of 1844 and 1862.

title: Orson Pratt owns the plurality of Gods from the stand: “one only wise God … an immense number of Gods”
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Apostle, Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse delivered in the Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City, October 7, 1854, at the October general conference (Journal of Discourses 2:54–61)

witnesses.scribe: Journal of Discourses 2:54–61 (BYU ContentDM page images)
witnesses.note: The scan against which the complete discourse was collated word for word at final review, with title, speaker line, date and occasion verified against the printed page.

quotes.excerpt: For instance, the world read in the revelations we have received, that there are more Gods than one. This is something that does not immediately concern us; but yet opposers get up and contend against us, and prejudice the minds of congregations against the people of God, because they profess to believe, not only in a plurality of wives, but also in a plurality of Gods; it is necessary to show them the reasons for our belief—the whys and the wherefores; and this I endeavored to do in some of my last publications; not because I had more light upon this subject than many others, but I endeavored to do it for the benefit of the people—to show them wherein we believe in the plurality of Gods, and yet acknowledge only one God. I believe both of these principles with all my heart. I believe there is one only wise God, and I believe there is an immense number of Gods.
quotes.note: Categories deliberately empty, on the precedent of pratt-infinite-gods-1855, and the two entries should be read as one argument in two halves: this is Pratt owning the numerical claim from the conference stand in October 1854, and the February 1855 sermon four months later is where he explains what he means by it — that "God" names one attribute-set of light and knowledge, numerically identical wherever it dwells, and the infinity is the count of tabernacles indwelt. Nothing here is successive. There is no predecessor, no line, no Father above the Father anywhere in the address, and INFINITE-CHAIN requires a series. Two further data. "Some of my last publications" is The Seer (see citesId), the work the First Presidency and the Twelve would repudiate in 1865 (fp-repudiation-1865) — so this is Pratt defending the Seer material publicly, eleven years before it was disavowed and one day before Brigham Young's October 8 discourse rebutting his pre-existence teaching (young-adam-god-chain-1854). And note the register: the doctrine is handled as a liability to be explained to opponents rather than as something to preach — "this is something that does not immediately concern us."

quotes.excerpt: I feel thankful to God this day that I stand in the midst of a great and good people, that are willing to practice the principles of eternal truth and righteousness; and those mysteries about the plurality of Gods, and the plurality of worlds also are good in their places; God has revealed them, and they are intended for our good and instruction, or He never would have revealed them.
quotes.note: The mysteries defended rather than deferred: revealed, good "in their places," and given for instruction. Tagged MANY-WORLDS for the plurality of worlds, which Pratt states as revealed doctrine; the plurality of Gods gets no tag for the reason set out on q1. Worth dating against the other side of the argument — this is five years before Brigham Young told a conference to stop "inquiring after the origin of the Gods" (young-origin-caution-1859), and Pratt is the apostle that caution was aimed at.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1854/1854-10-pratt-perpetual-emigrating-fund-emigration.md, collated at final review against the BYU ContentDM images of Journal of Discourses volume 2, pp. 54–61 (Internet Archive leaves n61–n68). Hearsay C: shorthand report, published without the speaker's review. Filed as original with a citation edge to pratt-seer, which is the body of work Pratt is defending. The value of the entry is that it is a bare-formula plurality statement in the one decade where such statements are most often read as chain evidence, made by the one speaker whose metaphysics demonstrably will not support that reading. Anyone citing an 1850s "immense number of Gods" line as backward-chain evidence has to clear both this entry and pratt-infinite-gods-1855 first. The setting is worth recording as well: the doctrinal passage is an aside in a fundraising discourse on the Perpetual Emigrating Fund, delivered on Pratt's return from a two-year mission — the same conference at which Brigham Young delivered what Bergera calls his most explicit Adam–God statement to date, in part as a rebuttal to Pratt.

title: Brigham Young: the gods never had a beginning — “could you have a father without having a grandfather?”
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference discourse, afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (The Complete Discourses of Brigham Young 2:845–848)

witnesses.scribe: Brigham Young Papers manuscript report
witnesses.note: Provenance as printed in The Complete Discourses: “Ms/219, 81; CR 1234, 48-12, BYC. LJA 12-55-7, 11; TPBY 3:343-6; EBY 86-103; BYA 2:224-237.” Four independent manuscript and print witnesses; the sermon's authenticity is not in question.

witnesses.scribe: Gary James Bergera, Conflict in the Quorum, 125–26
witnesses.note: Independent transcription, used here to resolve words the Complete Discourses scan garbles (“intelligence,” “will”). Bergera does not quote the Emerald Isle sentence; “bom” → “born” in q3 is an uncontroversial OCR correction made here.

quotes.excerpt: I believe in the eternities of worlds, saints, angels, kingdoms, and gods: In eternity without beginning. I believe the gods never had a beginning, neither the formation of matter, and it is without end; it will endure in one eternal round swimming in space, basking, living, and moving in the midst of eternity. All the creations are in the midst of eternity, and that is one eternity, so they move in one eternal round. Consequently, when you hear philosophers argue the point how the first god came, how intelligence came, how worlds came, and how angels came, they are talking about that which is beyond their conception; about that which never was, and never will be worlds without end. It manifests their folly.
quotes.note: The chain claim in its strongest available form: not merely that gods are many but that the question of a first god is a question about “that which never was.” Referent is ambiguous here because the subject is the gods as a class, not the Father specifically — the Father-referent claim arrives two pages later.

quotes.excerpt: He is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, both body and spirit; and He is the Father of our spirits, and the Father of our flesh in the beginning. You will not dispute the words of the Apostle, that He is actually the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Father of our spirits. You may add these words to it, or let it alone, it is all the same to me, that He is not only the Father of our spirits, but also of our flesh. He being the founder of that natural machinery through which we have all obtained our bodies. Do you wish me to simplify it? Could you have a father without having a grandfather; or a grandfather without having a great grandfather?
quotes.note: Quoted whole and in printed order on purpose. Compilations routinely stop at “…and the Father of our spirits,” which asserts nothing about a regress at all; the regress is the grandfather sentence that immediately follows, and it is the sentence scholarship actually cites. Note also what the grandfather argument is arguing for: Young is establishing that God is the Father of our flesh as well as our spirits — the ancestral premise is doing Adam-God work, not standing alone as a cosmological thesis.

quotes.excerpt: I never heard of one circumstance that varied from this rule, and that was a son of the Emerald Isle who said he was born of one of his aunts. Does this unlock to your understandings how the Lord Almighty is our natural Father; He set the great machine to working. If you cannot see this truth now, you will if you are faithful, and patient.
quotes.note: Kept as context because it names the argument's target in Young's own words: “how the Lord Almighty is our natural Father.” The grandfather analogy is a step in that argument, not its conclusion.

notes: Re-pulled in full from The Complete Discourses of Brigham Young 2:844–848 (digital scan pp. 252–256; the printed pagination of that edition and the scan's own page numbers differ by 592) and collated word by word against Gary James Bergera's independent transcription in Conflict in the Quorum, 125–26, which supplies the readings the scan's OCR destroys. Context that must travel with this entry: Bergera identifies the discourse as Young's “most explicit Adam-God statement to date,” delivered as a deliberate rebuttal to Orson Pratt's Seer series on the pre-existence (see pratt-seer) and probably to Pratt's conference sermon of the previous day; Wilford Woodruff called it “the greatest sermon that ever was Deliver[e]d to the Latter Day Saints since they have been a People.” The same discourse teaches that God is “the Father of our flesh in the beginning,” and later pages carry the Adam-God material proper. Citing the grandfather sentence as a free-standing regress proof-text, without the Adam-God frame, is the single most common handling error attached to this sermon — Blake Ostler's rejection of the chain turns precisely on that frame. Hearsay C: a contemporaneous manuscript report of a spoken sermon, not reviewed by Young in this form.

title: Parley P. Pratt: a plurality of Gods under “one Supreme Head”
speaker: Parley P. Pratt
office: Apostle
venue: Key to the Science of Theology (1855), ch. V “Keys of the Mysteries of the Godhead,” pp. 34–36

witnesses.scribe: Third edition (Salt Lake City: Deseret News, 1874), pp. 34–36
witnesses.note: Collated independently; wording identical apart from “firstborn” (1855) printing as “first born.”

quotes.excerpt: It may then consistently enough be said, that there are, in a subordinate sense, a plurality of Gods, or rather of the sons of God; although there is one Supreme Head, who is over all, and through all, and in all His sons, by the power of His Spirit.
quotes.note: The terminus, stated at the head of the argument. Pratt's plurality is a plurality of sons, and it is bounded from the start.

quotes.excerpt: All these are Gods, or sons of God—they are the Kings, Princes, Priests, and Nobles of Eternity. But over them all there is a Presidency or Grand Head, who is the Father of all. And next unto him is Jesus Christ, the eldest born, and first heir of all the realms of light.
quotes.note: The structure is a presidency, not a genealogy: gods ranked under a Grand Head, with Christ as first heir directly below him. Pratt never asks whether the Head has a Head, and never allows for one.

quotes.excerpt: Again it follows, that in the use of this power, by consent and authority of the head, any one of these Gods may create, organize, people, govern, control, exalt, glorify and enjoy worlds on worlds, and the inhabitants thereof… All these are kingdoms which, together with their Kings, are in subordination to the great Head and Father of all, and to Jesus Christ the firstborn, and first heir, among the sons of God.
quotes.note: A clean forward chain — exalted beings create, people and govern worlds of their own — and note that even here the forward extension is licensed “by consent and authority of the head” and stays “in subordination” to it. The forward direction proliferates; the backward direction does not.

notes: Verified verbatim against the 1855 first edition (Internet Archive item keytoscienceofth00parl, printed pp. 34–36) and re-collated against the 1874 third edition and the archive's reflowed copy; the three agree. Judgment call recorded explicitly, because this text is filed in opposite directions by different compilers. Pratt is not a denial of the regress: he never argues against a chain, he simply never entertains one. Nor is he an INFINITE-CHAIN source: what he asserts is a bounded subordination hierarchy terminating in “one Supreme Head, who is over all,” “the Father of all.” In this project's sub-grades that is C-finite — a chain that ends — but the available category set has no tag for a terminating chain, and applying INFINITE-CHAIN would invert the claim while applying nothing at all would hide it, so the terminus quotes are carried untagged with the reasoning here. Reading either an affirmation or a denial of infinite regress into these pages is retrojection: Pratt is answering a different question, namely how a plurality of Gods can be reconciled with the oneness of God. What the same pages do supply, cleanly, is the forward chain.

title: Orson Pratt: “the number of Gods is infinite” — plurality without succession
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Apostle, Quorum of the Twelve
venue: Discourse delivered in the open air on the Temple Block, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 2:334–347)

witnesses.scribe: Journal of Discourses 2:334–347 (BYU ContentDM page images)
witnesses.note: Collation surface for the vault text; contemporaneous report, speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: …there are many Gods, and that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are Gods, and that all good men in this Church shall become Gods… In these expressions, God has reference to the great principles of light and truth, or knowledge, and not to the tabernacles in which this knowledge may dwell; the tabernacles are many and without number, but the truth or knowledge which is often personified and called God, is one, being the same in all; God is one, being a unity, when represented by light, truth, wisdom, or knowledge; but when reference is made to the temples in which this knowledge dwells, the number of Gods is infinite.
quotes.note: Categories deliberately left empty, and that is the entry's point. INFINITE-CHAIN requires a succession — Gods before Gods, a series with predecessors. Pratt's infinity has no succession in it at all: “God” names one attribute-set (light, truth, knowledge) that is numerically identical wherever it dwells, and the infinity is the count of tabernacles indwelt, a simultaneous multiplicity rather than a genealogy. No backward tag applies because nothing backward is claimed; no forward tag applies because no offspring, mechanism, or increase is named here; DIVINE-PROGRESSION does not apply because Pratt is not addressing whether God grows. Tagging this passage at all would be reading the later framework into it.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1855/1855-02-18-pratt-the-holy-spirit-and-the-godhead.md (“The Holy Spirit and the Godhead”), whose complete text was collated against the BYU JoD volume 2 page scan, pp. 334–347. Contemporaneous report, speaker unreviewed, hence C. This is the collection's essential control. Nineteenth-century “infinite Gods” language is routinely cited as evidence for an infinite regress; Pratt gets to literally infinite Gods by a route that is not genealogical, in the same decade and from the same pulpit as Brigham Young's genuinely serial statements. Anyone citing an 1850s “many Gods” or “infinite Gods” passage as backward-chain evidence has to clear this one first, because it demonstrates that the vocabulary alone does not settle the direction. Two consequences worth carrying: the arithmetic is compatible with a completed, non-successive plurality; and on this metaphysics — God as the finished attribute-set of knowledge, identical in all — there is nothing left for God to increase in, which is why Pratt's opposition to ongoing divine progression is structural rather than stated (his propositional denial lives in The Seer and the 1860 First Presidency exchange, not in this sermon corpus). Structurally this is also the earliest instance of a move the dataset sees again in 1984: defusing plurality by redefining what “God” refers to (see packer-parentage-1984). The rhyme is worth noting; unlike Packer, Pratt is constructing rather than walking anything back, so RETREAT-REFRAME is not applied.

title: Jedediah M. Grant: “My God is not lariatted out”
speaker: Jedediah M. Grant
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Bowery discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 4:122–129)

witnesses.scribe: BYU ContentDM scan of Journal of Discourses vol. 4, pp. 122–129
witnesses.note: Wayback capture of the BYU page images the vault text was collated against.

quotes.excerpt: Men have to be rewarded according to their works; if a man ceases to work, there is no more blessings for him. He is lariatted out, as Orson Pratt lariatted out the Gods in his theory; his circle is as far as the string extends. My God is not lariatted out.
quotes.note: Affirmation, by ridicule. The lariat is a staked rope: a tethered animal can graze only as far as the string reaches. Grant applies the image to Orson Pratt's published position that the Gods have all knowledge and cannot increase in it, and refuses it for his own God — the shortest statement of the affirmative side of the progression question in the nineteenth-century corpus. The target is named, which is what makes the quote usable: this is the Young/Pratt controversy conducted from the pulpit, nine years before the First Presidency condemned Pratt's propositions (see fp-repudiation-1865).

quotes.excerpt: I do not want the old men to think that they have done enough, but to exert themselves to the last, and not to believe in a God that is lariatted out, nor be lariatted out themselves, and say, “I have worked ten, fifteen, or twenty-five years, and I do not want to work anymore, my rope is long enough now.”
quotes.note: Context, not an independent claim: Grant's whole use of the image is homiletic — a God who has stopped growing licenses men who have stopped working. Recorded here because it shows the doctrinal claim being deployed as an argument about labor, which is how the affirmative side of the progression question was normally preached rather than argued.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1856/1856-10-grant-those-who-are-in-darkness.md, whose text was collated against BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses vol. 4, pp. 122–129. Journal of Discourses, so C: a Pitman-shorthand report of a Bowery discourse, published without the speaker's review; the printed heading is “Those Who Are in Darkness Cannot Discern the Light—Exhortations to Male and Female to Seek After the Light of the Holy Ghost—Women Who Leave Their Husbands, Etc.” Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 39, pairs this with a Brigham Young “lariat rope” sermon of the same month; Young's version could not be located in the vault (the October 1856 Young files in the corpus are the handcart-rescue discourses), so only Grant's is entered here, and any Young lariat entry should be sourced from the printed Journal of Discourses directly rather than from England. Grant was Second Counselor in the First Presidency and died five weeks after this discourse, on 1 December 1856.

title: W. W. Phelps, “There Is No End” (now the hymn “If You Could Hie to Kolob”)
speaker: William W. Phelps
office: Latter-day Saint printer, poet, and former scribe to Joseph Smith
venue: Poem “There Is No End,” Deseret News, 19 November 1856, p. 2; hymn no. 284 in Hymns of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

quotes.excerpt: Do you think that you could ever, Through all eternity, Find out the generation Where Gods began to be?
quotes.note: The regress question in interrogative form, and the tagging turns on that form. What the quatrain states is that the beginning of the Gods is not findable — the C-agnostic move — and that is all it states. It does not assert an endless line, it does not name the Father, and it does not say the Gods have generations in a single descending line rather than merely a plural existence. The INFINITE-CHAIN reading is the answer a rhetorical question invites, not a claim the hymn makes, so under the no-retrojection rule it is argued in the entry note rather than tagged here. Note also that “Gods” is unqualified: the referent is the class of Gods, not demonstrably the Father, hence “ambiguous” — unlike roberts-endless-line-1895-q2, where Roberts reprints this same quatrain in a context that has already made the Father its subject.

quotes.excerpt: Or see the grand beginning, Where space did not extend? Or view the last creation, Where Gods and matter end? Methinks the Spirit whispers, “No man has found ‘pure space,’ Nor seen the outside curtains, Where nothing has a place.”
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose, and it is the load-bearing stanza for how this entry is graded. Verse 2 is where the hymn answers itself, and the answer it gives is a limit on knowledge, not a cosmology: the Spirit whispers that no man has found the bounds. That answer is addressed to the spatial question (“pure space,” “the outside curtains”) rather than to the genealogical one in verse 1, which is left standing unanswered. Recorded so the entry shows that the hymn's own reply to its own questions is agnostic.

quotes.excerpt: The works of God continue, And worlds and lives abound; Improvement and progression Have one eternal round. There is no end to matter; There is no end to space; There is no end to spirit; There is no end to race.
quotes.note: The “There is no end to…” litany, which runs on through verses 4 and 5 (virtue, might, wisdom, light, union, youth, priesthood, truth; glory, love, being, and “no death above”). Tagged MANY-WORLDS for “worlds and lives abound.” Deliberately not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION: “Improvement and progression Have one eternal round” says progression is a permanent feature of the universe, not that God is progressing, and reading God into it is exactly the conflation this dataset exists to prevent. Deliberately not tagged INFINITE-CHAIN either: what the litany declares endless is matter, space, spirit, and race — never a line of Gods. The chain is the one thing the endlessness list conspicuously omits.

notes: Provenance resolved: this is not a Times and Seasons text. Phelps published it as the poem “There Is No End” in the Deseret News, 19 November 1856, p. 2 — twelve years after Joseph Smith's death and nine years into the Utah period — and it entered the hymnody later under its present title. The Deseret News attribution is taken from Michael Hubbard MacKay et al., eds., Producing Ancient Scripture, p. 440 n.134 (https://corpus.noahairmet.com/b/producing-ancient-scripture-joseph-smith-s-4e4d/440), which cites the poem to that issue and identifies it as hymn 284 in the 1985 hymnal; the 1856 newspaper page itself was not inspected for this entry, so the printing date is carried on that scholarly authority rather than on a page image. The hymn text quoted here was verified verbatim against the live churchofjesuschrist.org hymn page on 2026-08-10, where it stands as no. 284 with the text credited to “William W. Phelps, 1792–1872,” the tune KINGSFOLD arranged by Ralph Vaughan Williams, and the scripture references Abraham 3:1–4, 9 and Moses 1:3–4, 33–39. Graded current-correlated on that basis: it is a currently hosted, currently sung hymn. Caveat for a later pass: the hosted text is the 1985 hymnal, which the new Hymns—For Home and Church (2024–) is progressively superseding; whether the hymn and its number survive that rollout is not asserted here. Why this entry matters to the timeline: it is the only place in current correlated worship material where the beginning-of-the-Gods question is put to a congregation at all, and it is put as a question that is never answered. B. H. Roberts saw the opportunity and closed it — in A New Witness for God (1895) he prints the prose claim that “there has been and there now exists an endless line of Gods,” then prints this hymn in full immediately after as its hymnodic form (see roberts-endless-line-1895, quote q2, which reproduces this same quatrain in the older “D'ye think that you could ever” wording). No citesId is set on this entry, because citation edges run from the citing source to the cited one and the hymn is the earlier text; the reciprocal edge belongs on roberts-endless-line-1895 and adding it is out of scope here. The practical consequence is the one Roberts's own note anticipates: the prose statement fell out of General Authority usage, and the question survived in the hymnbook.

title: Heber C. Kimball: a Father connected with one still farther back
speaker: Heber C. Kimball
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference discourse, Bowery, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 5:18–23, at 5:19)

quotes.excerpt: We must be grafted into the true vine, and continue to partake of its fatness, and then we shall go back to our Father and God, who is connected with one who is still farther back; and this Father is connected with one still further back, and so on; and just so far as we respect our superiors and try to save our children, so shall we receive blessings from this time forth and forever, and shall become as numerous as the sands upon the seashore.
quotes.note: The chain runs in both directions inside one sentence — ancestors “still further back” and posterity “as numerous as the sands upon the seashore.” One of the cleanest explicit-chain sentences in the Journal of Discourses.

notes: Verified verbatim against the printed Journal of Discourses. Pitman shorthand report; the speaker did not review the text before publication — hence hearsay C under the v2 rebasing of Journal of Discourses material.

title: Wilford Woodruff: God Himself is increasing and progressing
speaker: Wilford Woodruff
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 6:115–121, at 6:120)

quotes.excerpt: If there was a point where man in his progression could not proceed any further, the very idea would throw a gloom over every intelligent and reflecting mind. God himself is increasing and progressing in knowledge, power, and dominion, and will do so, worlds without end. It is just so with us. We are in a probation, which is a school of experience.
quotes.note: Affirmation. The argument runs from the intolerability of a ceiling on human progress to God's ongoing progression — anthropology first, theology second. Later official denials attack the conclusion without engaging this premise. “God himself” is not further specified, hence the ambiguous referent.

notes: One of only two unambiguous affirmative divine-progression sentences located in the Journal of Discourses corpus; the other is Brigham Young's of 13 January 1867 (JD 11:282–291), see young-progressing-eternally-1867. No later pulpit affirmation was located. Watt shorthand, not reviewed by the speaker.

title: Brigham Young: instead of inquiring after the origin of the Gods
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 7:282–291)

quotes.excerpt: Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause of all things; but it would be as easy for an ant to number the grains of sand on the earth.
