It is not for man, with his limited intelligence, to grasp eternity in his comprehension. … Instead of inquiring after the origin of the Gods—instead of trying to explore the depths of eternities that have been, that are, and that will be—instead of endeavouring to discover the boundaries of boundless space, let them seek to know the object of their present existence, and how to apply, in the most profitable manner for their mutual good and salvation, the intelligence they possess.
quotes.note: Delivered the day after the “never was a time when there were not Gods” discourse (by-chain), in the same October 1859 conference: the same speaker holds the most explicit chain language and the earliest discouragement of the question on consecutive days.

notes: This is the caution the by-chain entry's earlier placeholder pointed at — it belongs to its own sermon (“Intelligence, Etc.,” October 9, 1859), not to the October 8 discourse. The 1997 Teachings of Presidents: Brigham Young manual (ch. 4) excerpts this passage; log that manual as its own citation entry when added.

title: Richard F. Burton: “gods in an ad infinitum ascending series”
speaker: Richard F. Burton
office: English explorer and travel writer; non-Mormon visitor to Great Salt Lake City in 1860
venue: The City of the Saints, and Across the Rocky Mountains to California, ch. IX, p. 388

quotes.excerpt: This body consists of three, viz., Eloheim, Jehovah, and Michael, which is Adam. From the Christian apostles and the Apocalypse, the Mormons deduce the dogma of gods in an ad infinitum ascending series: man, however, must limit his obedience to the last heavenly Father and Son revealed by the Holy Spirit.
quotes.note: Quoted with the preceding sentence attached, because the two cannot be separated honestly. Burton's Godhead is Eloheim, Jehovah and Michael-who-is-Adam: he is describing Adam-God, and the ascending series sits inside that description — the same pairing found in Brigham Young's discourse of 8 October 1854. The second clause is a real observation about how the doctrine functioned in practice: an infinite series upward, obedience owed only to the nearest link.

quotes.excerpt: And as God is perfect man, so is perfect man God: any individual, by faith and obedience, can, as the Brahminical faith asserts, rise to the position of a deity, until, attaining the power of forming a planet, peopling, redeeming it, and sitting there enthroned in everlasting power.
quotes.note: The forward chain as an outsider heard it in 1860, complete with world-forming. The comparative gloss “as the Brahminical faith asserts” is Burton's own frame, not his informants' — he read everything through comparative religion.

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive scan of the Harper (New York) printing, at printed p. 388 in chapter IX; the 1861 date is the London first edition, and the entry is dated to it while the pagination cited is the printing actually collated. The scan's OCR renders “ad infinitum” as “ad mjinitum” and “there” as “therq”; both are plainly scanner artifacts and are corrected silently. Hearsay B rather than A: the prose is Burton's own published writing, but every doctrinal statement in the chapter is his summary of what Mormon informants told him during his 1860 visit, with no Latter-day Saint source quoted for the regress claim — so as evidence of the doctrine it stands one remove from any Latter-day Saint speaker. Its evidential value is precisely that distance. It shows that in 1860 the ascending series and Adam-God were publicly legible, and legible together, to a well-read non-Mormon visitor who had no stake in either.

title: Brigham Young relays Joseph Smith: a God who had not a Father — nor a mother
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 9:286–289)

quotes.excerpt: The idea that the Lord our God is not a personage of tabernacle is entirely a mistaken notion. He was once a man. Brother Kimball quoted a saying of Joseph the Prophet, that he would not worship a God who had not a Father; and I do not know that he would if he had not a mother; the one would be as absurd as the other. If he had a Father, he was made in his likeness. And if he is our Father we are made after his image and likeness.
quotes.note: Three stacked claims in one breath: past mortality (“He was once a man”), the Father's Father (the relayed Joseph Smith saying), and the mother clause — which is Young's own hedged inference (“I do not know that he would”), not part of the reported saying.

notes: The relayed saying is an attribution chain three links deep — Joseph Smith (d. 1844) → Heber C. Kimball (earlier the same afternoon) → Young → Watt's shorthand — so while the sermon is a contemporaneous report (C), the Joseph attribution itself is an eighteen-year-old relay and should be weighed accordingly. Also excerpted in Widtsoe's Discourses of Brigham Young compilation.

title: Brigham Young: “the God that I serve is progressing eternally”
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 11:282–291)

witnesses.scribe: Edward L. Sloan, shorthand reporter, printed in Journal of Discourses 11:282–291
witnesses.note: Wayback capture of the BYU ContentDM page images. The printed header reads “Remarks by President Brigham Young, in the Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City, January 13th, 1867. Reported by Edward L. Sloan.”

quotes.excerpt: They appear to be bounded in their capacity for acquiring knowledge, as Brother Orson Pratt, has in theory, bounded the capacity of God. According to his theory, God can progress no further in knowledge and power; but the God that I serve is progressing eternally, and so are his children: they will increase to all eternity, if they are faithful.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the most explicit one from a Church President in the corpus. Two claims in one sentence, and they must be kept apart: God is progressing eternally (D), and his children will increase to all eternity (the forward promise, stated with no object — no offspring, no worlds, no mechanism). Young joins them with “and so are,” which is exactly the symmetry that later readers turn into an argument for a chain; he does not himself make a backward claim here, so nothing backward is tagged. Orson Pratt is named as the holder of the bounded view, which dates and localizes the dispute (compare pratt-seer and fp-repudiation-1865).

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1867/1867-01-young-weakness-of-the-human-mind.md, printed under the heading “Weakness of the Human Mind. Extortion. Imperfection of the Human Judgment. Introduction of Machinery.” Journal of Discourses, so C: Edward L. Sloan's shorthand report, not reviewed by the speaker before publication; the vault file is still status draft. This is the sentence Eugene England uses to open “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 33, where he sets it against Hyrum Smith's 1844 “I would not serve a God that had not all wisdom and power” to frame the whole two-modes argument; England's reproduction is lowercase OCR, so the text here is taken from the sermon, not from him. Note what the surrounding paragraphs are actually about: retail prices, judging cloth, and Saints who stop learning. The doctrinal claim arrives as an analogy for members who will not study, which is a recurring feature of this material and a reason it is easy to miss when sweeping by topic.

title: Orson Pratt: exaltation defined by increase — the angels who have none
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Thursday afternoon session, New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 13:183–196)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 13:183–196; reporter credited on the printed header. Speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: There is a difference between the classes of angels called celestial, terrestrial and telestial. The celestial angels have not attained to all of the power and greatness and exaltation of kings and priests in the presence of God; they are blessed with glory, happiness, peace and joy; but they are not blessed with the privilege of increasing their posterity to all ages of eternity, neither have they thrones and kingdoms, but they are servants to those of the highest order.
quotes.note: Exaltation defined by the presence of eternal increase, and the definition delivered by subtraction: the ministering angels get glory, happiness, peace and joy, and are still not exalted, because increase is what they lack. Euphemism rather than explicit: “increasing their posterity to all ages of eternity” names the increase and its endlessness but leaves the offspring's nature and the mechanism unstated — the same register as D&C 132's “continuation of the seeds forever.”

quotes.excerpt: We might inquire, have angels not also these affections which belong to the higher class of beings, inasmuch as they are resurrected beings? Yes, but herein they have lost, through disobedience, the privilege of attaining to the higher glory and exaltation. They have affections and desires that never can be gratified, and in this respect their glory is not full.
quotes.note: Context for q1, untagged: it makes no claim about increase itself, but it shows the argument's emotional engine — the deprivation is felt, not merely structural. This is the register in which mid-twentieth-century temple-marriage preaching would later carry the whole doctrine (see eldred-smith-no-increase-1948).

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1869/1869-10-pratt-celestial-marriage.md, whose opening and closing pages were collated against the BYU JoD volume 13 scan, pp. 183–196, with the printed header confirming David W. Evans as reporter. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. Its use to the collection is definitional: increase is not presented as a bonus attached to exaltation but as the differentia between the exalted and everyone else, D&C 132:17 preached as doctrine rather than cited as proof text. Same speaker, same sermon title, seventeen years after the 1852 discourse, and markedly more restrained — the mechanism has dropped out of view even though the entailment has not.

title: Orson Pratt: beget children, form and create worlds, send forth our spirit children
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 14:233–245)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 14:233–245; reporter credited on the printed header. Speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: Can spirits do this? No, they remain single. There are no marriages among spirits, no coupling together of the males and females among them; but when they rise from the grave, after being tabernacled in mortal bodies, they have all the functions that are necessary to people worlds. As our Father and God begat us, sons and daughters, so will we rise immortal, males and females, and beget children, and, in our turn, form and create worlds, and send forth our spirit children to inherit those worlds, the same as we were sent here, and thus will the works of God continue, and not only God himself, and His Son Jesus Christ have the power of endless lives, but all of His redeemed offspring. They grow up like the parents; that is a law of nature so far as this world is concerned. Every kind of being begets its own like, and when fully matured and grown up the offspring become like the parent. So the offspring of the Almighty, who begot us, will grow up and become literally Gods, or the sons of God.
quotes.note: The fullest forward chain located in the corpus, with every link named in one breath: resurrected sexed bodies retaining reproductive “functions,” literal begetting, spirit children, worlds created to receive them, and those children maturing into Gods. The clause that carries the most weight is the comparative one — “the same as we were sent here” — which declares our own origin identical to the process just described, making the Father a prior instance of it.

quotes.excerpt: We heard this forenoon that, when the Saints come into the possession of their everlasting inheritance and are exalted as glorified and eternal beings, to the increase of their posterity there would be no end. "No end!" What does that mean? It means that it will be eternal--that there never will be a period throughout all the future ages of eternity, but what they will be increasing and multiplying, until their seed are more numerous than the dust of the earth or the stars of heaven… They will not only people worlds, but they will create them. There is room enough to accomplish this when we consider that space is boundless.
quotes.note: Pratt glossing “no end” as a live arithmetical claim rather than a formula — the increase is genuinely unbounded and therefore requires boundless space. Double hyphens preserved from the vault transcription of the printed page.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1871/1871-08-pratt-o-the-redemption-of-the-earthpre-existencemarriage.md, a fresh ingestion collated against the BYU JoD volume 14 page scan, pp. 233–245, with both talk boundaries confirmed directly against the scan and an independent Internet Archive OCR pass of the same leaves. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand by David W. Evans, speaker unreviewed, hence C. This is the best single exhibit in the dataset for conflation trap #3. The symmetry pressure toward a backward chain is at its maximum here — the process is declared identical in both directions (“As our Father and God begat us… so will we rise… the same as we were sent here”), and the reader has only to run the sentence in reverse to reach an infinite regress. Pratt does not run it in reverse. Nothing is said about where the Father came from; INFINITE-CHAIN is carried for the succession of Gods the passage states in the forward direction — exalted couples begetting children who “will grow up and become literally Gods” — not for any backward regress. What the passage does state about the Father is narrower and worth keeping distinct: that He begat us viviparously, which is a claim about our origin, not His.

title: Brigham Young: spirits begotten, born, and brought forth by celestial bodies
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 18:257–264)

witnesses.scribe: George F. Gibbs (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 18:257–264. Speaker did not review. No Internet Archive page anchor exists for this range of volume 18.

quotes.excerpt: Mankind is composed of two distinct elements; the first is a spiritual organization in eternity, the second is a natural organization on this earth, formed out of the material of which this earth is composed. Man is first spiritual, then temporal. As it is written in the revelations of God to man, all things were first created spiritual, and secondly temporal. That is, spirits were begotten, born and educated in the celestial world, and were brought forth by celestial bodies.
quotes.note: Gestation and parturition, stated as exegesis rather than metaphor: begotten, then *born*, then brought forth *by bodies*. Three separate physiological terms in one sentence is what puts this past the reach of a figurative reading. The framing matters too — Young offers it as his gloss on the Moses/D&C “all things created spiritual first” passage and as “a part of my own visions upon this matter,” so it arrives as a president's interpretation, not as cited revelation.

quotes.excerpt: Those of the Latter-day Saints who will continue to follow after the revelations and commandments of God to do them, who are found to be obedient in all things, continually advancing little by little towards perfection and the knowledge of God, they, when they enter the spirit world and receive their bodies, will be able to advance faster in the things pertaining to the knowledge of the Gods, and will continue onward and upward until they become Gods, even the sons of God.
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose. This is plain theosis — becoming like God — from the same discourse, and the taxonomy's second trap is that theosis is not by itself a claim about generative exaltation or about anyone's ancestry. Recorded here so the pairing is visible: in one sermon Young states the viviparous mechanism and the deification promise without ever joining them into a chain.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1876/1876-10-young-philosophy-of-man-upon-the-earththe.md, collated against BYU JoD volume 18, pp. 257–264. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand by George F. Gibbs, speaker unreviewed, hence C; the vault entry is still marked draft, so the two quoted sentences deserve a page-image check before they carry public weight. Chronologically this sits between Pratt's Seer systematization and the 1909 First Presidency statement, and it shows the viviparous mechanism being taught from the general conference pulpit by the President of the Church — not merely written in a periodical by an apostle. The phrase later curriculum inherits is “begotten and born,” and this is one of its pulpit sources.

title: Joseph F. Smith: the exalted man is greater than the angel
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 23:169–176, at 23:173)

quotes.excerpt: The man who passes through this probation, and is faithful, being redeemed from sin by the blood of Christ, through the ordinances of the Gospel, and attains to exaltation in the kingdom of God, is not less but greater than the angels… in fact having passed from the condition of the angel to that of a God. He possesses keys of power, dominion and glory that the angel does not possess—and cannot possess without gaining them in the same way that he gained them, which will be by passing through the same ordeals and proving equally faithful.
quotes.note: Theosis, forward direction only. The comparison being drawn is between an exalted human and an angel, and the “same ordeals” are the ordeals the exalted man passed through, not ordeals attributed to God.

notes: Re-pulled and read at Journal of Discourses 23:169–176 (discourse “Man a Mortal and an Immortal Being,” Joseph F. Smith, Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday, June 18, 1882, reported by Geo. F. Gibbs) and verified verbatim. This entry exists chiefly to stop a persistent misfiling. The passage circulates in regress lists — usually cited from its Gospel Doctrine reprint rather than from the sermon — but it makes no claim about God's past, God's Father, or a chain of Gods; its subject is the rank of an exalted human relative to an angel. Under this project's taxonomy it is theosis and nothing more, and treating theosis as evidence for divine ancestry is the second conflation trap. The sentence such lists are actually reaching for — “We are precisely in the same condition… that God our Heavenly Father was when He was passing through this or a similar ordeal” — is not in this discourse at all; it belongs to a Joseph F. Smith sermon delivered twenty months later. See jfs-same-ordeal-1884. Hearsay C: Gibbs's contemporaneous report, published without the speaker's review.

title: Joseph F. Smith: “an eternal being, without beginning of days” and “precisely in the same condition,” in consecutive sentences
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Assembly Hall discourse, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon (Journal of Discourses 25:51–60, at 25:58); reprinted in Gospel Doctrine, 64

quotes.excerpt: God has a tabernacle of flesh and bone. He is an organized being just as we are, who are now in the flesh. Jesus Christ was born of His mother Mary. He had a fleshly tabernacle; He was crucified on the cross; and his body was raised from the dead. He burst the bonds of the grave and came forth to newness of life, a living soul, a living being, a man with a body, with parts and with spirit—the spirit and the body becoming a living and immortal soul. You and I have to do the same thing. We must go through the same ordeal in order to attain to the glory and exaltation which God designed we should enjoy with him in the eternal worlds. In other words, we must become like Him; peradventure to sit upon thrones, to have dominion, power, and eternal increase. God designed this in the beginning. We are the children of God. He is an eternal being, without beginning of days or end of years. He always was, He is, He always will be. We are precisely in the same condition and under the same circumstances that God our Heavenly Father was when He was passing through this or a similar ordeal.
quotes.note: Both halves, in printed order, in one paragraph. The order matters and is usually reported backwards: Smith asserts God's beginninglessness immediately BEFORE the same-condition sentence, not after it. He puts “He is an eternal being, without beginning of days or end of years. He always was, He is, He always will be” and “God our Heavenly Father… was passing through this or a similar ordeal” in consecutive breaths and shows no sign of feeling a tension between them. Quoting either half alone — which citations in both directions routinely do — manufactures a Joseph F. Smith who does not exist. Both directions of the Father-status axis are stated within this single passage — the same-ordeal claim and the beginningless-eternal-being claim sit five sentences apart; the tags record both. The Christological hinge is restored here rather than elided: the “same ordeal” takes its antecedent from Christ's death and resurrection, which complicates — though on the closing sentence it does not defeat — the past-mortality reading. The forward content is “dominion, power, and eternal increase,” the euphemism idiom, so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM replaces FORWARD-EXPLICIT.

notes: Re-pulled and verified verbatim at Journal of Discourses 25:51–60 (Joseph F. Smith, Assembly Hall, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon, February 17, 1884, reported by John Irvine); the quoted paragraph is at 25:58. Two provenance corrections worth carrying. First, this passage is frequently mis-cited to Journal of Discourses 23:173, which is a different discourse from June 1882 about angels and exalted men (see jfs-angel-to-god-1882) and contains none of this language. Second, the passage almost always travels in its Gospel Doctrine 64 reprint, and it is in that condensed reprint context that the counter-sentence gets dropped. Categorized as backward-mortality: Smith says we are in the condition God was in, which is a past-mortality claim, and he says nothing about God having a Father — so no chain tag. Hearsay C: Irvine's contemporaneous report, speaker-unreviewed.

title: Charles W. Penrose, “The Personality of God”: eternality in intelligence, not in ancestry
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Elder and editor of the Deseret News (ordained an Apostle 1904; later Counselor in the First Presidency)
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon (Journal of Discourses 26:18–27, at 26:23–27)

quotes.excerpt: But, if God is an individual spirit and dwells in a body, the question will arise, “Is He the Eternal Father?” Yes, He is the Eternal Father. “Is it a fact that He never had a beginning?” In the elementary particles of His organism, He did not. But if He is an organized Being, there must have been a time when that being was organized. This, some one will say, would infer that God had a beginning. This spirit which pervades all things, which is the light and life of all things, by which our heavenly Father operates, by which He is omnipotent, never had a beginning and never will have an end.
quotes.note: The anti-regress move, in the one paragraph where Penrose stages the objection and answers it. He concedes that God as an organized person had a beginning, and then locates eternality not in a line of ancestors but in an impersonal spirit of intelligence. Carried as context rather than tagged, because it asserts no ancestry in either direction — that is the point of it.

quotes.excerpt: And if you see a glorified man, a man who has passed through the various grades of being, who has overcome all things, who has been raised from the dead, who has been quickened by this spirit in its fullness, there you see manifested, in its perfection, this eternal, beginningless, endless spirit of intelligence. Such a Being is our Father and our God, and we are following in His footsteps. He has attained to perfection.
quotes.note: Past-mortality asserted as plainly as anywhere in the corpus — “raised from the dead” — but with the eternality predicated of the spirit of intelligence God embodies, not of God's person or lineage.

quotes.excerpt: The person whom I worship I acknowledge as my Father. Through Him I may learn to understand the secrets and mysteries of eternity, those things that never had a beginning and will never have an end. He has ascended above all things after descending below all things. He has fought his way from the depths up to the position He now occupies. He holds it by virtue of His goodness, of His might, of His majesty, of His power… He has won that position by His own exertions, by His own faithfulness, by His own righteousness.
quotes.note: Godhood by self-conquest. This is the alternative to a genealogy, not a step in one: nothing in the discourse says God received his position from a Father, and nothing asks who stood above him.

quotes.excerpt: As the Father had taken His upward course in worlds before this, so Jesus Christ followed in his footsteps in every respect; therefore he is entitled to sit down at the right hand of God in the heavens, to sit on his throne and be one with the Father in all things.
quotes.note: “Worlds before this” places the Father's progression in prior worlds — a real backward claim, and still not a parentage claim.

quotes.excerpt: The individual, the organized person may have had a beginning, but that spirit of which and by which they organized never had a beginning… The works of that eternal spirit of intelligence, the great Eternal God, manifested to us in our Father and through Jesus Christ, never had a beginning. There never was a first world or man; there will never be a last.
quotes.note: The closest Penrose comes to a chain, and it is deliberately not one: no first world and no first man, but no succession of divine fathers either. Structurally this is Orson Pratt's abstract “Great God” — the personages come and go, the intelligence is what is eternal — rather than Brigham Young's genealogy.

notes: The whole discourse (Journal of Discourses 26:18–27) was re-pulled and read for this entry, not just the paragraph that circulates. Verified verbatim. Two things follow from reading it whole. First, Penrose is a genuine backward-mortality source: God was organized, progressed through worlds before this one, was raised from the dead, and won his position by his own exertions. Second, he asserts no divine parentage anywhere in ten pages, and he explicitly heads off the regress by relocating beginninglessness into an impersonal “eternal, beginningless, endless spirit of intelligence” — so the entry carries no INFINITE-CHAIN tag and should not be recruited as one. It belongs with Nelson, Talmage and Widtsoe in the 1884–1915 cluster, where godhood is attained by progression through law from a beginning and eternality sits in impersonal intelligence, rather than with the Kimball–Young lineage stream. Discourse header: Elder Charles W. Penrose, Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon, November 16, 1884, reported by Arthur Winter. Hearsay C: a reporter's contemporaneous account, published without the speaker's review.

title: Erastus Snow: a Mother in heaven inferred from anatomy
speaker: Erastus Snow
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Quarterly conference discourse, Tabernacle, Provo (Journal of Discourses 26:213–227)

witnesses.scribe: John Irvine (third-person indirect report)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 26:213–227. Irvine reports in third-person indirect style (“Proceeding, he said…”) rather than as a first-person verbatim transcript, so the printed wording is a reporter's rendering of Snow's argument, not necessarily Snow's sentences.

quotes.excerpt: Now, it is not said in so many words in the Scriptures, that we have a Mother in heaven as well as a Father. It is left for us to infer this from what we see and know of all living things in the earth including man. The male and female principle is united and both necessary to the accomplishment of the object of their being, and if this be not the case with our Father in heaven after whose image we are created, then it is an anomaly in nature. But to our minds the idea of a Father suggests that of a Mother
quotes.note: The clearest statement in the corpus of how Heavenly Mother is actually reached: not by revelation and not by scripture, which Snow concedes are silent, but by an argument from nature in which her absence would be an anomaly. That candid “it is left for us to infer this” is the datum — the doctrine is presented as an inference, in a discourse by an apostle, and later usage will present it as settled.

quotes.excerpt: "In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me, I've a Mother there."
quotes.note: Eliza R. Snow's verse quoted from the pulpit as the poetic seal on the anatomical argument — see o-my-father. Punctuation and capitalization follow the Journal of Discourses printing, which differs slightly from the hymnal text. This is the earliest pulpit quotation of the hymn located in the Pulpit corpus; roughly fifty talks quote it in all, clustering 1904–1929 and again 1973–1991.

quotes.excerpt: Hence when it is said that God created our first parents in His likeness--"in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them"--it is intimated in language sufficiently plain to my understanding that the male and female principle was present with the Gods as it is with man. It needs only a common understanding of the organism of man and of all living creatures, and the functions of this organism to show the primary object of the Creator, and that is the multiplication of the species… We need only to study the anatomy and construction of the human system, and to understand its powers and capabilities, to comprehend the object and purpose of the Creator, even though the commandment had not been written to multiply and replenish the earth.
quotes.note: Marked implied. What Snow states outright is that the male and female principle exists among the Gods and that human anatomy reveals the Creator's purpose to be multiplication of the species; the sentences about multiplying and replenishing are about earthly generation. Divine viviparous reproduction is the conclusion the argument is built to support and the one his hearers would draw, but he stops at the premise, so the tag is carried as read-into rather than stated. Double hyphens preserved from the vault transcription of the printed page.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1885/1885-05-snow-e-the-creation-male-and-female-etc.md, a fresh ingestion whose complete text was collated against the BYU JoD volume 26 page scans, pp. 213–227, with the printed header confirming John Irvine as reporter. Filed as an original rather than a citation, with citesId recording the edge to o-my-father: the hymn verse is quoted, but the entry's value is the argument around it, which is Snow's own and is not in the hymn — the hymn asserts a Mother and stops, while Snow supplies a reason, and the reason is anatomical. Provenance caveat, and it is a real one: this is the weakest-fidelity text in the pulpit lane. Irvine reports in third-person indirect style rather than transcribing, so the wording is his rendering of Snow's argument. Graded C to match the Journal of Discourses convention, since the report is contemporaneous and published, but it sits at the bottom of that grade and the phrasing should never be pressed as Snow's ipsissima verba. The vault entry is also still marked draft.

dateDisplay: Couplet as published doctrine, 1880s–1901; origin story dated to 1840
title: Lorenzo Snow couplet
speaker: Lorenzo Snow
office: Apostle, later President of the Church
venue: Published poetry and addresses; origin narrated in later recollection

quotes.excerpt: As man now is, God once was: As God now is, man may be.
quotes.note: The couplet in isolation. Nothing in it settles whether "God" is the Father or the Son.

quotes.excerpt: As Abra'm, Isaac, Jacob, too, First babes, then men — to gods they grew. As man now is, our God once was; As now God is, so man may be... For John declares: When Christ we see Like unto him we'll truly be... The head of all his spirit-race.
quotes.note: Snow's own poem “Man's Destiny” (January 1892). His warrant is 1 John 3:2 — likeness to Christ. The closing “head of all his spirit-race” is a forward-explicit signal: an exalted man as progenitor of a spirit race.

quotes.excerpt: Again, Jesus said: “To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in His throne.” [Revelation 3:21.] That is a wonderful saying. Is there any truth in it? It is all true. It is the Lord Almighty that said it.
quotes.note: Address of 20 July 1901. The proof text is Revelation 3:21 — Christ's own exaltation. A being who was mortal, is now God, and has a Father above him fits the Son exactly and requires no theogony for the Father. Retagged: Revelation 3:21 describes attainment (“overcame, and am set down”), not mortality — and with referent Son, it does not establish either of the Father.

quotes.excerpt: [The 1840 origin narrative as printed in the manual: “In the spring of 1840, Lorenzo Snow was in Nauvoo, Illinois, preparing to leave for a mission in England. He visited the home of his friend Henry G. Sherwood, and he asked Brother Sherwood to explain a passage of scripture… ‘I formed the following couplet which expresses the revelation, as it was shown me.’ Snow ‘did not teach the doctrine publicly until he knew that the Prophet Joseph Smith had taught it.’]
quotes.note: Survives only through Snow's own recollection some six decades later — hence the D override on this quote alone, while the couplet as published doctrine stays A.

notes: The most consequential revision in v2. Both of Snow's own proof texts are about Christ, so on his own scriptural warrant the couplet is Christological and the Father-referent reading is imported from the King Follett milieu. Counterweight: he dated the insight to 1840 Nauvoo, attributed it to revelation, and his milieu pointed at the Father. Verdict: ambiguous, weighted toward the Son. The consequence for the site is concrete — the couplet should not be read as independent evidence for the Father's mortality; it inherits that meaning only when paired with the King Follett Discourse. That later Church usage exploits precisely this ambiguity (Hinckley's “more of a couplet than anything else”; the 2014 essay's “little has been revealed about the first half”) is itself one of the collection's findings.

title: Orson Pratt, The Seer
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Apostle
venue: The Seer (periodical), Washington, D.C.; §25 (p. 37) and §113 (p. 184)

quotes.excerpt: Each God, through his wife or wives, raises up a numerous family of sons and daughters... As soon as each God has begotten many millions of male and female spirits... he, in connection with his sons, organizes a new world.
quotes.note: The most systematic viviparous spirit-birth theology published by an apostle.

quotes.excerpt: The Father of our spirits has only been doing that which His Progenitors did before Him.
quotes.note: Father-referent and explicitly serial: progenitors, plural, before Him.

notes: A-tier by provenance (Pratt's own pen) but never official, and formally repudiated in part — see the 1865 First Presidency statement, the first official retreat in this dataset, 132 years before the Hinckley interviews. Pratt's systematization is the high-water mark from which the correlated era slowly walks back.

title: First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve, statement on The Seer
speaker: Brigham Young, Heber C. Kimball, and eleven members of the Quorum of the Twelve
office: First Presidency and the Twelve
venue: Latter-day Saints' Millennial Star 27, no. 42 (21 October 1865): 657–663, reprinted from the Deseret News

quotes.excerpt: When we commenced this article, we did not think of extending our comments beyond the work already alluded to. We consider it our duty, however, and advisable for us to incorporate with this which we have already written, our views upon other doctrines which have been extensively published and widely received as the standard and authoritative doctrines of the Church, but which are unsound. The views we allude to, and which we deem objectionable, have been published by Elder Orson Pratt.
quotes.note: The hinge sentence of the declaration, printed pp. 658–659. The document opens as a repudiation of Lucy Mack Smith's Biographical Sketches (which Pratt had published in Liverpool) and then widens, mid-article, into a doctrinal disavowal. Note the framing the First Presidency themselves supply: these are teachings that had been "widely received as the standard and authoritative doctrines of the Church."

quotes.excerpt: Seer, page 117, par. 95:— “Then there will be no Being or Beings in existence that will know one particle more than what we know; then our knowledge and wisdom and power will be infinite, and cannot, from thenceforth, be increased or expanded in the least degree.” Same page, par. 96:— “But when they (the Saints) become one with the Father and the Son, and receive a fulness of their glory, that will be the end of all progression in knowledge, because there will be nothing more to be learned. The Father and the Son do not progress in knowledge and wisdom, because they already know all things past, present and to come.” Par. 97:— “There are none among them (the Gods) that are in advance of the others in knowledge; though some may have been Gods as many millions of years as there are particles of dust in all the universe, yet there is not one truth that such are in possession of, but what every other God knows.” “None of these Gods are progressing in knowledge, neither can they progress in the acquirement of any truth.”
quotes.note: The propositions themselves, printed p. 660. Two provenance facts the England summary flattens. First, these are not the First Presidency's paraphrase of Pratt — they are verbatim quotations of The Seer, par. 95–97, set out under their paragraph numbers so the reader can check them. Second, they reach the 1865 declaration by way of an earlier First Presidency comment on Pratt's remarks of 29 January 1860, published in the Deseret News of 25 July 1860 and signed by Brigham Young, Heber C. Kimball and Daniel H. Wells; the 1865 signers reproduce that comment inside their own document and then, in the passage quoted below, extend the disavowal to the whole body of Pratt's speculative writing. The direction is what matters for this collection: the earliest official retreat here is a retreat against the denial of divine progression, not against its affirmation. Pratt's own recorded concession, quoted immediately before this on p. 660, is “So far as revelation from the heavens is concerned, I have had none in relation to those points of doctrine.”

quotes.excerpt: They are mere hypotheses, and should be perused and accepted as such, and not as doctrines of the Church… But the Seer, The Great First Cause, the article in the Millennial Star of October 15th, and November 1, 1850, on the Holy Spirit, and the first half of the tract, also on the Holy Spirit, contain doctrines which we cannot sanction, and which we have felt impressed to disown, so that the Saints who now live, and who may live hereafter, may not be misled by our silence, or be left to misinterpret it. Where these objectionable works, or parts of works, are bound in volumes, or otherwise, they should be cut out and destroyed; with proper care this can be done without much, if any, injury to the volumes.
quotes.note: The operative disavowal, printed p. 663. This is the sentence the entry previously had only in England's summary form: The Seer is named by title and put outside the doctrines of the Church, with the physical instruction to excise it from bound volumes. Small caps and italics in the printed text (“the Seer, The Great First Cause”, “the Holy Spirit”) are rendered here as plain roman.

quotes.excerpt: It ought to have been known, years ago, by every person in the Church—for ample teachings have been given on the point—that no member of the Church has the right to publish any doctrines, as the doctrines of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, without first submitting them for examination and approval to the First Presidency and the Twelve… While upon this subject, we wish to warn all the Elders of the Church, and to have it clearly understood by the members, that, in the future, whoever publishes any new doctrines without first taking this course, will be liable to lose his Priesthood.
quotes.note: The closing paragraphs, printed p. 663, immediately above the signatures. Worth keeping alongside the doctrinal content because it is the procedural half of the retreat: 1865 is where prior-approval-before-publication is asserted as the rule for doctrinal writing, with loss of priesthood named as the penalty. The pattern recurs — compare the treatment of mcconkie-mormon-doctrine ninety-three years later.

notes: Verified in v2 against the printed original. The declaration, headed “HEARKEN, O YE LATTER-DAY SAINTS, AND ALL THE INHABITANTS OF THE EARTH WHO WISH TO BE SAINTS, TO WHOM THIS WRITING SHALL COME” and credited “(From the Deseret News.),” fills pp. 657–663 of the Latter-day Saints' Millennial Star vol. 27, no. 42, Saturday 21 October 1865. All four excerpts were read off the Internet Archive page scans (item per_utah-and-the-mormons_the-latter-day-saints-millennial-star_1865-10-21_27_42, leaves n0–n6 = pp. 657–663) and collated against the page images at full resolution, not merely the OCR layer; the leaf-to-page mapping was fixed from the scan's own page_numbers.json and the printed folio “663” visible above the signatures. Two corrections to the previous draft. (1) Daniel H. Wells did not sign. The signatures, in printed order, are Brigham Young, Heber C. Kimball, Orson Hyde, John Taylor, Wilford Woodruff, George A. Smith, Amasa M. Lyman, Ezra T. Benson, Charles C. Rich, Lorenzo Snow, Erastus Snow, Franklin D. Richards, George Q. Cannon — the First Presidency less Wells, plus eleven of the Twelve. Wells's name appears only on the embedded 1860 First Presidency comment. (2) The propositions about the Father and the Son not progressing are quotations of The Seer, par. 95–97, not the Presidency's own wording; the entry's citesId link to pratt-seer is therefore exactly right, and the sourceType of citation is retained. Remaining gap: the date field (23 August 1865) is the Deseret News printing date carried over from secondary itemization. The Millennial Star reprint carries no date of its own beyond “(From the Deseret News.),” and there is no 1865 Deseret News scan on the Internet Archive to check it against, so that one datum is still second-hand while the wording, venue, page range and signatories are now first-hand.

title: Brigham Young on the succession of Gods — and his caution
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 7:333)

quotes.excerpt: How many Gods there are, I do not know. But there never was a time when there were not Gods and worlds, and when men were not passing through the same ordeals that we are now passing through. That course has been from all eternity, and it is and will be to all eternity.
quotes.note: Succession of Gods, not merely plurality of worlds — this is what the tightened INFINITE-CHAIN tag requires.

notes: Hearsay raised from E to C in v2. Most Journal of Discourses material derives from George Watt's contemporaneous shorthand, edited for publication and in the early years reviewed by Young's office — that is contemporaneous secondhand with an editing layer, not untraceable attribution. E is now reserved for genuinely orphaned attributions. The pairing is what makes this entry valuable: the same speaker holds the most explicit chain language and the earliest official discouragement of the question. Quote verified verbatim against the printed Journal of Discourses 7:333 (page-scan collation). The “origin of the Gods” caution formerly held here as a placeholder belongs to a different discourse — see young-origin-caution-1859, delivered the next day of the same conference.

title: “Our Mother in Heaven”: the companion hymn that named her a “goddess bride”
speaker: Wm. C. Harrison
office: Contributor to the Juvenile Instructor (hymn text; music by A. Hardy)
venue: “Our Mother in Heaven: Companion Hymn to E. R. Snow's ‘Invocation,’” words by Wm. C. Harrison, music by A. Hardy, Juvenile Instructor 29, no. 8 (15 April 1894): 263–264

witnesses.scribe: George Q. Cannon's reprint of verses 3 and 4 in “Topics of the Times: The Worship of Female Deities”
witnesses.note: An independent typesetting of the same stanzas thirteen months later, on p. 316 of the 15 May 1895 issue. It agrees word for word with the 1894 music page and differs only in accidentals — Cannon prints “powers” for “pow'rs,” “his goddess bride” for “His goddess bride,” “didst” for “did'st,” and adds line-end commas the engraved music omits.

quotes.excerpt: Oh my mother, thou that dwellest In thy mansions up on high, Oft methinks I still remember When you bade your child good by; How you clasped me to your bosom, Bade me a true son to be E're I left my Father's mansion, To dwell in mortality.
quotes.note: Verse 1, and the point of the whole exercise: Eliza R. Snow's opening line is repeated almost unchanged, “O my Father” becoming “Oh my mother.” The printed subtitle makes the dependence explicit — “Companion Hymn to E. R. Snow's ‘Invocation.’” Line breaks in the engraved setting are run together here with the syllable hyphens closed up; the spelling “E're” is as printed.

quotes.excerpt: 'Tis recorded in your journal How you stood by Father's side, When by pow'rs that are eternal Thou wast sealed His goddess bride; How by love and truth and virtue E'en in time thou did'st become Through your high, exalted station Mother of the souls of men. When of evil I've repented, And my work on earth is done, Kindest Father, loving mother, Pray forgive your erring son.
quotes.note: Verses 3 and 4, the two Cannon would single out a year later. Two claims are stacked here that the taxonomy keeps apart. First, generative exaltation, stated of a divine person rather than of mortals: sealing by eternal powers gives her a “high, exalted station,” and through that station she “did'st become … Mother of the souls of men” — and “E'en in time” places her becoming inside time rather than in eternity past. Second, and this is what drew the rebuke, the hymn does not merely describe her but addresses her, and asks her jointly with the Father to forgive a sin. Verses 3 and 4 are contiguous in the setting and are printed here without a break; the second half of verse 4 (“When my pilgrimage is ended, And the victor’s wreath I’ve won, Dearest mother, to your bosom Will you welcome home your son?”) is simply not carried.

notes: Verified verbatim against the archive.org page images of the engraved music on printed pp. 263–264 (item juvenileinstruct298geor, IA leaves 33–34), read directly rather than from OCR, because a music page sets each verse twice — once under the obligato solo staff and once under the “Voices Subdued” staff — with the lyrics broken into sung syllables. The two settings on the page were collated against each other and then against Cannon's 1895 reprint of verses 3–4 (see witnesses), and all three agree on the wording; the transcription here closes the syllable hyphens and runs the staff-by-staff line breaks together, with punctuation taken from the melody line. Provenance of the venue: the Juvenile Instructor was the organ of the Deseret Sunday School Union, edited by George Q. Cannon of the First Presidency, which is why an unofficial lyricist's hymn counts as historical-official here — and also why Cannon had to answer for it in print. Filed first in the pair so that cannon-female-deities-1895 can cite it. The hymn was never taken into a hymnbook.

title: B. H. Roberts: an endless line of Gods stretching back into the eternities
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: Member of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: A New Witness for God (Salt Lake City: George Q. Cannon & Sons, 1895), ch. XXX, p. 466

witnesses.scribe: Mormon Texts Project transcription of the 1895 first edition
witnesses.note: Independent full-text transcription; collated against the page scan and agrees word for word.

quotes.excerpt: But if God the Father was not always God, but came to his present exalted position by degrees of progress as indicated in the teachings of the prophet, how has there been a God from all eternity? The answer is that there has been and there now exists an endless line of Gods, stretching back into the eternities, that had no beginning and will have no end. Their existence runs parallel with endless duration, and their dominions are as limitless as boundless space.
quotes.note: The most explicit published chain statement by a General Authority in the nineteenth century, and note its logical role: Roberts offers the endless line as the solution to a problem the King Follett Discourse creates. If God was once a man, how has there been a God from all eternity? Because there has always been another one behind him. The regress here is a piece of apologetic repair work, not an independent revelation claim.

quotes.excerpt: D'ye think that you could ever, Through all eternity, Find out the generation Where Gods began to be?
quotes.note: Roberts prints W. W. Phelps's “If You Could Hie to Kolob” in full immediately after the prose statement, as the hymnodic form of the same claim. This is why the chain outlives the prose that carries it: the hymn stayed in the hymnbook long after General Authorities stopped writing sentences like the one above.

notes: Verified verbatim twice over against the 1895 first edition: the Internet Archive page scan (printed p. 466) and the Mormon Texts Project's independent transcription. Chapter XXX is titled “Evidence of Divine Inspiration in Joseph Smith Derived from the Prophet's Teaching in Regard to the Extent of the Universe, Man's Place in It and His Doctrine Respecting the Gods—Concluded”; the passage sits directly after Roberts's block quotation of the King Follett Discourse (see kfd-1844), which is what raises the question the endless line answers. Graded never-official: Roberts sat in the First Council of the Seventy and the book was issued by the church-affiliated George Q. Cannon & Sons, but it carried no First Presidency commission — unlike Talmage's Articles of Faith four years later — and it functioned as a missionary apologetic rather than as a doctrinal standard.

title: George Q. Cannon: “This language approaches to worship”
speaker: George Q. Cannon
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency; editor of the Juvenile Instructor (the column is bylined “The Editor”)
venue: “Topics of the Times: The Worship of Female Deities,” Juvenile Instructor 30, no. 10 (15 May 1895): 314–317

quotes.excerpt: Now, to my mind this is rank idolatry, and is as false as the worship of “the queen of heaven” was by the women of Judah in the days of Jeremiah. It is most dangerous doctrine to be taught to the rising generation of our people. If adopted as a belief and persisted in, it would undoubtedly lead to as dreadful consequeces in these days as it did to those who pursued a similar course in the days of the prophet Jeremiah.
quotes.note: Printed p. 315. Referent discipline matters here: “this” is Elizabeth Cady Stanton's proposal in The Woman's Bible — quoted by Cannon in the preceding column — that the rising generation recognise “an ideal Heavenly Mother, to whom their prayers should be addressed, as well as to a Father.” The column is triggered by a feminist reading of Genesis in a local paper, not by Latter-day Saint teaching, and it only turns on the Saints' own hymnody on the following page. “consequeces” is a compositor's error in the original and is preserved.

quotes.excerpt: That great care must be exercised among the Latter-day Saints upon this point there can scarcely be a question. The late Sister Eliza R. Snow composed a hymn which opens with “O my Father, thou that dwellest.” About a year ago a companion hymn to this invocation of Sister Snow's, entitled “Our Mother in Heaven,” was published in the Juvenile Instructor. In this hymn there is too much of this inclination to deify “our mother in heaven” manifested to make it such a hymn as ought to be sung and to become a household hymn among the Latter-day Saints. There is no ground to think that the author had any design to teach any wrong ideas when he wrote this hymn; neither did the publishers. But if the Editor's attention had been called to this before it appeared in the columns of the Juvenile Instructor, he would have suggested some changes.
quotes.note: Printed p. 316. The retraction proper, and notice its shape: the hymn is not condemned, its author is not accused, and Cannon concedes that the fault was editorial inattention — his own, since he was the editor. What is withdrawn is not the doctrine but the hymn's fitness to be sung, and specifically its fitness “to become a household hymn,” which is to say its fitness to do what “O My Father” had already done.

quotes.excerpt: This language approaches to worship. Our mother is called a “goddess bride.” But this is not all: she is appealed to with the Father to forgive her erring son. Poetical license may warrant the use of language to an extent that might be considered improper in prose; but, as Latter-day Saints, we cannot be too careful concerning the use of language that may lead to wrong impressions, especially regarding the Being whom we worship. In this poetry the mother is placed side by side and on an equality with the Father.
quotes.note: Printed p. 316, immediately after Cannon reprints verses 3 and 4 of the hymn. The three named faults are the boundary markers: calling her a goddess, addressing petition to her, and placing her “on an equality with the Father.” Note the phrase “Our mother” — Cannon says our mother, unhedged, in the same breath in which he forbids appealing to her. Existence is not what is at issue.

quotes.excerpt: We know also that our Father in heaven should be the object of our worship. He will not have any divided worship. We are commanded to worship Him, and Him only. In the revelation of God the Eternal Father to the Prophet Joseph Smith there was no revelation of the feminine element as part of the Godhead, and no idea was conveyed that any such element “was equal in power and glory with the masculine.” Therefore, we are warranted in pronouncing all tendencies to glorify the feminine element and to exalt it as part of the Godhead as wrong and untrue, not only because of the revelation of the Lord in our day, but because it has no warrant in scripture, and any attempt to put such a construction on the word of God is false and erroneous.
quotes.note: Printed p. 317, the column's conclusion. This is the reframe stated as a rule, and it is narrower than it is usually reported to be. Cannon denies two things — that the feminine element belongs to the Godhead, and that worship may be divided — and he grounds the denial on absence of revelation rather than on contrary revelation. He nowhere denies that Latter-day Saints have a Mother in heaven; he has called her “our mother” on the previous page. “and Him only” is italicised in the original.

notes: Verified verbatim against the archive.org page images of printed pp. 315, 316, and 317 (item juvenileinstruct3010geor, IA leaves 23–25), collated against the item's full text; the column heading and the byline “The Editor” come from the issue's own table of contents, which lists “Topics of the Times — The Worship of Female Deities — Fast Day and the Sacrament — Passing the Sacrament … The Editor 314.” The 314–317 span in the standard citation covers all three topics in the column; the Heavenly Mother material occupies pp. 314–317, and the hymn discussion pp. 316–317. Cannon was First Counselor to Wilford Woodruff and editor of the magazine, so this is the First Presidency correcting a church periodical in that periodical — the earliest clean retreat-and-reframe in the dataset, and the template for a boundary that gets redrawn in almost the same terms much later (compare hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991, which affirms the inference to a Mother in Heaven and forbids praying to her). Three conflation traps this entry should not be used to spring. First, the trigger is Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Woman's Bible, not Latter-day Saint teaching; the Harrison hymn is reached as a domestic application of an argument aimed outward. Second, Cannon does not deny Heavenly Mother's existence, and the dataset should not cite him for that. Third, the sanction is on worship and on Godhead membership, not on the generative doctrine — nothing in the column touches eternal increase or spirit birth, which continued to be taught without interruption.

title: Orson F. Whitney: “our eternal Father and Mother were once man and woman in mortality”
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Bishop of the Salt Lake City Eighteenth Ward (later a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles)
venue: Remarks made at the large Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday, May 12, 1895; printed in Woman's Exponent 24, no. 2 (June 15, 1895): 9–10

quotes.excerpt: Thirdly, that if we be the children of God; if it be true, as we have sung, and as I doubt not, that in the heavens parents are not single, but that we have a Mother as well as a Father there, then it follows that we, as the sons and daughters of God, bear within us the embryotic germs of Deity, and are capable by advancement, by progression, of becoming like our Father and our Mother in heaven; that it is possible, in other words, for man to become God, and if this be true, it teaches that there was a time when that being whom we now worship—that our eternal Father and Mother were once man and woman in mortality.
quotes.note: The rarest thing in the Heavenly Mother corpus: past mortality predicated of the Mother, in print, by name. Two things make it unusual. First, the direction of the argument — Whitney does not begin from the Snow couplet and extend it; he begins from the forward claim (we may become as God), treats it as established, and runs it backwards as an entailment, “and if this be true, it teaches that there was a time when…” That is the symmetry inference stated outright by the speaker rather than read into him, which is why it is tagged rather than confined to a note. Second, the Mother is carried through the whole inference on the same terms as the Father, so the mortality claim is joint. Tagged FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE only, not FATHER-BECAME-GOD: what Whitney asserts is that the Father and Mother were once mortal, and the attainment is present in the argument's structure rather than in a statement about them, which is exactly the line the bare-couplet precedent draws. Referent “father” because the enum has no joint value; the point of the quote is that the Mother is included, and the entry note says so. The hymn allusion — “as we have sung… that in the heavens parents are not single” — is a direct paraphrase of Eliza R. Snow, hence the citesId to o-my-father.

quotes.excerpt: Secondly, that Deity, which created man and woman, male and female, in its own image, after its own likeness, must of necessity involve and comprehend the male and female principles.
quotes.note: The second of the three thoughts Whitney draws from Genesis 1:26–27, and the premise the Mother claim rests on. Note the argument-form: Deity “must of necessity involve and comprehend” both principles, which is a deduction from the image-of-God text rather than an appeal to revelation. Same move Erastus Snow made in 1885 (snow-heavenly-mother-1885) and Joseph Fielding Smith would make in 1960 (jfs-agq-mother-in-heaven-1960) — the doctrine is defended from reason and scriptural inference throughout its history, which is the vulnerability the twentieth-century retreat later exploits.

quotes.excerpt: Progress is written upon everything that God has made. The stars that glitter in the blue vault of heaven are educated worlds, homes of the redeemed and glorified or of those who, like ourselves, yet hope for glorification. This earth is but one of millions of planets that have preceded it, and have become the habitations of the righteous
quotes.note: Plurality of worlds in the full nineteenth-century idiom, and note the temporal claim inside it: this earth is one of millions “that have preceded it.” A sequence of inhabited, glorified worlds stretching back before ours is the cosmological setting the backward inference in q1 assumes. Not tagged INFINITE-CHAIN — Whitney says the worlds are many and prior, not that the Gods over them form a line.

quotes.excerpt: These are well-known Mormon doctrines, and they ought to be well known Christian doctrines, for they are sustained by the Scriptures, which, when properly understood and interpreted, will be found to teach, by implication at least, these truths.
quotes.note: Untagged register datum, and the sentence that immediately follows q1. “Well-known Mormon doctrines” — in 1895 the divine mortality of the Heavenly Mother could be described from the Tabernacle stand as common knowledge and offered to Christendom as something it should adopt. Compare the handling a century later in hinckley-1997 and essay-2015. Note the small hedge that survives even here: the scriptures teach it “by implication at least.”

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive scan of the bound Woman's Exponent for 1895 (item exponent1895, IA leaf 41 = printed p. 9; the address continues onto p. 10). The masthead on that leaf reads “Vol. 24 … SALT LAKE CITY, UTAH, JUNE 15, 1895 … No. 2,” and the piece is headed “BISHOP O. F. WHITNEY” with the bracketed line “[Remarks made at the large Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday, May 12, 1895.]” Whitespace and line-break artifacts in the OCR have been normalized in the excerpts; no words are changed, and the printed spelling “embryotic” is preserved. Provenance chain: the target list flagged this item from Paulsen and Pulido, “‘A Mother There': A Survey of Historical Teachings about Mother in Heaven,” BYU Studies 50/1, p. 89 n.31 (https://corpus.noahairmet.com/b/50-1-0c17/89), whose summary — that Whitney taught both a Mother in Heaven and her mortal probation — is confirmed by the primary text quoted here. Correlation graded never-official: the Woman's Exponent was an independently produced periodical, edited and published by Latter-day Saint women without Church ownership, though closely associated with the Relief Society and freely printing General Authority remarks. The occasion matters: this is a Sunday Tabernacle meeting at which women spoke first (Whitney is introduced as following “the eloquent ladies who have already addressed you”), the topic in the room was woman suffrage, and Whitney's Heavenly Mother argument is offered as theological support for it. Hearsay graded A on the convention that published periodicals rate A, with the caveat that the Exponent prints an unsigned report of oral remarks delivered a month earlier and no reporter is named; the text is smooth and continuous and reads as a prepared transcript rather than as notes, but it is not a stenographic record and the wording should not be pressed word by word. This is the strongest single datum in the dataset for the Mother's past mortality, and it should be read against whitney-father-and-mother-1907, where the same man, now an apostle speaking in general conference, makes the Heavenly Mother argument again and drops the mortality half entirely.

title: B. H. Roberts in the Improvement Era: “God and the Father of God”
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: Member of the First Council of the Seventy; co-editor of the Improvement Era
venue: “Religious Faiths, X.—The Claims, Doctrines, and Organization of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, II.: The Doctrine of the Church in Respect of the Godhead,” Improvement Era 1, no. 10 (August 1898): 754–769

quotes.excerpt: I call special attention to the words written above in italics—“unto God and his Father,” which can only mean God and the Father of God, which certainly conveys the idea of a plurality of Gods.
quotes.note: Roberts's own sentence, not a quotation — his exegesis of Revelation 1:6 on printed p. 765. “God and the Father of God” is about as compact a statement of the backward direction as the nineteenth century produces, and it is offered as plain reading rather than as speculation. Note the proof-text: the same Revelation 1:6 move reappears in official curriculum 120 years later (see nt-manual-2018). The words “italics” and “unto God and his Father” are set in italic type in the original; the markup is flattened here, the wording untouched.

quotes.excerpt: Commenting on this text the prophet said: If Jesus Christ was the Son of God, and John discovered that God, the Father of Jesus Christ, had a Father, you may suppose that he had a Father also. Where was there ever a son without a father? And where was there ever a father without first being a son? Whenever did a tree or anything spring into existence without a progenitor? And everything comes in this way. Paul says that that which is earthly is in the likeness of that which is heavenly. Hence, if Jesus had a Father, can we not believe that he had a Father also? I despise the idea of being scared to death at such a doctrine, for the Bible is full of it.
quotes.note: Roberts's footnote §, running from the foot of p. 765 to the foot of p. 766, quoting Joseph Smith's Sermon in the Grove (16 June 1844) from Millennial Star 24:109 — the citation Roberts himself gives. This is the C-infinite reading rather than a bare C-indefinite one, and the recursion is carried by two clauses rather than by the famous first sentence: “where was there ever a father without first being a son?” makes every father a former son, and “Whenever did a tree or anything spring into existence without a progenitor? And everything comes in this way” generalises the rule with no terminus offered. Provenance is why this quote carries C rather than the entry's A: the Era printing is a published magazine, but the words are a scribal report of an 1844 sermon relayed through the Millennial Star. Two artifacts of the printed page preserved as found: the footnote closes with a quotation mark that was never opened after “the prophet said:”, and the “he” in “you may suppose that he had a Father also” is italicised in the original.

quotes.excerpt: An infinitude of worlds and systems of worlds rising one above the other in ever-increasing splendor in limitless space and eternal duration, would have, as a concomitant, an endless line of exalted men, to preside over and within them as priests, kings, patriarchs, Gods!
quotes.note: Printed p. 769, the article's peroration; the sentence begins at the foot of p. 768 (“How, then, would the teaching of the Prophet Joseph respecting the Gods rise to meet the conceptions of the extent and grandeur of the universe, as now known to our astronomers!”). Deliberately not tagged INFINITE-CHAIN: Roberts's “endless line” here runs sideways across a plurality of worlds, not backwards through a genealogy of divine fathers, and the entry's backward claims are carried by q1 and q2. The near-identical phrase three years earlier — “an endless line of Gods, stretching back into the eternities” (roberts-endless-line-1895) — is the genealogical one, and the difference between the two sentences is exactly the distinction this dataset exists to keep.

notes: Verified verbatim against the archive.org scan of Improvement Era 1, no. 10: the item's full text was collated word for word against the page images for printed pp. 765 and 769 (item improvementera110unse, IA leaves 67 and 71). The article was identified from the issue's own table of contents (“Religious Faiths, X. — The Claims, Doctrines and Organization of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, II., B. H. Roberts, 754”) and from the byline on p. 754; the running head is “Religious Faiths” and the section heading is “The Doctrine of the Church in Respect of the Godhead.” Why the venue matters: the masthead of this issue lists Jos. F. Smith — then Second Counselor in the First Presidency — and B. H. Roberts as editors, and the magazine is styled the organ of the Young Men's Mutual Improvement Associations, published by the General Board. So the strongest divine-ancestry statement in a nineteenth-century church periodical was printed by an author who was also one of the magazine's editors, alongside a member of the First Presidency. On p. 764 Roberts footnotes his own “New Witness for God, Ch. XXX” — the chapter carrying the 1895 endless-line passage — which is why roberts-endless-line-1895 is named in citesId alongside sermon-grove-1844.

title: James E. Talmage: a God who is Himself progressive
speaker: James E. Talmage
office: Author writing under commission of the First Presidency (ordained an Apostle 1911)
venue: The Articles of Faith, Lecture XXIV, “Practical Religion” (1899 first edition, p. 442)

quotes.excerpt: We believe in a God who is Himself progressive, whose majesty is intelligence; whose perfection consists in eternal advancement; the perpetual work of whose creation stands “finished, yet renewed forever;”—a Being who has attained His exalted state by a path which now His children are permitted to follow; whose glory it is their heritage to share.
quotes.note: Affirmation — the canonical statement of ongoing divine progression in an officially commissioned doctrinal work. Contrast Talmage in the April 1915 Conference Report (“was once a Man, and has progressed … to His present position”), which is completed past progression, not this claim — the same apostle, sixteen years apart, saying two different things that sound identical.

quotes.excerpt: In spite of the opposition of all other sects, in the face of direct charges of blasphemy, the Church proclaims the eternal truth, “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.”
quotes.note: The Snow couplet proclaimed as “eternal truth” against blasphemy charges — a useful register datum for 1899 confidence, three sentences after the progression claim. 1899 first-edition wording (“all other sects”); the 10th edition (1917) reads “all the sects.”

notes: Text verified against the printed lecture. The book was prepared and published under First Presidency commission and served as a semi-official doctrinal standard for decades; it is not current curriculum. Edition caveat: wording and pagination verified against the 1899 first-edition scan (archive.org articlesoffaiths1899talm) after the GSA copy proved to be a post-1917 revision presenting as 1899.

witnesses.scribe: Gospel Scholar Archive copy
witnesses.note: Reflowed modern ebook carrying only the first-edition preface but a post-1917 text; do not quote 1899 wording from it. See talmage-af-kingdom-excision-1917 for the documented edition changes.

title: George Q. Cannon: “the power of procreation is promised”
speaker: George Q. Cannon
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, first day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1899, pp. 17–21)

quotes.excerpt: That the man who has done his duty in his sphere here on the earth faithfully will have an enlarged sphere hereafter; will have greater power, more opportunities for development; shall have every God-like power; every power and attribute that we have derived from our ancestry—that is, from God our Eternal Father. We shall have room for infinite gratification, unlimited gratification, going on from one degree of power to another, and exercising it as our Father exercises it in the midst of the eternities.
quotes.note: The run-up, kept untagged on purpose. “Every God-like power” and “exercising it as our Father exercises it” is theosis at full strength and asserts nothing generative by itself — the A-framing trap, handled the same way as whitney-father-and-mother-1907-q3. What makes the passage matter is that Cannon then names the power. Printed p. 20.

quotes.excerpt: If I have children; if I have a wife, I shall have them in eternity. I shall preside over that family no matter how small it may be, or how large it may extend. They will be my kingdom; for this is the promise of God. … that that union shall be perpetuated throughout eternity, and that there shall be an increase of that love and of that union and an increase also of that power, because the power of procreation is promised—the greatest power that man possesses on the earth. That is promised unto those who are faithful.
quotes.note: The naming. “Increase” is not left as a euphemism for one sentence longer than it takes to say what it is: the power of procreation, identified as the same power man possesses on earth, promised to the faithful. This is why the entry is FORWARD-EXPLICIT rather than FORWARD-EUPHEMISM. Elision covers Cannon's intervening sentence about those with whom our lives are entwined. Printed p. 20.

quotes.excerpt: Therefore, it can be said of us as it was said of our Lord and Savior, "to the increase of His kingdom there shall be no end." Why? Because of this principle that I spoke of—the principle of procreation. By it, and through that principle the worlds are peopled. The planetary orbs which stud our heavens so gloriously are peopled by that principle—the principle of procreation. God possesses it, and we as His children inherit the power. If we do what is right He promises to bestow it upon us.
quotes.note: The cosmological reach, in three sentences: procreation peoples the worlds, God possesses it, and His children inherit it. MANY-WORLDS is earned outright — “the planetary orbs which stud our heavens.” Note what is *not* here, and why the entry stops where it does: Cannon never says spirit children and never describes a premortal birth, so SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS would be retrojection even though the mechanism claim in q4 points that way. What he says is that the peopling of worlds runs on the principle we already know. Printed p. 20.

quotes.excerpt: I know the world say this is materialistic; that we take wrong views of this; that we are not spiritual enough. Well, I am willing to have that charge levelled against me. I want to be materialistic in this sense. I want to enjoy that which we enjoy here, purified, exalted, and increased beyond my comprehension or your comprehension at the present time; and we are to have this glory and this power; the Lord promises it unto us.
quotes.note: Marked implied because the antecedent of “that which we enjoy here” is supplied by the previous sentences rather than restated — but the antecedent is unambiguous in context, and this is the closest Cannon comes to a mechanism: not a new power but the earthly one continued, “purified, exalted, and increased.” The register is worth as much as the doctrine. The materialism charge is anticipated, embraced, and answered from the pulpit at general conference by a member of the First Presidency, in the same conference year Talmage published the Articles of Faith. Printed p. 20.

notes: Verified word-for-word against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (item conferencereport1899a, file conferencereport691chur_djvu.txt; the address runs printed pp. 17–21 and every excerpt above is on p. 20), not merely against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1899/1899-04-cannon-scriptures-and-living-revelation.md. That distinction matters here: the vault transcription of this talk renders nearly every sentence-final period as an em dash, a systematic transcription artifact that is not in the printed page, so the excerpts above follow the scan rather than the vault. OCR line-break hyphenation removed and spacing around dashes normalized; two OCR misreadings in the quoted span ("gloriouslv", "sixtj'-nine") corrected against the surrounding text. No words changed. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. The address is a survey of what the Restoration has done for the world in sixty-nine years — the printed subject line above it reads "The great and beneficent physical and spiritual effects brought to the world by the organization of the Church" — and the peroration on procreation arrives as the answer to "what has the organization of this Church done for us in regard to the future?", not as a doctrinal excursus. It is the sixty-ninth anniversary of the Church's organization to the day, which is what "sixty-nine years ago today" in the closing paragraphs fixes the date on. Read directly against cannon-female-deities-1895: four years earlier the same man, in the same office, shut down a Heavenly Mother hymn as approaching worship, and the 1895 entry's third caveat — that the sanction fell on worship and Godhead membership, not on the generative doctrine — is confirmed here in the plainest possible way. Cannon preaches procreation as an inherited divine power in general conference with no hedge at all.

title: Nels L. Nelson: how our Father became God
speaker: Nels L. Nelson
office: Professor of English, Brigham Young University
venue: Scientific Aspects of Mormonism; or, Religion in Terms of Life (New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1904), ch. XXV “Jehovah,” pp. 273–274, and ch. XXVI “How Our Father Became God,” pp. 275–276

quotes.excerpt: As respects the eternal principles underlying His purposes, He never changes; these form the very warp and woof of His divine perfection; but as respects the methods or devices for bringing about these purposes, He changes as the exigency requires; and the variations possible to His invention are practically infinite… It is by reason of this very principle of mutation in God that we perceive all things to be in a state of evolution here on earth.
quotes.note: Affirmation — but a bounded one, and the boundary has to be quoted with it. Nelson's God changes in method, not in principle, and the sentences just above hold that on attaining Godhood “how could He be other than immutable?
