For change would then imply degeneracy.” Lifting “this very principle of mutation in God” out of that setting produces a stronger divine-progression claim than Nelson makes.

quotes.excerpt: But since by this conception He is made to belong to the same order of beings as Christ, His Son,—the same order, indeed, as man himself,—and must consequently have attained to Godhood or creative power, it becomes a pertinent question to consider how He reached such divine sovereignty.
quotes.note: The chapter's opening question, carried as context because it is routinely quoted as though it were the chapter's answer. Note the original begins “But since by this conception…” — the concessive “But” is part of the sentence and is preserved here.

quotes.excerpt: A sufficient general answer, therefore, would be that God became God because He fulfilled the law of becoming perfect as His Father in heaven was perfect; or, in the terms of science, because He fulfilled the supreme requirements of psychic evolution.
quotes.note: Explicit divine parentage — “His Father in heaven,” a phrase Nelson builds by turning Matthew 5:48 back on God himself — with no chain length stated and no interest in stating one. The gloss “psychic evolution” is the Spencerian idiom that marks this whole cluster of Utah writers.

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive scan of the 1904 Putnam's first edition (item scientificaspect00nelsrich), reading continuously from printed p. 273 through p. 276 so the page breaks between the three quotes are known rather than assumed: the divine-progression material closes ch. XXV at pp. 273–274, and ch. XXVI “How Our Father Became God” opens at p. 275 with the question and answers it on pp. 275–276. Nelson was a BYU English professor writing for a national trade press, not for the Church; never-official. He is one of the few authors in the dataset who is both a backward-explicit source and a divine-progression source, which is precisely why his two claims should not be merged into one: the parentage is asserted, the ongoing mutability is heavily qualified, and neither entails the other.

title: B. H. Roberts, The Seventy's Course in Theology
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: One of the seven Presidents of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: Seventy's Course in Theology (five volumes); later The Truth, The Way, The Life

quotes.excerpt: It is customary for us to say, that there are three grand estates of existence through which intelligencies pass in the course of their exaltation to resurrected, immortal, divine beings…: first, their pre-existence as spirits, sons and daughters of God, in the spirit world; second, these spirits clothed upon with mortal bodies—earth-life of men and women; third, spirits inhabiting bodies that have been resurrected, immortal beings clothed with imperishable bodies prepared for eternal advancement in the kingdoms of God. But the doctrine of the Prophet and of the scriptures he gave to the world, require us to recognize before the first estate as set forth in the above order, the existence of the self-existent intelligencies before they are begotten spirits, sons and daughters of God. So that it could be said that there are four estates in which intelligencies exist instead of three; namely; self-existent, uncreated and unbegotten intelligencies, co-eternal with God; second, intelligencies begotten of God spirits; third, spirits begotten men and women, still sons and daughters of God; fourth, resurrected beings, immortal spirits inhabiting imperishable bodies, still sons and daughters of God, and in the line of eternal progression, up to the attainment of divine attributes and powers.
quotes.note: The framework stated as an amendment, which is the thing worth seeing. Roberts is not reporting a received three-stage model; he is arguing that the customary three estates are one short and that an uncreated intelligence must be recognised *before* the spirit. Printed pp. 11–12, note 7, headed “Effect of the Doctrine of the Eternal Existence of Intelligences on Our Terminology.” Elision covers a parenthetical cross-reference to Jaques's Catechism, ch. vi. The printed text really does read “namely;” with a semicolon and omits “first,” before the opening member of the list — verified against the page image, not the OCR. Roberts then offers the concession that has made the model portable ever since: counting changes rather than statuses, “we may still say that so far as the matter has been revealed there are three estates.”

quotes.excerpt: The difference, then, between “spirits” and “intelligencies,” as here used, is this: Spirits are uncreated intelligencies inhabiting spiritual bodies; while “intelligencies,” pure and simple, are intelligent entities, but unembodied in either spirit bodies or bodies of flesh and bone. They are uncreated, self-existent entities, possessed of “self-consciousness,” and “other-consciousness”—they are conscious of the “me” and the “not me”; they possess powers of discrimination… they discern between the evil and the good; between the “good” and “the better.”
quotes.note: The definition the whole framework rests on, printed p. 11, note 6. This is the tier that is *not* begotten, and it is why the entry carries SPIRIT-BIRTH-ADOPTION alongside the begetting quotes below: on Roberts's account what is born in the pre-existence is a body, and what inhabits it was never made. Compare abraham-3 and kfd-1844, which supply the uncreatedness he is systematising.

quotes.excerpt: “This body which ye now behold is the body of my spirit”—the house, the tenement of that uncreated intelligence which had been begotten of the Father a spirit, as later that spirit-body with the intelligent, uncreated entity inhabiting it, will be begotten a man.
quotes.note: The three stages compressed into a single sentence, printed p. 10, note 6, reasoning from Ether 3:16 and Christ's spirit body outward to all men. Roberts's verb is “begotten” at both transitions, which is why this quote takes the begetting tag and q2 takes the adoption tag: the two are not in tension for him, they are the two halves of the synthesis. No physiology is described anywhere in the lesson — the gestational mechanism that later attaches to this model comes from Melvin J. Ballard, not from here (see ballard-increase and eom-premortal-life-1992).

quotes.excerpt: According to this, then, there is a “Father of Spirits.” It follows, of course, that “spirits” have a father—they are begotten… Fatherhood to spirits is manifestly a relationship established independent of man's earth-existence; and, of course, in an existence which preceded earth-life, where the uncreated intelligences are begotten spirits.
quotes.note: Printed p. 14, Lesson II, note 2, arguing from Hebrews 12:9. The closing clause is the framework's load-bearing formula — “the uncreated intelligences are begotten spirits” — an uncreated subject undergoing a real begetting. Roberts is explicit that Paul's “Father of spirits” cannot mean “Fathers of our flesh,” so the fatherhood is premortal and literal.

notes: Placeholder closed in v2 against the printed volumes. The excerpts are from The Seventy's Course in Theology, Second Year: Outline History of the Dispensations of the Gospel (Salt Lake City: Skelton Publishing Co., 1908), Part I, “Prelude to the Dispensations,” Lesson I (“Intelligencies and Spirits”) notes 3–7 and Lesson II notes 1–2, printed pp. 8–14 — read from the Gospel Scholar Archive copy of the collected Course (PDF pp. 278–284) with pp. 10, 11, 12 and 14 additionally checked against the rendered page images, since the OCR layer of this volume introduces stray commas and hyphenation at line breaks. Line-break hyphenation is closed up; one stray comma in the OCR (“spiritual, bodies”) is not in the print and has been dropped. Roberts's own footnote to Lesson I records where the material came from and settles the status question: the notes are taken from his article “Immortality of Man,” Improvement Era, April 1907 — the Era being, in the volume's own words, “the Organ of the Seventies and of the Young Men's Mutual Improvement Associations” — and the Era printed it with the editorial line, “Elder Roberts submitted the following paper to the First Presidency and a number of the Twelve Apostles, none of whom found anything objectionable in it, or contrary to the revealed word of God, and therefore favor its publication.” correlationStatus is therefore changed from never-official to historical-official, matching roberts-progress-of-god-1911: rationale — the Year Books were prepared by Roberts in his office as President of the First Council of the Seventy, copyrighted “for the First Council of Seventy,” and prescribed as the study course for Seventies quorums, and this particular material had been read by the First Presidency and members of the Twelve before publication, so grading the same series two different ways cannot be defended on the evidence. That grade is about the standing of the *source*, not the canonical standing of the *claim*: the four-estate scheme was never canonised, Roberts himself presents it as a correction to customary usage, and Joseph Fielding Smith attacks it by implication in 1963 (see jfs-agq-intelligences-1963). One housekeeping note for the maintainer: the excerpts are from the 1908 Second Year volume, so the entry's 1907–1911 range still covers them, but venue could be tightened to name the Second Year specifically.

title: Orson F. Whitney: a Mother in heaven defended as philosophy
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1907)

quotes.excerpt: Why, then, should it be deemed unphilosophic for man, the child of God, — man and woman, male and female, — to become like their Father and their Mother in heaven? We are at the defiance of the world to prove this doctrine unphilosophical.
quotes.note: A Mother in heaven asserted in passing and then used as a premise, which is the tell: Whitney does not argue for her, he assumes her and dares the world to refute the package. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER only. “Become like their Father and their Mother in heaven” is theosis, not generative exaltation, and carries no FORWARD tag by itself — the A-framing trap. Spacing before the question mark normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed.

quotes.excerpt: You earthly parents expect your children to become men and women like yourselves. You know that it is only a question of time, when, if they live, your little toddling children will become men and women, and will marry and have children of their own.
quotes.note: Marked implied. The sentence is literally about mortal children. But it is the immediate warrant for the claim in q1 — the analogy is offered so that the hearer will complete it — and what completes it is offspring, not merely likeness. Whitney stops one step short of saying so, so the forward-generative reading is carried as read-into rather than stated.

quotes.excerpt: It revealed anew the sublime fact that man is verily the child of Deity, and can become, by development, like unto his Father and his God. It taught the great truth that man is divinity in embryo, and capable, by education, through human experience, and by obedience to the principles of eternal progress, of rising to the plane whereon stands the Universal Father, who desires to make His children equal with Himself, and to put into their possession all things.
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose. “Divinity in embryo,” “equal with Himself,” “rising to the plane whereon stands the Universal Father” — this is theosis at full nineteenth-century strength and it still asserts nothing about spirit offspring or about a chain behind the Father. Recorded so the entry shows what Whitney does and does not claim in the same breath.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1907/1907-10-whitney-defending-the-saints.md, whose Final Review collated the full body against the archive.org scan conferencereport1907sa, leaves n45–n53, word for word against the printed page. A heavyweight pass had earlier split a separate George F. Richards address out of this file and re-anchored the leaf, so the URL points at where Whitney's own remarks begin. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. No hymn quotation appears in this talk, which is why the entry carries no citesId — Whitney reaches the Mother without Eliza R. Snow, through the same argument from nature that Erastus Snow used in 1885 (see snow-heavenly-mother-1885), but stripped of the anatomy and recast as a reply to outside critics. The setting matters: the talk is an apologetic defense of the Saints “against calumny and misrepresentation,” and the Heavenly Mother claim is deployed as an asset rather than defended as an embarrassment. Read against packer-parentage-1984 and hinckley-1997, which handle the same apologetic pressure by subtraction.

title: Heber C. Iverson: the hymn credited to Joseph Smith's inspiration
speaker: Heber C. Iverson
office: Bishop of the Second Ward
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon overflow session (Conference Report, April 1908, pp. 69–72)

quotes.excerpt: In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there.
quotes.note: The couplet as printed in the Conference Report; Iverson quotes the first three stanzas and stops here. Spacing before the question mark, semicolon and exclamation point normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed. See o-my-father.

quotes.excerpt: That doctrine was ridiculed seventy years ago, when announced by this hymn, teaching what had been given by inspiration flowing first through the mind of the Prophet Joseph Smith, that we have a mother in heaven.
quotes.note: The provenance claim that the whole later tradition rests on, made explicit from the pulpit: the hymn is not Eliza R. Snow's poetic inference but a vehicle for revelation given first to Joseph Smith. Set this beside snow-heavenly-mother-1885, where an apostle says the opposite in as many words — “it is left for us to infer this” — and beside hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991, where the argument has shrunk to the observation that Joseph made no correction to what Sister Snow had written. The date arithmetic is loose: “seventy years ago” from 1908 lands in 1838, while the poem was published in 1845.

quotes.excerpt: He discourses very learnedly upon the dual sequence of the term Elohim, and proves conclusively by his deduction that there is a feminine element existing with the Deity, and that we have in Deity a mother as well as a father. There are mothers of our spirits.
quotes.note: Two things worth having. First, the corroboration is outside and secular — an unnamed writer in “one of the leading magazines of this country” arguing from the plural form of Elohim — which is a Latter-day Saint apostle-era bishop reaching for a non-Mormon philologist to underwrite a Mormon doctrine. Second, and easy to miss, the plural: “There are mothers of our spirits.” Iverson slides from one Mother to many without remark, twenty years after the Manifesto and in a Church still living with plural marriage, and the plural never becomes a doctrine anyone defends.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1908/1908-04-iverson-rejoicing-and-responsibility.md, whose heavyweight pass verified the talk boundary, speaker, session and supplied title against the archive.org Conference Report scan conferencereport1908a at printed pages 69–72, and whose Final Review pass is recorded as complete. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. Filed as an original rather than a citation, with citesId preserving the edge to o-my-father: the hymn is quoted at length, but the entry's value is the three claims Iverson builds around it — that the doctrine came by inspiration through Joseph Smith, that a secular philologist independently confirms it, and that our spirits have mothers plural — none of which is in the hymn. He is a ward bishop speaking in an overflow session, so this is not authoritative teaching; it is evidence of what a well-read local leader took the hymn to have settled, which for the reception history is the more useful thing.

title: First Presidency, “The Origin of Man”
speaker: Joseph F. Smith, John R. Winder, Anthon H. Lund
office: First Presidency
venue: Improvement Era (official statement)

quotes.excerpt: All men and women are in the similitude of the universal Father and Mother and are literally the sons and daughters of Deity… man, as a spirit, was begotten and born of heavenly parents and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father, prior to coming upon the earth in a temporal body to undergo an experience in mortality.
quotes.note: The strongest viviparous statement in the corpus, and the only one that says both begotten and born.

quotes.excerpt: Man is the child of God, formed in the divine image and endowed with divine attributes, and even as the infant son of an earthly father and mother is capable in due time of becoming a man, so the undeveloped offspring of celestial parentage is capable, by experience through ages and aeons, of evolving into a God.
quotes.note: Tagged BACKWARD-MORTALITY per the v2 revision, but flagging a tension for review: as excerpted, the sentence runs forward (man evolving into a God), not backward (God having been man). It reads as a First Presidency forward-progression claim — arguably FORWARD-EUPHEMISM, since no mechanism is named — and only yields a backward claim by running the couplet's inference in reverse. Confirm the exact wording against the 1909 Improvement Era text, then settle the tag. Retag resolved: with BACKWARD-MORTALITY retired, this moves to FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than onto the Father axis. The sentence runs forward — man evolving into a God, no mechanism named — and never claims the Father was mortal. Confirm the Improvement Era wording; if it does contain a backward clause, move it to FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE.

quotes.excerpt: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, basing its belief on divine revelation, ancient and modern, proclaims man to be the direct and lineal offspring of Deity. God Himself is an exalted man, perfected, enthroned, and supreme.
quotes.note: Two paragraphs above the quoted closer, and the answer to the entry's own open question: the 1909 statement does carry a plain Father-status claim, in a different sentence than the one q2 examines. q2 stays FORWARD-EUPHEMISM.

notes: Verify quote 2's wording before relying on it; if confirmed it makes 1909 a stronger forward-progression statement than it is usually remembered as being. The February 2002 Ensign reprint is filed separately as a citation — its timing, five years after the Hinckley interviews, is the datum.

title: B. H. Roberts: God's immutability does not exclude advancement or progress of God
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: Member of the First Council of the Seventy (senior President from 1924)
venue: The Seventy's Course in Theology, Fourth Year: The Atonement (Salt Lake City: The Deseret News, 1911), 69–70

witnesses.scribe: Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression: Two Complementary Ways to Talk About God,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 41 (GSA scan p. 43), citing The Seventy's Course in Theology (Deseret News Press, 1911), 69–70
witnesses.note: England's catalogue entry, which is what led here; his reproduction is lowercase OCR and drops the “so” from “should not be so understood.” The excerpts below are from the Roberts volume, not from England.

quotes.excerpt: But God's immutability should not be so understood as to exclude the idea of advancement or progress of God. Thus, for example: God's kingdom and glory may be enlarged, as more and more redeemed souls are added to his kingdom: as worlds and world-systems are multiplied and redeemed and enrolled with celestial spheres, so God's kingdom is enlarged and his glory increased. So that in this sense there may come change and progress even for God.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the ground it stands on matters: Roberts derives divine progress from the enlargement of God's kingdom and glory — the very same “dominions, not knowledge” move that Bruce R. McConkie would later use to *deny* progression (see mcconkie-heresies-1980 and millet-mcconkie-life-beyond-1986). The difference is that Roberts does not stop there; see the next quote.

quotes.excerpt: an absolute immutability would require eternal immobility—which would reduce God to a condition eternally static, which, from the nature of things, would bar him from participation in that enlargement of kingdom and increasing glory that comes from redemption and the progress of men.
quotes.note: The argument stated negatively: an unqualified immutability is not reverence but paralysis. The same stagnation-is-death reasoning runs through Hugh B. Brown's April 1956 conference address (see brown-deify-man-1956), where it has been transferred from God to man.

quotes.excerpt: So with the All-knowing attribute, Omniscience: that must be understood somewhat in the same light as the other attributes considered: not that God is Omniscient up to the point that further progress in knowledge is impossible to him; but that all knowledge that is, all that exists, God knows.
quotes.note: The sharper half of the claim, and the one England does not quote: Roberts takes progression into knowledge, not merely dominion. This is the precise proposition Joseph Fielding Smith calls “very dangerous” forty-three years later (jfsmith-doctrines-salvation-1954) and McConkie calls a deadly heresy in 1980, and it is here in a Church-published quorum study course written by the President of the First Council of the Seventy.

notes: Verified by pulling the printed pages themselves from the Gospel Scholar Archive copy of the collected Seventy's Course in Theology (PDF pp. 802–804 = printed pp. 68–70 of Year Book IV), and confirming from the volume's own title page (PDF p. 727) that the 1911 Deseret News imprint England cites is Fourth Year: The Atonement. Line-break hyphenation has been closed up; one phrase carrying scan damage is elided. The passage sits in a numbered section headed “7. Limitation in the Attributes of God,” immediately after Roberts's treatments of Omnipotence, Omniscience and Omnipresence, and is footnoted to a long quotation from Sir Oliver Lodge — the philosophical provenance England and Matthew Bowman both trace to Herbert Spencer-era British thought. correlationStatus is graded historical-official here because the Year Books were prepared by Roberts as a member of the First Council of the Seventy, so styled on the volume's own title page, issued by the Church's own press, and used as the prescribed course of study for Seventies quorums; note that the existing bh-roberts-tripartite entry grades the same series never-official, and the two should be reconciled by the maintainer rather than left divergent. This entry is deliberately *not* the tripartite-framework entry: bh-roberts-tripartite covers intelligence → spirit → body and still needs its own excerpt pulled from the Year Books; this one covers only the progression claim.

title: Charles W. Penrose: the gift of endless, perpetual increase
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, October 1911, pp. 48–54)

quotes.excerpt: One of the grand things referred to by President Smith as in the revelations of God to the Prophet Joseph, was the eternity of the marriage covenant, by which the man and the woman may be joined together according to God's order, and though death may part them, yet in the resurrection they shall come forth to be husband and wife, to be parents of children, to have the gift of endless, perpetual increase, the beginning of their kingdom and their glory in worlds without end. That is real life, the power to continue and the power to produce and to increase, the power of vitality in the spirit and in the body.
quotes.note: Explicit rather than euphemistic: resurrected couples are named as “parents of children,” and the increase is qualified twice over as endless and perpetual. “Worlds without end” here is the liturgical idiom for eternity, not a claim about plural worlds, so MANY-WORLDS is not applied. The Conference Report OCR prints “bv President Smith”; corrected to “by,” a scan artifact, with no other change to the wording.

quotes.excerpt: And those who follow in the footsteps of Jesus Christ, who is now to all purposes like the Father, will inherit similar glory, and it will never fade away, and it will be exemplified in them to the full. The spirit of life will be within them in body and in spirit, and they will increase forever and ever, and like the blessing that comes to our elder brother, Jesus Christ, of the increase of their kingdom there shall be no end.
quotes.note: The forward chain closed against Christ's own case: the exalted inherit what the Son inherited, and the increase of their kingdom is unending. The vault transcription prints a stray period in “elder .brother,” an OCR artifact of the printed column; removed here, wording otherwise untouched.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1911/1911-10-15-charles-w-penrose-remarks-15.md. Conference Report, so A. That file has an unusually heavy repair history — two long passages were scrambled by two-column OCR and were later de-interleaved directly against the archive.org page images (leaves n48–n56, printed pp. 48–54) — but neither quoted passage falls inside the repaired blocks, and both read cleanly apart from the two isolated scan artifacts noted on the quotes. Two corrections to how this source is usually described. First the date: the pulpit report gives 6 October, but the vault frontmatter and the printed session heading place it in the second day afternoon session, 7 October 1911. Second the office: he is frequently cited as First Presidency here, but Penrose was not called as a counselor until December 1911, so in October he was still of the Twelve. Why it matters: this is post-Manifesto, official, and undiminished. Twenty-one years after plural marriage ended, the full generative package is preached in general conference without hedging — which is the evidence that the early twentieth century softened the vocabulary of deification, not the doctrine of increase.

title: George F. Richards: God “has become what He is” by obedience unto law and authority
speaker: George F. Richards
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning overflow meeting (Conference Report, April 1913)

quotes.excerpt: We are His children in very deed, having been born of Him in the spirit, and we have inherited the very attributes which He possesses. They are in us, and they make us God's embryo. We believe that as we are now God once was, and by the practice of virtue and righteousness, by obedience unto law and authority, He has become what He is, and as He is, man may become, on the same principle.
quotes.note: Three claims in one breath, and the middle one is what makes the entry worth having. The couplet is not left bare: Richards supplies the mechanism on both ends of it — God “has become what He is” by the practice of virtue and by obedience unto law and authority, and man ascends “on the same principle.” That is FATHER-BECAME-GOD on top of FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE under the Father-status precedent, and it puts a lawful, earned theogony in an April 1913 general conference. Referent is the Father throughout: the God who once was as we are is the same God of whom we are “born … in the spirit” two sentences earlier. The spirit-birth tag is for the birth language itself (“born of Him in the spirit,” “born of God”); no physiology is described, so this sits with the 1916 exposition rather than with the 1909 statement in explicitness. Printed reading retained: the Conference Report has “they make us God's embryo,” where the same speaker says “gods in embryo” in October 1914 (richards-gods-in-embryo-1914); the singular may be a compositor's or scan artifact but it survives Final Review against the scan, so it is quoted as printed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1913/1913-04-24-george-f-richards-remarks-24.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1913a, leaves n81–n84, running head “ELDER GEORGE F. RICHARDS.”) and Final-Reviewed by column reading-order reconstruction against the same scan with no body change required. Conference Report, so A. The vault frontmatter gives the generic “General Authority”; Richards had been ordained an Apostle in April 1906 and was of the Twelve in 1913. He presided at this overflow meeting, which is why the address closes the session rather than appearing in the Tabernacle sequence. Context worth carrying: the couplet arrives inside a sermon whose entire argument is obedience to law — the elements obey, man alone does not — so the theogony is stated as a corollary of the obedience thesis rather than as a doctrinal excursus, which is how it has stayed invisible in most sweeps of this decade.

title: Orson F. Whitney: souls “capable of endless increase,” and the things even God cannot do
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, October 1913)

quotes.excerpt: And yet, through that transgression, and the consequent fall of man, God's purpose was accomplished, in the coming of a race of spirits to take upon themselves bodies, thus becoming souls, capable of endless increase and everlasting progression.
quotes.note: Euphemism in the strict sense: “endless increase” is named as a capacity conferred by embodiment, and nothing in the sentence says what is increased — no offspring, no spirit children, no mechanism. What the passage does add is a reason: it is the body that makes the increase possible, which is the argument Whitney builds the whole fall-and-atonement section on. The surrounding definitions are the setting — “Exaltation is salvation added upon; it is an extension of that idea or condition, just as salvation is an extension of redemption” — and a few lines later he says, without comment, that “The most profitable work that men or gods can engage in is the salvation of souls,” a plural that is left entirely unexplained.

quotes.excerpt: There is nothing possible of achievement that God cannot do, but there may be things that He has not time to do, and which may be done for Him. There are some things, however, that even God cannot do. I speak it with all reverence. For instance, He cannot make something out of nothing, though many pious Christians ascribe to Him that power — if such it can be called. There is another thing that God cannot do — He cannot be present in all places at the same time, in His own proper person.
quotes.note: Deliberately untagged, and the restraint is the point. An apostle enumerating what God cannot do sits in the same 1913–16 argument as jfs-ignoramuses-1914 and jfs-he-knows-all-1916, but the propositions are not the same one: Whitney denies creation ex nihilo and personal omnipresence, neither of which says anything about whether God still progresses in knowledge or power. Tagging this DIVINE-PROGRESSION would be trap #4 — a limit on God read as a claim about God's growth. Kept because the register is evidence: this is what a Latter-day Saint apostle could say about divine limitation from the pulpit six months before the President of the Church called the men who limit God “learned fools.”

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1913/1913-10-37-orson-f-whitney-remarks-37.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1913sa, leaves n97–n100, running head “ELDER ORSON F. WHITNEY.”) and Final-Reviewed against the same scan at 0.959 similarity with all candidates resolved as scan noise; the vault's earlier draft had truncated the second half of the talk at a page boundary and it was restored in the heavyweight pass, so quote 2 comes from text that is present only in the repaired file. Conference Report, so A. The vault frontmatter gives the generic “General Authority”; Whitney had been ordained an Apostle in April 1906. Note what this entry does not contain: no Heavenly Mother, though Whitney is the apostle most associated with that argument in 1907 (whitney-father-and-mother-1907) and returns to it in 1920 (whitney-mother-in-heaven-1920).

title: Joseph F. Smith: “a few ignoramuses, ‘learned fools’” who limit God to the capacity of man
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference opening address, first day morning session (Conference Report, April 1914)

quotes.excerpt: It is true that we have, now and then, here and there, occasionally, persons who would, if they possibly could, limit the power, the knowledge, the wisdom of God Almighty, to the capacity of men. We have a few of them among us, and some of them have been, and may be, school teachers.
quotes.note: Denial, and the one detail that fixes its target: “school teachers.” This is 1914, three years after the Brigham Young University modernism dismissals, and the finite-God, God-still-learning position was being taught by Church educators — compare nelson-scientific-aspects-1904, written by a BYU professor. The claim being rejected is that God's knowledge and power are bounded by what man can conceive.

quotes.excerpt: I say again that there are just a few ignoramuses, “learned fools,” if you please, who would make you believe, if they could, that Almighty God is limited in His power to the capacity of man. Don't you believe it, not for one moment.
quotes.note: Denial, in the register the phrase is famous for. Read the intervening text before using it as a straight progression datum: the specific charges Smith enumerates are that the miracles were “mere symbols,” that Christ could not turn water into wine or walk on water, and that the Father and Son did not appear to Joseph Smith in person. The proposition on the page is a denial of miracle and of divine omnipotence, not the technical claim that God is still acquiring knowledge; “the knowledge, the wisdom” of the previous quote is the only part that reaches the progression question directly.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1914/1914-04-00-smith-opening-address.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1914a, leaves n2–n10) and Final-Reviewed against an independent column-order reconstruction of the same scan. Conference Report, so A. The talk was missing from the vault's original ingest and was recovered whole in a later pass, which is why it does not appear in earlier sweeps of the 1914 conference. Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 40, files this under the deniers of divine progression alongside Joseph Fielding Smith; the excerpt is taken from the Conference Report rather than from England's lowercase OCR rendering, and the note above records where England's framing runs ahead of what the printed text says. The pairing that makes the entry worth having is chronological: Roberts publishes the progression claim in a Church-issued priesthood course in 1911, and the President of the Church calls its holders learned fools from the pulpit in 1914.

title: Melvin J. Ballard: the Father “complied with it Himself, and through compliance with it became God”
speaker: Melvin J. Ballard
office: President of the Northwestern States Mission (ordained an Apostle in January 1919)
venue: General conference, first overflow meeting (Conference Report, April 1914)

quotes.excerpt: Jesus Christ said, "I came not to do my own will, but the will of the father who sent me." The law that He announced and established, was under the direction of the Father, and so even the Father could not abridge it, or make it null and void. He complied with it Himself, and through compliance with it became God.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and about as unhedged as the axis gets. The referent is fixed by the sentence's own grammar — “the father who sent me,” “even the Father,” “He complied with it Himself” — so this cannot be read Christologically. FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone, not FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE: Ballard says the Father attained Godhood by obedience to a law standing above Him, and says nothing about a mortality. That is the precedent's “attainment language without explicit mortality” case, and it is the cleaner half of the King Follett package to find on its own. The argument it serves is a legal one — the whole sermon runs on the analogy of a will whose terms cannot be varied — which is why the claim is deployed as the strongest available proof that no one may negotiate the terms of salvation: not even God did.

quotes.excerpt: When men begin trying to discover, as they say, the origin of life upon this world, they manifest the lack of sufficient reasoning power, they should remember that in the midst of this creation there are worlds infinitely older than ours. … Likewise in the mighty universe, we would have to go to those worlds that are older than ours to discover some of those secret wonders of nature that we try to discover on this earth.
quotes.note: Plural worlds under one God, argued from astronomy rather than from revelation: the preceding paragraphs walk the congregation out through Jupiter, the sun, fifty million suns and the four-light-year gap to the nearest star. No succession of Gods is implied or stated, so this is MANY-WORLDS and not INFINITE-CHAIN. The move that follows is the interesting one — since older worlds hold the answers, “would it not be wise for us to listen to the words of those who are better informed than we are, to obtain information upon conditions in the worlds that existed prior to the organization of this world?” — revelation recast as testimony from older inhabited worlds. The Conference Report's OCR prints “df” for “of” in several places in this file, including once inside this passage; corrected here, with no other change to the wording.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1914/1914-04-13-melvin-j-ballard-remarks-13.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1914a, leaves n47–n53) and Final-Reviewed against an independent column-order reconstruction of the same scan, the single prepass candidate resolving as a running-head bleed already correctly excluded. Conference Report, so A. Office matters for how the quote is weighted: Ballard is speaking in 1914 as president of the Northwestern States Mission, five years before his ordination as an Apostle, so this is not yet apostolic teaching — but it is the same man who supplies the corpus's fullest statement of eternal increase eight years later (ballard-increase), and the 1922 sermon's forward chain and this sermon's backward attainment are the two halves of the same picture. Space-before-punctuation and a handful of single-letter OCR artifacts of the printed column are normalized in the excerpts; no words changed. Speaking the day after Joseph F. Smith's opening address in the same conference (jfs-ignoramuses-1914), Ballard states in an overflow meeting the proposition Smith's address is usually read as guarding against, which is a useful measure of how little tension the two were felt to be in.

title: George F. Richards: “gods in embryo, having been born of God”
speaker: George F. Richards
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first overflow meeting, Assembly Hall (Conference Report, October 1914)

quotes.excerpt: He is the very eternal Father of the spirits of men, for we all had a spiritual birth, a spiritual existence and experience and we were born of God. Think of it, brethren and sisters, sons and daughters of God inheriting from Him through our spiritual birth the very attributes and qualities of Deity, which in our Father in heaven are perfect and make Him what He is. We are placed here upon the earth for the purpose, in part, of improving, magnifying and perfecting those qualities and attributes; so that, while we are now but gods in embryo, having been born of God, in His likeness, in His image, and having received from Him the attributes of Deity, through perfecting those attributes in time and in eternity we will be like Him in very deed, and be glorified with him in His kingdom.
quotes.note: Birth language three times over — “a spiritual birth,” “we were born of God,” “having been born of God” — which is why this reads viviparous rather than as the bare literal-parentage claim of the 1916 exposition, though no physiology is described anywhere in the address. What Richards adds to the mechanism is heredity: the spirit birth is what transmits “the very attributes and qualities of Deity,” so deification becomes the maturation of inherited traits rather than a gift conferred, and mortality is where the inherited attributes are “improved, magnified and perfected.” No backward claim is made here, so nothing on the Father-status axis is tagged; the theosis conclusion (“we will be like Him in very deed”) is A in the working taxonomy and carries no category of its own. The Conference Report OCR prints “pefect”; corrected to “perfect,” with no other change.

quotes.excerpt: I rejoice in the testimony which I bear this morning that God, the eternal Father, lives, an immortal and glorified being, whose power has no limitations.
quotes.note: The sentence immediately preceding the spirit-birth passage, kept untagged for setting. Six months after Joseph F. Smith denounced from the same pulpit those who “limit the power, the knowledge, the wisdom of God Almighty, to the capacity of men” (jfs-ignoramuses-1914), a member of the Twelve opens his testimony with a God “whose power has no limitations.” It is an assertion about power only — nothing about knowledge and nothing about growth — so it does not reach the progression question and is not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION; the same discipline is applied at jfs-ignoramuses-1914-q2 and whitney-endless-increase-1913-q2.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1914/1914-10-04-george-f-richards-remarks-4.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1914sa, leaves n14–n20) and Final-Reviewed against an independent column-order reconstruction of the same scan, which restored a dropped clause elsewhere in the address and corrected one print artifact; neither touches the quoted passages. Conference Report, so A. Richards presided over the Assembly Hall overflow meeting that ran concurrently with the opening Tabernacle session, which is why the printed volume places his remarks after the Smith/Penrose/Lund sequence rather than at the head of the conference. Read against richards-obedience-couplet-1913 eighteen months earlier: the same apostle, the same inheritance-of-attributes argument, but the backward half — “as we are now God once was … He has become what He is” — is simply absent here, and the address stays entirely on the forward side.

title: John A. Widtsoe: a progressive God, and Many Gods who are peers rather than ancestors
speaker: John A. Widtsoe
office: President of the Agricultural College of Utah (ordained an Apostle 1921)
venue: Rational Theology As Taught by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (General Priesthood Committee, 1915), ch. 6 “God and Man,” pp. 23–25

quotes.excerpt: However, if the great law of progression is accepted, God must have been engaged from the beginning, and must now be engaged in progressive development, and, infinite as God is, he must have been less powerful in the past than he is today. While it is folly for man to attempt to unravel in detail the mystery of the past, yet it is only logical to believe that a progressive God has not always possessed his present position.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and an unusually unhedged one — “must now be engaged in progressive development,” present tense. This is the claim Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie later call dangerous and heretical.

quotes.excerpt: We may be certain that, through self-effort, the inherent and innate powers of God have been developed to a God-like degree. Thus, he has become God… His Godhood, however, was attained by the use of his power in simple obedience to the laws he discovered as he grew in experience.
quotes.note: Untagged deliberately. This is completed past attainment, not past mortality and not parentage: Widtsoe's God rose from among co-existing intelligences by self-effort, and no Father of God appears anywhere in the chapter. Tagging it backward-mortality would import the King Follett frame Widtsoe is quietly declining to use.

quotes.excerpt: Next to God, there may be, therefore, other intelligent beings so nearly approaching his power as to be coequal with him in all things so far as our finite understanding can perceive. These beings may be immeasurably far from God in power, nevertheless immeasureably far above us mortal men of the earth. Such intelligent beings are as Gods to us. Under this definition there may be a great number of intelligent beings who possess to a greater or less degree the quality of Godhood.
quotes.note: The section is headed “Many Gods,” and this is the sentence that gets recruited as regress evidence. It is the opposite: Widtsoe's Many Gods are contemporaries thrown up by parallel progression from a common field of intelligences — some near-coequal, others “immeasurably far from God in power” and “as Gods to us” — not a line of ancestors. Nothing in the chapter stands behind God.

quotes.excerpt: Man is, nevertheless, moving on, in eternal progression. “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.” In short, man is a god in embryo. He comes of a race of gods, and as his eternal growth is continued, he will approach more nearly the point which to us is Godhood.
quotes.note: The Snow couplet is the only backward-mortality content in the chapter, and Widtsoe imports it as a summary rather than deriving it. “He comes of a race of gods” is about man's ancestry, not God's.

notes: Verified verbatim against a scan of the 1915 first edition, whose title page reads “Published for the Use of the Melchizedek Priesthood by the General Priesthood Committee, 1915” — hence historical-official rather than never-official, though the book was never canonical and is long out of print. Printed pp. 23–25 in that edition carry chapter 6, matching the pagination Eugene England uses. Watch the edition when quoting: the Paulsen and Fisher review in FARMS Review 15/2 quotes the 1965 Deseret Book printing, which reads “if the law of progression be accepted” where the 1915 text collated here reads “if the great law of progression is accepted,” and the surrounding sentences differ likewise. Recorded as a divine-progression affirmation and emphatically not as a chain source: this is the taxonomy's fourth trap in its purest form, a source that affirms ongoing divine progression while asserting no divine ancestry at all. Structurally it belongs with Penrose (1884) and Nelson (1904).

title: George F. Richards: sealed couples “shall have eternal increase in the kingdom of God”
speaker: George F. Richards
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day outdoor meeting at the Bureau of Information, Temple Block (Conference Report, April 1915)

quotes.excerpt: If it shall prove true, as we believe, and as the scriptures plainly teach, that a worthy man and woman joined together as husband and wife, under solemn covenant for time and for all eternity, that union solemnized in the Temple of the Lord as He has directed, by the authority which he has delegated to men, and those relationships maintained and recognized in the life beyond, and that they shall have eternal increase in the kingdom of God, — and that all other unions will not be so recognized, — what a satisfaction it will be to those who have accepted this divine truth, this great hope, and have yielded obedience unto it
quotes.note: “Eternal increase” named as the outcome of temple sealing, with nothing said about what increases — no offspring, no spirit children, no mechanism — which is the euphemistic register exactly. Stance is affirms rather than hedges despite the conditional opening: “if it shall prove true, as we believe, and as the scriptures plainly teach” is the rhetorical spine of the entire address, a wager frame Richards applies in turn to the existence of God, to baptism, to work for the dead and to sealing, and in each case the antecedent is asserted, not doubted. The exclusive clause is worth as much as the increase clause — all other unions “will not be so recognized” — because it makes eternal increase the discriminating blessing of the temple rather than a general promise.

quotes.excerpt: there is no other plan instituted by the Gods for the salvation of the children of men
quotes.note: The closing clause of the testimony, untagged. A capitalized plural — “instituted by the Gods” — dropped into the last sentence of a general conference address without gloss, explanation, or apparent awareness that it needs one. It establishes nothing on its own: no succession, no worlds, no council named. Its value is as a register datum for how unremarkable plural-Gods language still was in 1915 speech.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1915/1915-04-16-george-f-richards-remarks-16.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1915a, leaf n67) and Final-Reviewed against a word-coordinate reading-order reconstruction of the same scan, the single candidate resolving as a running-head artifact in the witness rather than in the vault text. Conference Report, so A; the vault frontmatter's generic “General Authority” understates the office, since Richards was of the Twelve from 1906. The setting is the outdoor overflow held in front of the Bureau of Information while the Tabernacle and Assembly Hall both ran full, which is where the address's opening apology for the standing crowd comes from. Same conference as talmage-conference-1915 and jfs-perfect-in-our-sphere-1915: the April 1915 conference carries the Father's mortality, a graded limit on human perfection, and eternal increase within three days of each other.

title: Joseph E. Robinson: the exalted “build yet other mansions for our Father, thus adding to His glory”
speaker: Joseph E. Robinson
office: President of the California Mission
venue: General conference, first day outdoor meeting at the Bureau of Information, Temple Block; Easter Sunday (Conference Report, April 1915)

quotes.excerpt: With Him and in His presence, in the eons of years yet to come, we shall come into a fulness of divinity, and build yet other mansions for our Father, thus adding to His glory as we add to the glory and perpetuity of our own homes and families.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and on precisely the ground B. H. Roberts had staked out four years earlier: God's glory is enlarged by what His redeemed children go on to do (roberts-progress-of-god-1911, “as worlds and world-systems are multiplied and redeemed … so God's kingdom is enlarged and his glory increased”). This is the dominion-and-glory form of the claim, not the knowledge form, so it is the version Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie would later concede while denying progression proper — but stated as an affirmation of increase in God rather than as a limit on it. The building metaphor is doing real work: the exalted are not merely glorified, they are contributors to a Father whose glory is therefore not yet complete.

quotes.excerpt: And the Latter-day Saint looks for the place where he shall build, as he began to build in this life for an eternal home, for the family relationship, for father and for mother, for wife and husband, for parents and children, to associate together until they shall come into a fullness of all that their fond hearts have desired and their minds have conceived of ; and it shall be an endless home of eternal progression in the presence of the Christ and with the Father, who is God over all.
quotes.note: The eternal-family form of the euphemism, and a weak one: every relation named — father and mother, wife and husband, parents and children — is a relation the hearers already have, continued rather than extended. Nothing is increased, no new children are named, no mechanism appears. Hedges, and recorded because the contrast with the sentence tagged above is instructive: Robinson is explicit about God's glory growing and vague about what the family does to grow it.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1915/1915-04-18-joseph-e-robinson-remarks-18.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1915a) and Final-Reviewed by manual collation of leaves n71–n78 in column reading order after a prepass boundary false positive; the body matches the print verbatim, including preserved typographical errors elsewhere in the address. Conference Report, so A. Delivered Easter Sunday 1915 at the outdoor overflow, immediately after George F. Richards's address at the same meeting (richards-eternal-increase-1915), and the sermon is a resurrection sermon throughout: the argument from nature — that every longing in creation has its complement, so the longing for immortality must have one too — is what the divine-progression clause is the peroration of. Robinson is a mission president, not a general authority, which is the right weight to give the entry; its value is that the Roberts position is being preached as ordinary conference fare in 1915, one year after the President of the Church called those who limit God “learned fools” and four years after Roberts published it.

title: Reed Smoot: “the God whom we worship has passed through all the experience that we are now passing through”
speaker: Reed Smoot
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles; United States Senator from Utah
venue: General conference, second day morning session (Conference Report, April 1915)

quotes.excerpt: When strangers have said, "We believe in God the Eternal Father," I have stated, "Yes, as far as you understand Him; but our idea, our conception of God, leads us to believe He is entirely a different God from the one in whom you believe, whom, you say, is a god without body parts or passions." … I simply say, with you, that the God whom we worship has passed through all the experience that we are now passing through. He is an exalted being, a personality, and I predict the time will come when, instead of a handful of people believing in the personality of God, the great body of the people of the world will acknowledge that fact.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the referent is fixed by what Smoot is expounding: the sentence is his gloss on the first Article of Faith, “We believe in God, the Eternal Father,” offered against the creedal God “without body parts or passions,” so the being who passed through our experience is the Father. Tagged FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE only. “He is an exalted being” describes a present status, not a narrated attainment, and reading it as FATHER-BECAME-GOD would import more than the sentence carries — contrast penrose-exalted-man-1916, where the Father is said to have passed through everything Christ afterwards passed through, and hart-once-as-we-are-1917, where the heights are ones “he has now attained.” What is distinctive here is the framing: the past mortality of God is presented not as a mystery but as the ordinary LDS conception of Deity, the thing that makes the first Article of Faith mean something different from what a stranger reading the card would assume. Two scan artifacts of the printed column are corrected in the excerpt and nothing else: “bodv” for “body” in the last clause, and a stray apostrophe splitting “body' parts or passions” across a line break in the creedal formula; the printed Report almost certainly reads “body, parts or passions,” but the comma is not legible in the OCR, so the phrase is given unpunctuated rather than emended.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1915/1915-04-23-reed-smoot-remarks-23.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1915a, leaves n88–n93) and Final-Reviewed against the column reconstruction with no body change and no prepass candidates. Conference Report, so A; the vault's generic “General Authority” understates the office — Smoot had been an Apostle since 1900 and was a sitting United States Senator, which is why the address turns on the Smoot hearings and quotes the prosecutor's summation at length. No backward chain is asserted: this is trap #1 in its clean form, past mortality with no Father above the Father and no succession, and the entry should not be counted toward the regress. Register datum: he says it in passing, declines to develop it (“I am not going to take the time”), and predicts the world will come round to it — the confidence of 1915, eleven years after the hearings that made his Mormonism a national question. Two hours later in the same conference James E. Talmage will make the harder version of the claim (talmage-conference-1915).

title: James E. Talmage: the Eternal Father was once a Man, by right of conquest
speaker: James E. Talmage
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning session (Conference Report, April 1915, p. 123)

quotes.excerpt: you can't change the fact that He is the Son of that Father, and that Father, the Eternal Father, the Father of Jesus Christ, the Father of His spirit and the Father of His body, was once a Man, and has progressed, not by any favor but by the right of conquest over sin, and over death, to His present position of priesthood and power, of Godship and Godliness, as the Supreme Being whom we all profess to worship.
quotes.note: BACKWARD-MORTALITY, and emphatically not DIVINE-PROGRESSION. Every verb is completed: was once a Man, has progressed, to His present position. The progression is a finished ascent that terminates in Godship, not an ongoing increase — Talmage is here answering the question of how the Father came to be God, not whether He is still growing. The referent is unmistakable and unusually over-specified: he names the Eternal Father four ways in one clause, so this cannot be read Christologically the way the Snow couplet can. “Right of conquest” is the distinctive contribution: exaltation earned rather than conferred.

quotes.excerpt: It was crystallized into what we may call an aphorism, by President Lorenzo Snow: "As man is God once was; as God is man may be". We know that Christ is God, and that He lived upon the earth as a Man. In the sense in which Christ was perfect in His sphere, we may become perfect in ours.
quotes.note: The couplet, and immediately a Christological gloss on it — “We know that Christ is God, and that He lived upon the earth as a Man” — which is exactly the ambiguity catalogued at snow-couplet. Referent ambiguous for this quote even though the entry's referent is the Father, because Talmage's own next sentence supplies the Son as the illustration. Note also the demotion in status: the couplet is “what we may call an aphorism,” not revelation. Spacing around the semicolons in the vault transcription reflects OCR of the printed Report and has been normalized; no words changed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1915/1915-04-34-james-e-talmage-remarks-34.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report and verified against a word-coordinate reading-order reconstruction of the archive.org DjVu OCR (conferencereport1915a, leaf anchor n121); the Final Review pass found no body change needed. Conference Report, so A. The office is given as the generic “General Authority” in the vault frontmatter; Talmage had been ordained an Apostle in December 1911 and was of the Twelve in April 1915. This entry exists chiefly to be read against talmage-af-1899, and the pairing is the point: the same author, sixteen years apart, makes two claims that sound identical and are not. In 1899 he wrote of “a God who is Himself progressive… whose perfection consists in eternal advancement” — present tense, ongoing, DIVINE-PROGRESSION. Here in 1915 he says the Father “was once a Man, and has progressed… to His present position” — past tense, completed, BACKWARD-MORTALITY. Conflating the two is trap #1 running in the opposite direction from usual, and it is how a single author gets cited on both sides of the twentieth-century progression debate.

title: Joseph F. Smith: perfect “in our sphere,” not in God's higher and more exalted sphere
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference closing address, third day (Conference Report, April 1915)

quotes.excerpt: I sincerely hope … that we will be able to continue to build on the foundations of the Gospel of the Son of God until we become perfect even as our Father in heaven is perfect, according to the sphere and intelligence that we act in and possess. I do not expect that any of us will ever become in mortality quite so perfect as God is perfect ; but in the spheres in which we are called to act, and according to the capacity and breadth of intelligence that we possess, in our sphere and in the exercise of the talent, the ability and intelligence that God has given to us, we may become as perfect in our sphere as God is perfect in His higher and more exalted sphere. I believe that.
quotes.note: Not a denial of deification and not a hedge about it — a graded reading of Matthew 5:48 that keeps the promise and relocates it. Two limits are stacked in one sentence and they are not the same limit: “in mortality” is temporal and would be conceded by anyone, while “in our sphere … as God is perfect in His higher and more exalted sphere” is permanent, and it is the second that does the work. Tagged RETREAT-REFRAME as an operation performed on “be ye perfect,” not as a position on the Father-status axis, which the passage never touches. The formula was in the air that week: James E. Talmage had used it in the Tabernacle earlier the same day — “In the sense in which Christ was perfect in His sphere, we may become perfect in ours” (talmage-conference-1915-q2) — but where Talmage's sphere language sits beside an unqualified statement that the Father was once a Man, the President of the Church supplies the qualification and nothing else. The Conference Report OCR prints “capacjty”; corrected to “capacity,” and space-before-semicolon artifacts of the printed column are normalized; no words changed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1915/1915-04-41-joseph-f-smith-remarks-41.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1915a, leaf n137) and Final-Reviewed against a word-coordinate reading-order reconstruction of the same scan, the single candidate resolving as a running-head artifact in the witness. Conference Report, so A. Provenance correction the vault has already applied and that matters for citation: this is the closing address of the third day, April 6, not a second-day session — the printed Report places it after the sustaining of the authorities and before Patriarch Hyrum G. Smith's benediction. The passage is the last doctrinal sentence of the conference, spoken immediately before the closing blessing, which is worth noting when weighing its force: it is a valediction, not an argument, and Smith adds “I believe that” as though the qualification were the personal part.

title: Joseph F. Smith: “His knowledge comprehends them all … and He knows all”
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference opening address, first day morning session (Conference Report, April 1916)

quotes.excerpt: It is a physical, a theological, an unreasonable, inconsistency to imagine that even God the Eternal Father would be in two places, as an individual, at the same moment. It is impossible. But His power extends throughout the immensity of space, His power extends to all His creations, and His knowledge comprehends them all, and He governs them all and He knows all.
quotes.note: Denial, and unlike the 1914 address this one reaches the progression question squarely: “He knows all” is an unqualified omniscience claim, which is the exact proposition B. H. Roberts had denied five years earlier in a Church-issued priesthood course — “not that God is Omniscient up to the point that further progress in knowledge is impossible to him” (roberts-progress-of-god-1911-q3). Note the structure of the paragraph, because it is the mid-century position in embryo: personal omnipresence is rejected as impossible in the same breath in which total knowledge is asserted. Smith is not defending the creedal God; he is drawing the line between an embodied, located Person and a bounded one, and putting knowledge on the unbounded side.

quotes.excerpt: I am only a child, I am only learning, and I hope I shall not be ever learning and never come to the knowledge of the truth. I sincerely hope that as I learn little by little, line upon line and precept upon precept, here a little and there a little, day by day, and month by month, and year by year, that there will come a time when I shall have learned indeed the truth and shall know it as God knows it and be saved and exalted in His presence.
quotes.note: Untagged, and kept because of what it does to the sentence above. Three paragraphs before asserting that God “knows all,” the same speaker hopes to “know it as God knows it” — a terminus for human learning that is God's own knowledge. Neither statement is about whether God still progresses, so neither is retrojected into the other; but together they define the shape of the deniers' position, in which the ladder has a top and God is standing on it. The Conference Report OCR prints “clay by day”; corrected to “day by day,” with no other change.

quotes.excerpt: They have advanced ; we are advancing ; we are growing as they have grown ; we are reaching the goal that they have attained unto
quotes.note: Untagged: the subject is the dead prophets — Joseph, Brigham, John, Wilford — not God, and the claim is postmortal progression for men, whose minds “have expanded beyond their comprehension in mortal life.” Recorded because it is the one place in the address where advancement is affirmed without limit, and because Smith flags it himself as a position some will find “a little extreme.”

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1916/1916-04-01-joseph-f-smith-remarks-1.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1916a) with the true reading order reconstructed from the volume's DjVu XML after a column-interleaving fault was found and repaired elsewhere in the file, and Final-Reviewed by sampled collation against the same scan at 97.5–100% similarity; none of the quoted passages fall inside the repaired block. Conference Report, so A. The vault frontmatter's “General Authority” is a placeholder; Smith was President of the Church. Space-before-punctuation artifacts of the printed column are left as printed in quote 3 and normalized elsewhere; no words changed. The entry's pair is jfs-ignoramuses-1914 two years earlier: there the target was named (“school teachers”) and the charge was miracle-denial, with only “the knowledge, the wisdom” touching progression; here the same President states the omniscience claim positively and without a polemical target, which is the cleaner citation of the two.

title: Charles W. Penrose: an exalted Man who passed through all Christ passed through — “a repetition of the things that had been done from remote, eternal ages”
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, first day afternoon session (Conference Report, April 1916)

quotes.excerpt: Jesus of Nazareth, born of the virgin Mary, was literally and truly the Son of the Father, the Eternal God, not of Adam. Don't think so for a moment. Christ was the Son of God, of God the Father ; the Father of His Spirit was the Father of His body. He was an exalted man who had passed through all things that Jesus Christ, His Beloved Son, afterwards passed through. It was a repetition of the things that had been done from remote, eternal ages, the great plan of salvation for all the people of all the worlds that God has created.
quotes.note: The strongest sentence of the discourse and the referent is unmistakable — “He” is the Father named twice in the preceding clause. Both Father-status positions: mortality, because what Christ afterwards passed through was a mortal life and death, and attainment, because “exalted man … had passed through all things” describes a completed ascent rather than a standing condition, which is what separates this from smoot-passed-through-experience-1915. MANY-WORLDS for “all the people of all the worlds that God has created,” a plurality under one God with no succession named. Deliberately not INFINITE-CHAIN: “a repetition of the things that had been done from remote, eternal ages” asserts that the plan of salvation has recurred endlessly, not that a line of Gods produced one another, and reading a regress out of a repeated plan is the symmetry inference trap #3 warns against. It is the nearest thing to C-infinite in this batch, and it stops short.

quotes.excerpt: Now, if the Father, in the course of His great experience as revealed through the Prophet Joseph, had passed through the "estate" of mortals that He might be placed in the same conditions of trial, so was Jesus thus placed, and the Lord showed to Jesus all about this.
quotes.note: The same claim in conditional dress, twenty paragraphs earlier in the same address, and the pair is why both are recorded. Hedges: the protasis is “if the Father … had passed through the estate of mortals,” and the sentence's argumentative weight rests on the apodosis about Jesus, not on the Father's mortality — yet the interpolated clause “as revealed through the Prophet Joseph” treats the antecedent as settled revelation while the syntax treats it as a supposition. Penrose is using King Follett as a premise he does not stop to defend, and by the end of the discourse he will state it flat (q1). The quotation marks around “estate” are the printed text's.

quotes.excerpt: There still remains, I can tell by the letters I have alluded to, an idea among some of the people that Adam was and is the Almighty and Eternal God. … So Adam was neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Ghost, was he? Then, who was he? Why, we are told he was Michael in his first estate, and as Adam he will stand at the head of his race. … You see, do you not, that Michael became Adam and that Adam was not the Son Jehovah, and he was not Elohim the Father.
quotes.note: The reframe, and it is the reason the address exists: a counselor in the First Presidency devoting most of a general conference sermon to putting down Adam-God (young-adam-god-chain-1854), sixty-two years after Brigham Young preached it and fifty-one after the First Presidency's Pratt repudiation (fp-repudiation-1865). Two features are worth recording. The refutation is procedural rather than historical — Adam prayed, was taught the gospel, was baptized in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost, therefore he is none of them — and it never names Young or acknowledges that the doctrine had a source at the pulpit; it is attributed to “letters,” to “peculiar ideas” that “get into people's minds,” and to a stubborn Scotchman. And it is a live problem in 1916: “I am sorry that has not been rectified long ago … and yet it still lingers.”

quotes.excerpt: He who made the worlds, and as we heard today, controls and governs and directs them, is actually our Father, not in some mystical sense, not in some mere theory, but we were begotten of Him. In the revelation contained in the 76th Section of the Doctrine and Covenants we are told that the inhabitants of the worlds are "begotten sons and daughters unto God." There may be more in that than we see at the first glance, but the result of it all is in our minds, if we are at all logical, that the great Eternal God is our Father and we are begotten of Him or UNTO Him
quotes.note: Literal begetting insisted on against a figurative reading — “not in some mystical sense, not in some mere theory” — with no physiology anywhere in the address, which puts it at the explicitness of eom-god-the-father-1992 rather than of fp-1909. Two details repay attention. Penrose does gloss the D&C 76:24 quotation rather than leaving it bare, and his gloss is a hesitation: “There may be more in that than we see at the first glance.” And the alternative he leaves standing in the same sentence — “begotten of Him or UNTO Him,” the capitals the printed text's — preserves the ambiguity of the scriptural preposition instead of resolving it, which is the one place the address stops short of the 1909 statement. No Mother is mentioned anywhere.

quotes.excerpt: You know there are some of our brethren who have thought that Jesus, in His first estate, as we call it, or in His former state, was a resurrected being. I do not know where they get the idea from … I don't know of any that intimates at all that He could not be God unless He had passed through a mortal probation and had been tried and tempted and had suffered ; that He could not be God beforehand … There is no need for the theory that He must have had a body before coming to this earth, and there is nothing that establishes it by revelation.
quotes.note: Untagged, but it constrains how q1 and q2 should be read. Penrose is denying that Godhood requires a prior mortality — of the Son. He does not extend the denial to the Father; on the contrary, he affirms the Father's mortal experience in the same address. So the sermon holds both that Jesus was God before any body and that the Father was an exalted man who had passed through all Jesus later passed through, and never remarks on the asymmetry. Anyone tempted to read the Son's case back onto the Father, as the Snow couplet's Christological gloss invites (snow-couplet), should note that Penrose himself does not.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1916/1916-04-04-charles-w-penrose-remarks-4.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1916a) with reading order reconstructed from the volume's DjVu XML; the heavyweight pass established that three separate vault files were a single continuous address wrongly split at page turns and merged them, and Final Review spot-collated the merged text against the same scan with no divergence found. Conference Report, so A. Two provenance points. The vault frontmatter says “General Authority”: Penrose had been Second Counselor in the First Presidency since December 1911, and the printed running head styles him “PRESIDENT CHARLES W. PENROSE,” so this is First Presidency teaching, not an apostle's opinion — which is what makes both the Adam-God repudiation and the King Follett affirmation weigh as much as they do. Space-before-punctuation artifacts of the printed column are left as printed; several single-letter OCR errors were corrected in the heavyweight pass and none fall in the quoted passages. Delivered the same day as jfs-he-knows-all-1916, in the session immediately following it, and the pairing is the finding for April 1916: the President of the Church asserts that God knows all, and his counselor asserts that God was once a man who passed through everything His Son later did, with no sense that the two remarks bear on each other. citesId names the Adam-God discourse because this address is a repudiation of it, on the pattern of fp-repudiation-1865 → pratt-seer; Penrose quotes Brigham Young nowhere and never names him.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith: a kingdom “where the crowning glory is the continuation of the family union and eternal increase”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles (signed “Joseph F. Smith, Jr.”)
venue: “Birth Control,” The Relief Society Magazine 3, no. 7 (July 1916): 363–368, at p. 368

quotes.excerpt: There is no promise of eternal salvation and exaltation for such as they, for by their acts they prove their unworthiness for exaltation and unfitness for a kingdom where the crowning glory is the continuation of the family union and eternal increase which have been promised to all those who obey the law of the Lord.
quotes.note: Euphemism, not explicitness: the celestial kingdom's crowning glory is named as “continuation of the family union and eternal increase,” and nothing in the sentence says what is increased. No new spirit children, no offspring of any kind, no mechanism — which is precisely the register worth recording, because the same apostle will be entirely explicit about spirit offspring in later decades (see jfsmith-doctrines-salvation-1954). The sentence's argumentative work is also worth noting: eternal increase is deployed here as a threat, as the blessing forfeited by those who limit their families, rather than as doctrine expounded for its own sake.

notes: Verified verbatim against the archive.org page image of printed p. 368 (item relief-society-magazine_1916-07_3_7, IA leaf 6); the passage is signed “Joseph F. Smith, Jr.” at the foot of the same page. Provenance and register both matter here. The piece is not an article but one of five signed contributions to a symposium the magazine's editor solicited by letter — Rudger Clawson, George F. Richards, David O. McKay, Orson F. Whitney, and Joseph F. Smith, Jr. — introduced with “We present herewith the views of five members of the quorum of the Twelve apostles, and ask that our Relief Society officers shall read these stirring and splendid comments in the various meetings of our Society” (p. 364). So the doctrinal clause was written to be read aloud in ward Relief Society meetings, which is why it is graded historical-official rather than as private apostolic opinion. George F. Richards makes the same forward move in the same symposium on p. 365, calling the doctrine of limited families “pernicious” because “it robs both man and his Maker of their glory and increase” — another B1 formulation that names increase without naming offspring. The context needs stating plainly rather than eliding: the paragraphs on either side of the quoted sentence are an anti-“birth control” polemic that runs into explicit nativism and “survival of the fittest” language about immigrants displacing “the old Colonial stock.” None of that bears on the taxonomy label, but a reader who follows the URL will meet it immediately, and the entry should not pretend otherwise.
