title: The Articles of Faith loses “and from kingdom to kingdom”: Talmage revises his own book
speaker: James E. Talmage
office: Apostle (ordained December 1911), revising the book he wrote in 1899 under First Presidency commission
venue: The Articles of Faith, Lecture XXII (Article 11), §25 — p. 421 in the first edition (Salt Lake City: The Deseret News, 1899) and p. 421 in the tenth edition (February 1917)

witnesses.scribe: Second edition (December 1901), p. 421 — clause still present
witnesses.note: Its own Preface to the Fifth Edition says the second edition “differed but little from the first edition, the few alterations that were made consisting ‘in the correction of typographical and other minor errors, and in the introduction of additional notes.’”

witnesses.scribe: Fifth edition (November 1909), p. 421 — clause still present
witnesses.note: The archive.org identifier for this scan is mislabeled “word-of-wisdom”; the item is in fact the fifth edition of The Articles of Faith, Deseret News, 1909, twenty-third thousand. Its preface says the fifth edition “embodies a few changes in phraseology, otherwise it is uniform with the earlier electrotype issues” — and the clause survives those changes.

witnesses.scribe: Eleventh edition (October 1919), p. 421 — clause gone
witnesses.note: The Publishers' Note to the Eleventh Edition states it “is printed from the electrotype plates used for the last preceding edition,” i.e. the tenth. The 1919 reading is therefore the tenth-edition reading, which is how the change is dated to February 1917.

witnesses.scribe: A Study of the Articles of Faith (1924 revision), p. 409 — clause gone and the question explicitly closed
Gospel Scholar Archive e-text of The Articles of Faith (post-1917 text)
witnesses.note: The GSA copy is a 2020 OK Publishing / Musaicum reflowed ebook carrying only the Preface to the First Edition, so it presents as 1899 but reads “within each of the three specified kingdoms” — it is a tenth/eleventh-edition text. Anyone quoting 1899 wording from the GSA copy is quoting the revision.

quotes.excerpt: It is reasonable to believe, in the absence of direct revelation by which alone absolute knowledge of the matter could be acquired, that, in accordance with God's plan of eternal progression, advancement from grade to grade within any kingdom, and from kingdom to kingdom, will be provided for. But if the recipients of a lower glory be enabled to advance, surely the intelligences of higher rank will not be stopped in their progress; and thus we may conclude, that degrees and grades will ever characterize the kingdoms of our God. Eternity is progressive; perfection is relative; the essential feature of God's living purpose is its associated power of eternal increase.
quotes.note: BEFORE — first edition, 1899, p. 421. The tag is marked implied deliberately: the passage's direct subject is resurrected souls advancing between degrees of glory, not God, and only the clause “and from kingdom to kingdom” was later cut. What earns the DIVINE-PROGRESSION marker is the frame Talmage builds around it — the advancement is “in accordance with God's plan of eternal progression,” it is asserted of “the intelligences of higher rank” without a ceiling, and it closes on “perfection is relative,” the exact proposition Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie later had to deny in order to deny divine progression. Twenty-one printed pages further on, the same first edition says “We believe in a God who is Himself progressive… whose perfection consists in eternal advancement” (p. 442; see talmage-af-1899).

quotes.excerpt: It is reasonable to believe, in the absence of direct revelation by which alone absolute knowledge of the matter could be acquired, that, in accordance with God's plan of eternal progression, advancement from grade to grade within each of the three specified kingdoms will be provided for. But if the recipients of a lower glory be enabled to advance, surely the intelligences of higher rank shall not be stopped in their progress; and thus we may conclude that degrees and grades will ever characterize the kingdoms of our God. Eternity is progressive; perfection is relative; the essential feature of God's living purpose is its associated power of eternal increase.
quotes.note: AFTER — tenth edition, February 1917, p. 421, verified through the eleventh edition printed from the tenth's plates. One surgical substitution against the immediately preceding (fifth, 1909) edition: “within any kingdom, and from kingdom to kingdom” becomes “within each of the three specified kingdoms.” (Two smaller changes visible against the 1899 text above — “will not be stopped” → “shall not be stopped” and the loss of the comma in “conclude, that” — were already made in the second edition of 1901.) Everything else is untouched, including the now-orphaned next sentence about “the recipients of a lower glory” being “enabled to advance,” which in the original meant advancing out of that glory and now can only mean advancing inside it. That leftover is the strongest internal evidence that this was an excision rather than a rewrite.

quotes.excerpt: It is reasonable to believe, in the absence of direct revelation by which alone absolute knowledge of the matter could be acquired, that, in accordance with God's plan of eternal progression, advancement within each of the three specified kingdoms will be provided for; though as to possible progress from one kingdom to another the scriptures make no positive affirmation. Eternal advancement along different lines is conceivable. We may conclude that degrees and grades will ever characterize the kingdoms of our God. Eternity is progressive; perfection is relative; the essential feature of God's living purpose is its associated power of eternal increase.
quotes.note: The 1924 rewrite (A Study of the Articles of Faith, p. 409) finishes the job: it is no longer enough to have deleted the claim, the possibility is now named in order to be declared unsupported — “though as to possible progress from one kingdom to another the scriptures make no positive affirmation.” The consolation offered in its place, “Eternal advancement along different lines is conceivable,” is the same dominions-not-knowledge substitution that runs through the whole D debate. The orphaned “recipients of a lower glory” sentence, still sitting there in 1917, is gone by 1924.

notes: The edition diff is real and both states are verified verbatim. Chain of witnesses, all read as full text and page-anchored: first edition (Deseret News, 1899), p. 421 — clause present, confirmed independently in two scans (BYU's articlesoffaiths1899talm leaf 439 and Google's articlesfaithas00talmgoog); second edition (December 1901), p. 421 — present; fifth edition (November 1909), p. 421 — present; tenth edition (February 1917), p. 421 — absent, read through the eleventh edition (October 1919), whose Publishers' Note states it was printed from the tenth edition's plates; 1924 revision, p. 409 — absent and explicitly disclaimed. The tenth edition is therefore the edition that dropped it, and its own Preface (signed Salt Lake City, February 1917) says the issue “presents some departures from the earlier imprints in wording, in the substitution of several rewritten paragraphs” — Talmage announces that paragraphs were rewritten without saying which. NOT VERIFIED, and deliberately not asserted anywhere above: the footnote-mined scholarly claim that the “from kingdom to kingdom” language was originally inserted at the request of the First Presidency's reviewing committee. The 1899 Preface names that committee (Francis M. Lyman, Abraham H. Cannon and Anthon H. Lund of the Twelve; George Reynolds of the Seventy; John Nicholson; Karl G. Maeser) and thanks them for their “painstaking and efficient examination of the manuscript prior to the delivery of the lectures,” but nothing in the printed book attributes this clause to them; that half of the claim rests on Talmage's journals and should be run down there before it is published. Two corrections for the maintainer regarding the existing talmage-af-1899 entry, both found while doing this diff: (1) its q2 reads “the opposition of all the sects,” but the 1899 first edition reads “the opposition of all other sects” — “all the sects” is the tenth/eleventh-edition wording, and the 1924 revision reads “the opposition of the sects”; (2) the venue gives the progression passage as “p. 430 in early printings,” but in the 1899 first edition it is p. 442; p. 430 is its page in the 1924 A Study of the Articles of Faith. Both discrepancies trace to the same cause as the GSA witness note above — the corpus e-text of Articles of Faith is a post-1917 text, not the first edition.

title: John W. Hart: “God is a material being, an exalted, immortal man. He was once as we are”
speaker: John W. Hart
office: President of the Rigby Stake, Idaho
venue: General conference, first day (Conference Report, October 1917)

quotes.excerpt: As Latter-day Saints — "Mormons," as we are known — we believe that God is a material being, an exalted, immortal man. He was once as we are, and it is possible for us to attain to the heights that he has now attained ; and we base our faith on the circumstance that transpired in the death, crucifixion, and resurrection of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
quotes.note: Both Father-status positions, stated flatly and offered as the denominational position: past mortality (“He was once as we are”) and attainment (“the heights that he has now attained”). Referent ambiguous rather than father, and the reason is in the sentence itself: the warrant Hart gives is Christ's death and resurrection, and the Bible passage he then reads to his interlocutor is the risen Jesus saying “a spirit hath not flesh and bones as ye see me have.” The being described is plainly the God of worship — the exchange culminates in “we must know God the Father, before we can intelligently and consistently worship him” — but the evidence supplied is the Son's body, which is the ambiguity catalogued at snow-couplet and marked the same way at talmage-conference-1915-q2. What the quote is good for is register, not novelty: a stake president reports saying this, unprompted and without qualification, to a Christian Scientist state senator in a Boise hotel room, and reports it to general conference as an example of what every member should be ready to do.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1917/1917-10-32-john-w-hart-remarks-32.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1917sa, leaves n95–n97) and Final-Reviewed against an independent reading-order reconstruction of the same scan, which fixed nine single-character OCR artifacts elsewhere in the address; the quoted sentence needed none. Conference Report, so A. The quotation is doubly framed — Hart quoting himself quoting the Latter-day Saint position in a conversation he is recounting from the pulpit — so it is his own first-person composition of what he said, not a transcript of the Boise conversation; the hearsay grade covers the Conference Report's fidelity to Hart, not Hart's fidelity to his own remembered words. One unresolved discrepancy in the file: the vault frontmatter assigns the address to the first day afternoon session, while Hart twice says “this morning” and refers to holding services in the open air, which suggests an outdoor overflow meeting; the date is not in question.

title: Melvin J. Ballard narrows the couplet: not “that all men are going to become what God is”
speaker: Melvin J. Ballard
office: President of the Northwestern States Mission (ordained an Apostle in January 1919)
venue: General conference, second day morning session (Conference Report, October 1917)

quotes.excerpt: I don't understand that the "Mormon" doctrine, announced by President Lorenzo Snow, and so often quoted by us : "As God is man may become, and as man is God once was," means that all men are going to become what God is, not by any manner of means. It is possible they may become ; yes, when men keep and obey the fulness of the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ.
quotes.note: A reframe that cuts in only one direction, which is what makes it useful. Ballard restricts the forward half — not all men, only those who obey the fulness — and leaves the backward half untouched, quoting “as man is God once was” as “the ‘Mormon' doctrine, announced by President Lorenzo Snow, and so often quoted by us,” hence FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE affirms alongside the RETREAT-REFRAME tag. Referent ambiguous: this is the bare couplet with no gloss identifying the God in question. Two textual notes. Ballard inverts Snow's order, putting the forward line first, which is consistent with the forward half being the part he means to correct. And the correction is aimed at universalism, not at deification: “It is possible they may become” concedes the doctrine in the same breath that it withdraws the entitlement — compare hinckley-1997, where eighty years later the same sentence is walked back from the other end.

quotes.excerpt: But I am satisfied of the fact that those only who gain a celestial glory will ever become what God is, for there are privileges that belong to that glory and exaltation that do not belong to any other.
quotes.note: The restriction restated as a positive doctrine of degrees, a few sentences later. Read with the previous quote it gives the whole shape of the 1917 narrowing: deification is not denied, it is made scarce, and the scarcity is enforced by kingdom rather than by qualification of the doctrine itself. Later in the same address Ballard states the affirmative side just as plainly — “those who keep the celestial law are pursuing a path that leads on to where God is. and what God is now they may become” — so the entry records a boundary being drawn around a teaching, not a retreat from it.

quotes.excerpt: Those who gain the highest place provided shall have a very superior physical equipment, capable of more intense and rapid growth, they shall be associated with the very fountain head, and those who inherit a lesser degree of glory shall learn from those who attain unto the highest places, and so they will go on, and there will come knowledge and progress to them of an infinite character.
quotes.note: Untagged — this is progression between and within kingdoms, a question the category set does not cover — but the date makes it worth keeping. Eight months after James E. Talmage quietly deleted “and from kingdom to kingdom” from the Articles of Faith (talmage-af-kingdom-excision-1917), Ballard preaches infinite progress for the inhabitants of the lower glories while denying that they can ever close the gap: his illustration is three men in an endless race with a handicap, “would one ever catch the other? No.” Endless progress and permanent inequality asserted together, which is the position Talmage's revision was moving toward and is not the same as the deletion it made.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1917/1917-10-37-melvin-j-ballard-remarks-37.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1917sa, leaves n105–n112) and Final-Reviewed against an independent column-order reconstruction of the same scan; roughly twenty-five single-character OCR artifacts were corrected in that pass and a page-image adjudication in July 2026 restored the printed calling parenthetical below the speaker heading. None of the repairs fall inside the quoted passages except ordinary space-before-punctuation, left as printed. Conference Report, so A. Ballard is still a mission president here, fifteen months from his ordination as an Apostle, and the address is also the source of his widely reprinted vision of meeting the Savior — which is the part of the sermon everyone remembers and the reason the couplet paragraph has stayed unnoticed. Read against ballard-became-god-1914 by the same speaker: in 1914 he says the Father became God by compliance with law, in 1917 he says not everyone will follow Him, and in 1922 he supplies the corpus's fullest account of what the exalted then do (ballard-increase). The narrowing and the explicitness belong to the same man and the same decade.

title: Orson F. Whitney: Genesis 1:27 means “we have a Mother as well as a Father in heaven”
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, April 1920)

quotes.excerpt: He is the God described by Moses in the first chapter of Genesis, thus: "God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him, male and female created he them." This is equivalent to saying that God is in the form of man, and that we have a Mother as well as a Father in heaven, in whose image or likeness we are, male and female.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and reached by exegesis rather than by hymn: the whole weight rests on the “male and female” clause of Genesis 1:27, the same argument Erastus Snow ran in 1885 (snow-heavenly-mother-1885) and Whitney himself had run from this pulpit in 1907 (whitney-father-and-mother-1907). “This is equivalent to saying” is the load-bearing phrase — the Mother is presented as a logical entailment of the verse, not as a separate revelation, which is what lets Whitney assert her in the opening paragraph of an address about restoring the knowledge of God and then never return to her. Note what the argument is being used for: the target is the creedal God “without body, parts, or passions,” and the Mother arrives as collateral evidence of divine embodiment. Anthropomorphism is the claim; she is the corollary.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1920/1920-04-orson-f-whitney-the-true-and-living-god.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report of the Ninetieth Annual Conference (Internet Archive conferencereport1920a, leaf n120 = printed p. 119) after page-by-page heavyweight collation against that scan, and Final-Reviewed at 0.982 similarity with no candidates; the only Final Review change was converting all-caps side-heads to headings. Conference Report, so A. Delivered in the centennial year of the First Vision and structured as a list of Joseph Smith's services to humanity, of which the recovery of the true knowledge of God is the first. Filed with no citesId, and the absence is deliberate: Whitney gets to the Mother through Genesis without touching “O My Father,” exactly as he did in 1907 and as Rudger Clawson would in 1924 (clawson-parents-in-heaven-1924) — the hymn-dependent argument that Clawson falls back on in 1929 is not yet necessary.

title: The Lectures on Faith removed from the Doctrine and Covenants
speaker: Doctrine and Covenants revision committee (George F. Richards, chair; Anthony W. Ivins, Melvin J. Ballard, James E. Talmage, John A. Widtsoe, Joseph Fielding Smith)
office: Committee of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles appointed by the First Presidency
venue: Explanatory introduction to the 1921 edition of the Doctrine and Covenants, p. v

witnesses.scribe: Joseph Smith Papers transcript of the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants, Lecture Fifth
witnesses.note: Printed pp. 52–53; the paragraph quoted below breaks across the two pages. The catechism quoted below is printed p. 55 (image 63).

witnesses.scribe: Joseph Smith Papers transcript of the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants, Lecture Third
witnesses.note: Printed p. 38, §§12–15 — the attribute list, including the always-God clause.

witnesses.scribe: Current Doctrine and Covenants introduction, churchofjesuschrist.org
witnesses.note: The removal notice is still printed in the current hosted scripture, in reworded form. See the entry note for the wording change.

quotes.excerpt: There are two personages who constitute the great matchless, governing and supreme power over all things—by whom all things were created and made … They are the Father and the Son: The Father being a personage of spirit, glory and power: possessing all perfection and fulness: The Son, who was in the bosom of the Father, a personage of tabernacle, made, or fashioned like unto man, or being in the form and likeness of man …
quotes.note: The removed text itself — Lecture Fifth, §2, 1835 Doctrine and Covenants pp. 52–53; the sentence breaks across the page turn at “supreme power over / all things,” and is quoted continuously here. Untagged deliberately. This is a claim about what the Father presently is (unembodied spirit, against the Son's tabernacle), not a claim about whether he was always God, and tagging it FATHER-ALWAYS-GOD would be reading the 1844 controversy backwards into an 1835 sentence that is not addressing it. It earns its place because it is the specific incompatibility: by 1843 the Prophet was teaching that “The Father has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's” (D&C 130:22), and by April 1844 that the Father “dwelt on an earth” — and Lecture 5 was still bound into the canon saying the opposite about the Father's nature. Note also the count: the Godhead here has two personages, with the Holy Spirit identified as the shared mind of the Father and the Son rather than as a third personage.

quotes.excerpt: Q. How many personages are there in the Godhead? A. Two: the Father and the Son. … Q. What is the Father? A. He is a personage of glory and power.
quotes.note: The catechism attached to Lecture Fifth, 1835 Doctrine and Covenants p. 55 — the form in which this material was actually taught, since the catechisms were written to be memorized by elders and missionaries. Recorded because it shows the two-personage Godhead was not a stray phrase in a discursive lecture but the drilled answer. Also untagged, for the reason given on q1.

quotes.excerpt: 12 From the foregoing testimonies, we learn the following things respecting the character of God. 13 First, That he was God before the world was created, and the same God that he was, after it was created. … 15 Thirdly, That he changes not, neither is there variableness with him; but that he is the same from everlasting to everlasting, being the same yesterday to-day and forever; and that his course is one eternal round, without variation.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the sharpest one in the removed material — Lecture Third, §§12–15, 1835 Doctrine and Covenants p. 38. God was God before the world was created and does not change. Read against the text the Church would print in the Ensign fifty years after the removal: “We have imagined and supposed that God was God from all eternity. I will refute that idea” (see ensign-king-follett-1971 and kfd-1844). Between 1835 and 1844 the canon contained both propositions; after 1921 it contained only the later one, and it contained it nowhere in the Doctrine and Covenants at all.

quotes.excerpt: Certain lessons, entitled “Lectures on Faith,” which were bound in with the Doctrine and Covenants in some of its former issues, are not included in this edition. Those lessons were prepared for use in the School of the Elders, conducted in Kirtland, Ohio, during the winter of 1834-1835; but they were never presented to nor accepted by the Church as being otherwise than theological lectures or lessons.
quotes.note: The editorial act, in the only words the Church printed to explain it. Tagged RETREAT-REFRAME for what the sentence does rather than for any doctrine it states: it removes canonized text and reclassifies it retroactively, and the reclassification is a claim about 1835 that the 1835 volume contradicts — the Lectures were headed “the Doctrine of the Church of the Latter Day Saints,” the second part of that volume was headed “Covenants and Commandments,” and the 1835 First Presidency's preface said the Lectures embraced “the important doctrine of salvation” and that they were prepared to “answer to every principle advanced.” Note what the notice does not say: it gives no reason connected to the Godhead. The Godhead reason surfaces only in private correspondence — see the entry note.

notes: Verified text, source by source, because this entry stitches three documents together. (1) The 1921 explanatory notice was read verbatim from a printing of the 1921 edition digitized at archive.org (item doctrinecovenant0000jose_n3n7, catalogued 1923, notice on p. v, IA leaf 11); the wording quoted here is the printed wording, and it differs slightly from the form usually reprinted in the secondary literature, which drops the “to” and reads “never presented nor accepted.” (2) Lectures Third and Fifth were read verbatim from the Joseph Smith Papers transcripts of the 1835 first edition, pp. 38, 52–53, and 55, not from a modern reprint. (3) The committee's composition and chronology are received scholarship, not something verified here from committee minutes: the standard account is Richard S. Van Wagoner, Steven C. Walker, and Allen D. Roberts, “The ‘Lectures on Faith’: A Case Study in Decanonization,” Dialogue 20/3 (1987): 71–77 (https://corpus.noahairmet.com/b/v20n03-e92a/73), which records that the First Presidency appointed George F. Richards to chair the committee on 18 March 1920 with Ivins, Ballard, and Talmage, that Widtsoe and Joseph Fielding Smith joined by June, and that the group turned to the Doctrine and Covenants after finishing the Book of Mormon. Treat the committee roster and dates as that article's reporting. The Godhead motive is likewise received rather than official: Van Wagoner et al. print Joseph Fielding Smith's 1940 reply to John W. Fitzgerald listing four reasons for the removal, of which the last two are that the Lectures “are not complete as to their teachings regarding the Godhead” and that Talmage and the committee thought it “better not to have them bound in the same volume as the commandments or revelations” so as “to avoid confusion and contention on this vital point of belief.” That is a private letter written nineteen years after the fact by one committee member, and it is the closest thing to an official rationale that exists; the printed notice offers none. Dated at year precision to the 1921 edition, since the removal has no announcement date — there was no vote, no conference action, and no notice beyond the paragraph quoted in q4. Correlation graded historical-official: the 1921 edition was the Church's own scripture. One live afterlife worth recording: the current hosted Doctrine and Covenants introduction still reports the removal, but has rewritten both the setting and the reason — “Beginning with the 1835 edition, a series of seven theological lessons was also included; these were titled the Lectures on Faith. These had been prepared for use in the School of the Prophets in Kirtland, Ohio, from 1834 to 1835. Although profitable for doctrine and instruction, these lectures have been omitted from the Doctrine and Covenants since the 1921 edition because they were not given or presented as revelations to the whole Church.” The 1921 committee said the Lectures had never been accepted as anything other than lectures; the present text says they were not revelations, which is a narrower and less contestable claim, and it adds the concession that they are “profitable for doctrine and instruction.” Two rationales, a century apart, for one deletion.

title: Charles W. Penrose: “We do not say that God is a man; he is a perfected man”
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Member of the First Presidency
venue: General conference, first day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1921)

quotes.excerpt: …he is a divine being, a personage, a perfect and perfected man so to speak. We do not say that God is a man; he is a perfected man; he is exalted above all mankind, and he is our Father. He begat us in our original being, as his sons and daughters, verily and literally and truly. Jesus Christ who uttered that prayer is his Son just as we are, in the spirit, only he was the first-born.
quotes.note: Two moves in one breath, pulling opposite ways. FATHER-BECAME-GOD is graded hedges, not affirms: “perfected,” “exalted above all mankind” is attainment language (the precedent that reads “exalted man” as attainment is hunter-exalted-man-1948), but Penrose surrounds it with qualifiers — “so to speak,” and the explicit refusal “We do not say that God is a man” — and never says the Father was mortal, so nothing here reaches FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE. The begetting clause is the opposite register: “verily and literally and truly” is about as emphatic as the literal reading gets in this period, which is why SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS is affirms rather than the hedges given to bare “spirit son or daughter” formulas like proclamation-1995. No physiology is described and no Mother is mentioned. Spacing before semicolons normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed.

quotes.excerpt: In the book of Doctrine and Covenants we have a number of lectures inserted in the first part; which are not revelations. There are seven lectures, and in the fifth lecture, particularly, we are told that there are two personages in heaven, the Father and the Son, and that the holy spirit is the mind of God. That is true, so far as it goes. But the revelation through the Prophet Joseph Smith as to the personality of the Holy Ghost came many years after; it was given in 1843.
quotes.note: A member of the First Presidency, from the conference pulpit, telling the Church that a canonised text is “not revelation,” true only “so far as it goes,” and superseded by a later one — in the same year the Lectures on Faith were dropped from the Doctrine and Covenants (see lectures-on-faith-decanonized-1921). The operation, not the content, is the datum: it is the clearest surviving statement of the reasoning behind the decanonisation, delivered under his own printed side-head “PERTAINING TO THE STATEMENT IN THE LECTURES ON FAITH.” Note also what he does not say: no First Presidency announcement of the removal is made here, and the address gives no hint that the Lectures are about to leave the book.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1921/1921-04-charles-w-penrose-the-reality-of-the-resurrection.md, whose Final Review collated the body line by line against the archive.org scan conferencereport1921a (leaves n9–n17) and repaired the OCR artifacts in and around this passage, including the stray bracket in “verily and [literally.” Both excerpts were re-checked here against the item's own djvu text layer. Conference Report, so hearsay A. The title is supplied by the vault, not printed. The address is doctrinally busier than its title suggests: most of it is an exposition of the Holy Ghost as a personage of spirit prompted by letters reaching the President's office, and both quoted passages sit inside that argument rather than inside a discourse on the Father's nature.

title: George F. Richards: “the Father is indeed a resurrected immortal and glorified being”
speaker: George F. Richards
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1922)

quotes.excerpt: …for almost a century, we have been trying to convince the world that God has spoken from the heavens; that He has revealed Himself and His Son, Jesus Christ, and that the Father is indeed a resurrected immortal and glorified being, having a body of flesh and bones, and spirit like His Son after His resurrection, and that the Son ascended to heaven with His resurrected body, and retains it in the heavens…
quotes.note: Marked implied, and the implication is carried by a single word. “Resurrected” applied to the Father presupposes a death and therefore a mortality, which is more than the ordinary anthropomorphic formula of D&C 130:22 (“a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's”) asserts — but Richards does not state the mortality, draw the inference, or mention a mortal probation. He is enumerating the Church's message to the world, and the Father's resurrection is listed as settled content of that message, in parallel with the Son's, without argument or hedge. “Glorified” here reads as the resurrection state shared with the Son rather than as separate attainment language, so no FATHER-BECAME-GOD tag. Spacing before semicolons normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1922/1922-04-16-george-f-richards-remarks-18.md (the filename encodes talk order, not the date; the printed session is the second day, April 7, 1922), and re-verified word for word against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1922a. Conference Report, so hearsay A; the vault Final Review collated the body against leaves n55–n59. Title supplied by the vault (“We Carry Our Religion into Our Daily Work”), which is why this entry is titled from the doctrinal sentence instead. Worth registering as a register datum: the sentence is not a doctrinal exposition but a missionary-progress complaint — the Father's resurrected corporeality is cited as one of the things “we have been trying to convince the world” of, and the complaint is that only “a mere handful, less than half a million” have accepted it. Compare the same speaker nine years later in george-richards-immortal-beings-1931, where he stops and defines what “immortal being” means before applying it to the Father.

title: George F. Richards: eternal increase as the argument against 27,104 unmarried members
speaker: George F. Richards
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1924)

quotes.excerpt: We are informed that such marriages as are performed in our temples are necessary for men and women to obtain a fulness of glory and exaltation in the celestial kingdom of our Father in Heaven; for those who attain to that glory are to have a continuation of the seeds, forever, an eternal increase.
quotes.note: The D&C 132:19 idiom carried over intact — “a continuation of the seeds, forever” — with “an eternal increase” appended as its gloss, which explains nothing the revelation had not already left unexplained (see dc-132). No offspring, no spirit children, no mechanism, so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM. Richards does not cite the section; “We are informed that” is the whole of his attribution. Spacing before the semicolon normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1924/1924-04-10-george-f-richards-remarks-10.md (the filename encodes talk order, not the date; the printed session is the first day afternoon, April 4, 1924) and re-verified against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1924a. Conference Report, so hearsay A. The doctrinal clause is deployed, not expounded: the address is built on Presiding Bishop's Office statistics showing 27,104 unmarried members over 21, and eternal increase appears as the reason celibacy is “a doctrine of devils.” Richards then extends the argument past temple marriage to family size, telling the congregation that “when God offers a man a blessing and he refuses to accept or receive that blessing, that man is damned” and that those who decline children “will know the loss which they are sustaining, and it will be hell and torment to many of them.” That passage is about mortal childbearing, not spirit offspring, so it carries no tag here — but it is the same use of increase-as-threat catalogued at jfsmith-crowning-glory-1916, where Richards was one of the five apostles in the same 1916 Relief Society symposium.

title: Rudger Clawson: “suffice it to say we also have a mother in heaven”
speaker: Rudger Clawson
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1924, pp. 24–25)

quotes.excerpt: Now, brethren and sisters and friends, as a matter of fact, and as these scriptures which I have read, and many other scriptures, indicate, we existed before we came here and belonged to a great family of spirits in heaven. We speak of our Father in heaven. Jesus said, When you pray, say, "Our Father which art in heaven." We were his children in spirit, in heaven, and suffice it to say we also have a mother in heaven. There were parents in heaven — parents and children.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head "WE WERE THE CHILDREN OF GOD IN THE SPIRIT WORLD." The register is the finding. There is no hedge, no argument, no hymn and no appeal to authority: "as a matter of fact" governs the paragraph, and the Mother arrives inside a subordinate clause — "suffice it to say" — as something too settled to need establishing. Five years later, from the same pulpit, the same apostle will say "we believe that we have a mother there," reach for "O My Father" to license it, argue for it from the existence of a father, and commend the whole idea as "interesting and worthy of profound consideration" (clawson-mother-there-1929). One speaker, one office, five years, and the epistemic frame has moved from fact to belief.

quotes.excerpt: Let me say to you that when the earth was organized and rolled into existence, the Lord had a great and glorious purpose in view, and it was that these sons and daughters in the spirit world should come down to the earth and inhabit it.
quotes.note: The following paragraph, kept for setting. Untagged: the premortal family is doing structural work in the sermon — it is the answer to Bruno Lessing's "conundrum" about the object of life — but this sentence asserts nothing about a Mother or about generation.

notes: Verified word-for-word against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1924sa, printed pp. 24–25), and separately present in the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1924/1924-10-06-rudger-clawson-remarks-6.md, whose Final Review collated leaves n24–n27 at 0.991 similarity. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. Two provenance corrections the vault file does not yet carry, both settled on the scan. First, the vault frontmatter labels this the First Day Morning Session; the printed Report puts it in the AFTERNOON SESSION that convened at 2 o'clock, immediately after Orson F. Whitney's morning remarks, which is also what the opening sentence says ("I am dependent this afternoon"). Second, the filename's "1924-10-06" is a collection artifact of the same sequential-numbering ingest that corrupted the 1929 files; the October 1924 conference ran October 3–5 and this is the first day, October 3. The printed Report supplies no formal talk title, only side-heads; "A Conundrum" in the vault is the first of them. Filed as an original with no citesId, and that absence is the point of comparison with clawson-mother-there-1929, which cites the hymn twice: in 1924 Clawson reaches the Mother without Eliza R. Snow, exactly as Orson F. Whitney had in 1907 (whitney-father-and-mother-1907).

title: Orson F. Whitney: “the lesser intelligences” who became God's sons and daughters
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1925, “Divine Revelation”)

quotes.excerpt: What Latter-day Saint can doubt that Adam was among “the noble and great,” referred to in the Book of Abraham as “rulers,” chosen before they were born into this world to play leading parts in the divine drama having as its purpose the uplift and promotion of “the lesser intelligences” who became God's sons and daughters — the end designed by the all-wise, all-benevolent Creator from the beginning?
quotes.note: Three tiers in one sentence — “the lesser intelligences,” who then “became God's sons and daughters,” who were then “born into this world” — which is why this takes the framework tag and the bare three-estates schemes of the same decade (clawson-three-estates-1937, clawson-king-priest-1939) do not: those run spirit → mortal → resurrection and never reach behind the spirit. What Whitney does not supply is the mechanism of the “became.” There is no begetting verb here and no denial of one, so no spirit-birth tag; the scare quotes around “the lesser intelligences” are his own, marking the term as borrowed. Compare Abraham 3:18–26 (abraham-3), which supplies the “noble and great ones” and the graded intelligences he is reading. Printed em dashes and spacing restored from the archive.org text layer; no words changed.

quotes.excerpt: In the heavens, before this earth was formed, he was Michael the Archangel, leader of the loyal spirit hosts that vanquished Lucifer and his rebellious legions, winning the right to take bodies upon this planet, to become “souls” capable of endless increase and advancement.
quotes.note: “Endless increase” named and immediately paired with “advancement,” which is what keeps it euphemism: nothing says what increases, and the coupling invites the reader to hear personal progress rather than posterity. Whitney reuses the phrase almost verbatim three years later — “capable of endless increase and eternal progression” — in whitney-mother-in-heaven-1928, which suggests a settled formula rather than a considered claim.

quotes.excerpt: It is the path to endless glory and exaltation, the plan of eternal progression, designed by the wisdom of the Gods before the foundation of the world.
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose, and recorded because of what it looks like. “The plan of eternal progression” here is man's progression, not God's — it is the name of the plan, not a claim that God advances — so it is not DIVINE-PROGRESSION, and the plural “the Gods” is the Abraham 4 council idiom with no chain, no ancestry and no ordering behind it. This is the single most conflatable sentence in the address and it asserts neither of the things it is routinely quoted for.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1925/1925-10-28-orson-f-whitney-divine-revelation.md (the filename encodes talk order, not the date; the printed session is the second day morning, October 5, 1925), and re-verified against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1925sa, whose printed reading uses em dashes and capitalises “Gospel” where the vault does not. Conference Report, so hearsay A. “Divine Revelation” is Whitney's own printed title. Context matters for the register: the address is a reply to William Jennings Bryan and the Scopes trial, and the pre-existence material appears under the side-head “ADAM'S ANTECEDENTS” as an anti-evolution argument — the staged premortal history is deployed to prove that Adam “was no ordinary character,” not expounded for its own sake.

title: Brigham S. Young: “The reason God is God is because he has acquired all for which we are laboring”
speaker: Brigham S. Young
office: Recently returned president of the Northwestern States Mission
venue: General conference, second overflow meeting, Assembly Hall, Salt Lake City (Conference Report, April 1927)

quotes.excerpt: The reason God is God is because he has acquired all for which we are laboring. To the degree that we fail in acquisition and development, to that degree must we wait before we can come into the presence of him who has overcome all things.
quotes.note: Godhood given a cause, and the cause is acquisition. This is the clean case of the Father-status precedent that assigns FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone: attainment stated outright, with no mortality anywhere in the address, so no FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE and no couplet. Note the tense, which cuts the other way on a different question: “has acquired all” and “him who has overcome all things” describe a completed acquisition, and the address never suggests God is still acquiring — but it does not deny it either, and reading a position on divine progression into a sentence built to motivate missionaries would be retrojection, so the entry carries no DIVINE-PROGRESSION tag.

quotes.excerpt: The glorious thing in this gospel to me is, as the Prophet has told us, that we must acquire capacity that we may learn how to be gods ourselves. The most tremendous thought that was ever revealed to the human family was, that we, the sons of God, may rise to be what he is. That is the most glorious thing that ever animated the human heart or stimulated the human mind, that we, weak, erring though we are, may be even as God, our Father.
quotes.note: Untagged, following the precedent set at whitney-father-and-mother-1907-q3: this is theosis at full strength — “learn how to be gods ourselves,” “rise to be what he is,” and later in the address “the soul which is a god in embryo” — and it still asserts nothing about spirit offspring, eternal increase, or a chain behind the Father. Recorded because the pairing is the point: the same speaker who gives Godhood a cause in q1 never once takes the next step to increase or to ancestry. “As the Prophet has told us” is a relay of the King Follett Discourse (see kfd-1844), whose “you have got to learn how to be gods yourselves” Young is paraphrasing rather than quoting; he also twice attributes “You must acquire capacity” to Joseph Smith, a saying not found in that form in the standard King Follett texts.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1927/1927-04-15-brigham-s-young-remarks-17.md (the filename encodes talk order, not the date) and re-verified against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1927a. Conference Report, so hearsay A. Provenance detail that bears on weight: this was the second overflow meeting in the Assembly Hall, presided over by Rulon S. Wells of the First Council of Seventy, not a Tabernacle session — and the speaker is a returning mission president, not a General Authority — the Report's own caption identifies him only as former president of the Northwestern States Mission, and no further office is claimed here. The doctrinal sentence is therefore printed in the official Report but carries no apostolic weight, which is precisely what makes it useful: it shows the attainment account of Godhood circulating as unremarkable common property in 1927.

title: Orson F. Whitney: the Great Creator “found himself” among the lesser intelligences
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon meeting, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1927)

quotes.excerpt: It was instituted in the heavens before the earth was formed, as the means of uplift and promotion for “the lesser intelligences,” in the midst of whom the Great Creator found himself at the beginning, and who became his sons and daughters, first in the spirit and afterwards in the flesh.
quotes.note: Whitney's sharpest version of the staging, and the load-bearing clause is “found himself.” The intelligences are already there when the Creator arrives; he does not make them, he finds them, and only afterwards do they become his children — first in the spirit, then in the flesh. Three tiers, both transitions, one sentence, which is why this takes TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK where the decade's three-estates schemes do not. SPIRIT-BIRTH-ADOPTION is graded hedges, not affirms, on the same reasoning as bh-roberts-tripartite-q2: Whitney's verb is “became,” never “begotten,” and the uncreatedness of the subject pulls toward a relationship entered into rather than a birth — but he never says adoption, never denies begetting, and describes no mechanism at all. Compare his own 1925 formulation (whitney-lesser-intelligences-1925), where the intelligences “became God's sons and daughters” with no “found himself” clause and no spirit/flesh ordering.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1927/1927-04-27-orson-f-whitney-remarks-33.md (the filename encodes talk order, not the date; the printed session is the second day afternoon, April 4, 1927) and re-verified against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1927a, where the phrase is broken across a line as “intelli-gences.” Conference Report, so hearsay A. The rest of the address is a survey of the gospel dispensations, Adam's presidency, and Adam-ondi-Ahman, with nothing further on premortal staging — the sentence quoted here is the second paragraph of the discourse, offered as a definition of what “Mormonism” is to “the stranger within our gates,” which is what makes the casualness of “found himself” worth recording. Read against the wider corpus, this is the most explicit conference-pulpit denial of creation ex nihilo for intelligences between B. H. Roberts's Seventy's Course (bh-roberts-tripartite) and the mid-century retrenchment (jfs-agq-intelligences-1963).

title: Orson F. Whitney: “what more reasonable than the conclusion that we have a Mother as well as a Father in Heaven”
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day morning meeting, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1928, “God's Work And Man's”)

quotes.excerpt: Joseph knew God, for he had seen him, had conversed with him, and received from him instruction. He declared God to be in human form, an exalted, glorified Man, and that was his first great service to humanity. He brought back the lost knowledge of the true and living God.
quotes.note: “An exalted, glorified Man” — attainment language, which per the Father-status precedent (and the reading given the same phrase at hunter-exalted-man-1948) is FATHER-BECAME-GOD on its own, with no mortality stated anywhere in the address and therefore no FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE. Register worth noting: Whitney does not argue for this, he attributes it to Joseph Smith's first vision and calls it “his first great service to humanity,” placing the corporeal, exalted God at the head of the restoration's contributions rather than at its speculative edge.

quotes.excerpt: And how reasonable, how logical it is. What simple, plain common sense. For if God made man in his own image, then God must be in the image of man. And if men and women are indeed God's children, his sons and daughters, what more reasonable than the conclusion that we have a Mother as well as a Father in Heaven, in whose likeness we are, male and female?
quotes.note: The argument from the image of God, run in two steps and reaching the Mother as a conclusion rather than assuming her — which is the difference from his own 1907 address (whitney-father-and-mother-1907-q1), where she is a premise the world is dared to refute. Graded affirms: the rhetorical question is a conclusion Whitney plainly endorses and files under “THE GOSPEL OF COMMON SENSE,” not a hedge. This is the same inference Rudger Clawson makes a year later (clawson-mother-there-1929) and Gordon B. Hinckley makes in 1991 (hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991); Whitney is the only one of the three who states the male-and-female likeness premise it depends on.

quotes.excerpt: We are placed here as spirits to take bodies and thus become souls, capable of endless increase and eternal progression
quotes.note: The 1925 formula again, almost word for word (whitney-lesser-intelligences-1925-q2), with “advancement” swapped for “eternal progression.” Increase is named and nothing else is — no offspring, no mechanism, no godhood — and it is followed immediately by the two-estate framing, not by any account of what increases. A settled phrase doing settled-phrase work, which is what FORWARD-EUPHEMISM is for.

quotes.excerpt: The elements are eternal; matter as well as spirit is uncreatable, indestructible. Out of the eternal elements God created the earth spiritually and temporally, with all that it contains.
quotes.note: Untagged, and recorded for the tension it holds open. “Spirit is uncreatable” is the premise on which the adoption reading of spirit birth rests — it is what Whitney's own “found himself” sentence of eighteen months earlier (whitney-creator-found-himself-1927) turns on — yet the same address asserts literal divine parenthood in q2 without ever noticing that the two need reconciling. Whitney is arguing against creation ex nihilo, not about spirit birth, which is exactly why the sentence is useful: the anti-creation premise circulated as plain common sense while the begetting language circulated beside it, unharmonised.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1928/1928-10-18-orson-f-whitney-remarks-23.md (the filename encodes talk order, not the date) and re-verified word for word against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1928sa. Conference Report, so hearsay A; “God's Work And Man's” is Whitney's own printed title. Provenance caveat carried over from the vault: this address had been absorbed entirely into the neighbouring John G. Allred file during the original ingest and was extracted from the scan afterwards, so it is a comparatively recent addition to the corpus — the four quotes above were checked directly against the item's text layer rather than trusted from the vault alone. The printed discourse ends on a Watts hymn quotation with no closing “Amen”; that is the scan's reading, not a truncation.

title: Rudger Clawson: “Who ever heard of a father where there was no mother?”
speaker: Rudger Clawson
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1929)

quotes.excerpt: We understand, from the scriptures, that Jesus Christ is our elder brother. If that be the case then we are his younger brothers and younger sisters; we belonged to a great family before we came into the world. It was the family of God, for Jesus said: "When you pray, say our Father which art in heaven. Our Father is there, and we believe that we have a mother there. That thought was beautifully expressed in the hymn that the choir sang this morning. I think you will agree with me that it is a very wonderful thought indeed. At least it is interesting and worthy of profound consideration.
quotes.note: Note the register: “we believe that we have a mother there,” and then the doctrine is commended as “interesting and worthy of profound consideration” rather than taught as known. The quotation mark before “When you pray” is never closed in the vault text collated against the scan, and is preserved here rather than silently repaired. Spacing before semicolons and colons normalized; no words changed. The hymn was sung by the Tabernacle Choir that morning, which is how it entered the discourse — worship first, doctrine after.

quotes.excerpt: "I had learned to call thee Father, Through thy spirit from on high, But until the key of knowledge Was restored, I knew not why." "In the heavens are parents single? No, the thought makes reason stare. Truth is reason. Truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there."
quotes.note: Punctuation follows the 1929 Conference Report printing, which differs from the hymnal text (commas for semicolons, a period after “stare”). See o-my-father.

quotes.excerpt: To say the least, if we are led to believe that we have a Father in heaven, I think we are justified in believing that we have a Mother there. Who ever heard of a father where there was no mother?
quotes.note: The Erastus Snow argument from nature, compressed to a single rhetorical question and shorn of the anatomy — and hedged twice over (“to say the least,” “I think we are justified in believing”). Sixty-two years later Gordon B. Hinckley will make the identical move in the identical words of logic: “Logic and reason would certainly suggest that if we have a Father in Heaven, we have a Mother in Heaven.” That the inference survives verbatim across the whole twentieth century, while the anatomical premise behind it disappears, is the point of filing this entry next to snow-heavenly-mother-1885 and hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1929/1929-10-31-rudger-clawson-remarks-38.md, whose Final Review collated §0 against the archive.org scan conferencereport1929sa, leaves n105–n109, fixing OCR errors and a page-break sentence split. Provenance caveat worth carrying: the October 1929 ingest suffered the same systemic corruption as April 1929 — sequential “remarks-N” filenames with fabricated dates and session labels assigned by file position — and the heavyweight pass reconstructed the true date (October 6, 1929) and session from the report's own headers, so the filename is not evidence of anything. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. The vault frontmatter gives the generic “General Authority”; Clawson had presided over the Quorum of the Twelve since 1921. Filed as an original with the citesId edge preserved because the argument in q3 is Clawson's own and is not in the hymn. This entry and grant-o-my-father-1938 open the 1925–1965 stretch in which the hymn keeps circulating while almost no one argues from it.

title: George F. Richards defines “immortal beings,” then applies it to the Father
speaker: George F. Richards
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1931)

quotes.excerpt: And what are they? They are immortal beings. And what are immortal beings? Immortal beings are those who have passed through the change by which there is a separation of the body and the spirit, and then the resurrection, which is a uniting of the body and the spirit, so that there will be no more any separation. … In these heavenly personages we see two immortal beings, two beings who are glorified and exalted, and one of them is the Father, and the other the Son — there can be no question about that, because the personage speaking said to the boy, “This is my Beloved Son, hear him.”
quotes.note: Still implied, but the implication is now spelled out as a definition. In 1922 Richards simply called the Father “resurrected” (george-richards-resurrected-father-1922); here he stops, asks what an immortal being is, answers that it is one who has died and been resurrected, and then applies the term to both personages of the first vision — the Father included — and says “there can be no question about that.” The mortality is entailed twice over and still never asserted: Richards nowhere says the Father lived a mortal probation, and the passage is an argument about corporeality against sectarian creeds, not an argument about the Father's past. That is the whole reason the tag is marked implied rather than plain. The elision covers one intervening sentence on the inseparable connection of body and spirit being necessary to eternal life.

quotes.excerpt: Those who attain to a fulness of glory [in] the celestial kingdom are to have an eternal increase and a continuation of the seeds forever. It is unthinkable and untrue that that condition could exist without sustaining the marriage relation in the other world.
quotes.note: The 1924 formula (george-richards-continuation-seeds-1924) with an inference bolted on, and the inference runs backwards from the one the pulpit usually draws: instead of arguing from eternal marriage to increase, Richards takes increase as given and argues from it to the necessity of the marriage relation persisting after death — “unthinkable and untrue” that it could be otherwise. Still euphemism: the D&C 132 idiom of seeds and continuation is repeated without gloss, and nothing names offspring or a mechanism. Bracketed “[in]” repairs an OCR artifact reading “m” that is present in the Internet Archive text layer for conferencereport1931sa and reproduced in the vault; the printed page reads “in.”

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1931/1931-10-george-f-richards-moronis-exhortation.md and re-verified against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1931sa (the same text layer the vault Final Review collated against, which is why the “m the celestial kingdom” artifact is common to both and is repaired in brackets rather than silently). Conference Report, so hearsay A; the title is supplied by the vault. Both passages sit in an address whose announced subject is Moroni 10 and the testimony of the standard works; the doctrinal content arrives under the printed side-heads “IMMORTAL BEINGS” and “MARRIAGE FOR ETERNITY” as consequences of the first vision, not as a discourse on the Father or on exaltation.

title: Rudger Clawson: “God is a glorified being, a glorified man… some people might regard this statement as blasphemy”
speaker: Rudger Clawson
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1935)

quotes.excerpt: But now, we are told in the Book of Genesis, that man is in the image of God, is made like him with this difference, that God is a glorified being, a glorified man. I know there are some people in the world at large who might regard this statement as blasphemy, but it is the truth, nevertheless…
quotes.note: “A glorified man” is attainment language and takes FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone; Clawson never says the Father was mortal, quotes no couplet, and the difference he is drawing between God and man is one of state, not of history. The blasphemy clause is the register datum and it is a direct echo of talmage-af-1899 (“in the face of direct charges of blasphemy, the Church proclaims the eternal truth”) thirty-six years on — the President of the Twelve, in general conference, naming the charge before anyone can make it and answering it with “but it is the truth, nevertheless.” Compare how carefully Penrose handles the same word fourteen years earlier (penrose-perfected-man-1921: “We do not say that God is a man”).

quotes.excerpt: The Temple marriage is different. When a couple is united by the ordinance of God's house they are married for time and all eternity, and thus is perpetuated the great principle of fatherhood and motherhood, as already mentioned.
quotes.note: Parenthood itself, rather than posterity, is what the temple perpetuates — “the great principle of fatherhood and motherhood” — which names the office and leaves the offspring entirely unspecified. Euphemism at one further remove than “eternal increase,” since not even increase is named. The back-reference “as already mentioned” points to his opening remarks about mortal mothers and fathers in Israel, so the sentence reaches eternity through a joke about the Singing Mothers rather than through any doctrinal exposition.

quotes.excerpt: We have learned that in the life of man there are three estates, and that the first was our preexistent estate which was wholly spiritual; that the second estate is the spiritual and temporal, or mortal, combined; and that the third estate is the glorification of the spiritual and the temporal through the resurrection.
quotes.note: Untagged deliberately, and the omission is the point. This is the mid-century three-estates scheme — spirit, mortal, resurrected glory — and it is routinely mistaken for the tripartite framework, which it is not: there is no intelligence tier behind the spirit and no account of how the spirit came to be. Contrast whitney-creator-found-himself-1927 and bh-roberts-tripartite, where the tier that precedes the spirit is the whole argument. Clawson repeats this scheme in 1937 and 1939 (clawson-three-estates-1937, clawson-king-priest-1939) without ever adding the missing tier. Apostrophe artifact in “that'the” normalized to “that the”; no words changed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1935/1935-04-06-clawson.md (vault id 1935-04-rudger-clawson-the-mystery-and-purpose-of-life) and re-verified against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1935a. Conference Report, so hearsay A; the title is supplied by the vault. Clawson reads Abraham 3:24–26 aloud in the body of the address as the scriptural warrant for the estates scheme, hence the citesId edge to abraham-3 — though notably he takes only the “added upon” verses and not the graded-intelligences verses that precede them, which is the half of Abraham 3 that would have supplied the tier his scheme is missing.

title: Stephen L Richards: “the fatherhood, — and motherhood too, of our individual spirits”
speaker: Stephen L Richards
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1936)

quotes.excerpt: The continuity of intelligence and intelligencies; the fatherhood, — and motherhood too, of our individual spirits; the free agency and choice which were ours in the pre-earth life; spiritual creation preceding mortal creation; the relationship of body to spirit in this life and in the hereafter, the transcendent scheme of eternal progression, — all these and many related items constitute a unified, logical, authoritative exposition without counterpart in Christian literature.
quotes.note: A list, not an argument, and that is what makes it valuable: three separately contested doctrines are enumerated as settled, distinctive contributions of Joseph Smith. TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK because all three tiers and both transitions are present in sequence — continuing intelligences, then spirits who are fathered and mothered, then “spiritual creation preceding mortal creation.” HEAVENLY-MOTHER is affirms: “motherhood too” is asserted, not hedged, though the em-dashed afterthought construction is itself the register datum — she is named in a subordinate clause of a list. SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS is graded hedges on the proclamation-1995 precedent: parenthood of spirits is asserted and no mechanism whatever is described. Note also that “spiritual creation” sits in the same list as the fatherhood and motherhood, with no sign that Richards saw creation and begetting as competing accounts. Line-break spacing artifacts “intelli-gencies” and “lif e” normalized from the printed OCR, and spacing before semicolons closed up; no words changed.

quotes.excerpt: One of the features of temple work should for emphasis be specially mentioned. It is the sealing of husband and wife in the eternal covenant of marriage. Joseph Smith taught that the family circle is the foundation of exaltation and that its projection into eternity is heaven itself.
quotes.note: “Its projection into eternity is heaven itself” — the family continued, with nothing said about what the continuation produces. Not even the word increase appears; the content is exhausted by persistence. Compare the same speaker nine years later at richards-eternal-increase-1945, where he does name increase and immediately flags that he mentions it “with a little hesitation,” and two years later at slrichards-eternal-increase-1938, where increase is named without any hesitation at all.

quotes.excerpt: There will be general salvation for all in the sense in which the term is generally used, but salvation, meaning resurrection, is not exaltation. In the hereafter, as in this life, there are degrees of glory, preferential places and conditions.
quotes.note: Untagged context, kept because it is the distinction the whole forward axis depends on and it is stated here with unusual bluntness. Everything the corpus files under eternal increase is predicated on exaltation being a narrower thing than salvation; Richards separates them in one sentence and then, two paragraphs later, gives the content of the narrower thing as the family projected into eternity (q2) — and no further.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1936/1936-10-stephen-l.-richards-certainty-came-with-first-vision.md and re-verified word for word against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1936sa. Conference Report, so hearsay A; the title is supplied by the vault. The address is an enumeration of “the unique and distinctive contributions of Joseph Smith,” explicitly disclaiming any attempt to rank them — which is why the doctrines above arrive in a list rather than an exposition, and why the entry records the enumeration itself rather than an argument for any item in it.

title: Rudger Clawson: three estates, and no tier behind the spirit
speaker: Rudger Clawson
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1937)

quotes.excerpt: We are told in the Pearl of Great Price that man's experience has come to him through certain estates. There is the first estate and the second estate and the third estate. In the first, pre-existent, estate man's experience was spiritual in its character. We were spirits there and we were happy. We belonged to a great family of spirits. … it is only when we have attained to that condition that we can rise in the resurrection, after taking up these bodies, to exaltation and glory in that future third estate; so that we have in this matter of three estates a perfect brief citation of the purpose and meaning of life.
quotes.note: Untagged, and the entry exists to record the untagging. This is the scheme most often mistaken for the tripartite framework, and the three tiers are spirit → mortal → resurrected exaltation: there is no intelligence behind the spirit, no account of how the spirit came to be, and no begetting or creating verb anywhere in the address. Where the spirits came from is answered only by “We belonged to a great family of spirits,” which names a relationship and no origin. Nothing else in the discourse touches the axes either — no eternal increase, no offspring, no Heavenly Mother, no claim about the Father's past — and “exaltation and glory in that future third estate” is bare theosis, which per whitney-father-and-mother-1907-q3 carries no forward tag on its own. The elision covers roughly two paragraphs on the body as the tabernacle of the spirit and on the spirits who kept not their first estate.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1937/1937-04-rudger-clawson-four-important-books.md and re-verified against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1937a. Conference Report, so hearsay A; the title is supplied by the vault. This is deliberately a negative entry, on the same principle as pratt-infinite-gods-1855 and fp-1925: the President of the Twelve gives what he calls “a perfect brief citation of the purpose and meaning of life,” and the citation contains none of the doctrines this corpus tracks. Its value is as a denominator — it is the middle term of Clawson's own three-address sequence (clawson-glorified-man-1935, here, clawson-king-priest-1939) in which the estates scheme is restated and the missing tier is never supplied. The bulk of the address is a survey of the four standard works and a long approving quotation from an editorial on caring for the body, credited in the printed Report to “Bernard McFadden, the publisher of the Physical Culture Journal.”

title: Stephen L Richards: eternal increase in the celestial kingdom, and “the lesser but potentially divine intelligences”
speaker: Stephen L Richards
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1938)

quotes.excerpt: The highest and most desirable is the celestial kingdom of our Father. In that kingdom and only there do intelligences attain their highest state of perfection. Only there do we have assurance of the reunion of families and the perpetuation of family relationship and eternal increase. In that kingdom man may ultimately become divine.
quotes.note: Increase named, located exclusively in the celestial kingdom, and left undefined — bracketed between family reunion on one side and “man may ultimately become divine” on the other, so that the hearer can take it as either posterity or growth in glory and Richards never has to say which. Euphemism, and unusually clean euphemism: the three claims are stacked without a connective that would commit him to the generative reading. Note the exclusivity construction, “Only there,” which is the standard mid-century way of making increase load-bearing for temple marriage without expounding it; compare eldred-smith-no-increase-1948, where the same doctrine appears only as the thing the unworthy forfeit.

quotes.excerpt: I propose as the next major phase of this new interpretation a unique and distinctive conception of the family of God. God, the Master Intelligence is the Creator and veritable Father of his children, the lesser but potentially divine intelligences who make up his family and populate his kingdom.
quotes.note: Graded hedges because the sentence holds both mechanisms at once and settles neither: “Creator and veritable Father,” with “veritable” insisting the fatherhood is not figurative and “Creator” sitting immovably beside it. What the children are called matters too — “intelligences,” not spirits — and there is no spirit-birth stage anywhere in the address, which is a real narrowing from his own list eighteen months earlier (slrichards-fatherhood-motherhood-1936-q1), where the intelligences, the fathered-and-mothered spirits and the mortal creation were three distinct items in sequence. No Heavenly Mother appears here at all. The graded hierarchy — a “Master Intelligence” over “lesser but potentially divine intelligences” — is the Widtsoe-style ordering by degree rather than by descent; it asserts nothing about a chain, so no INFINITE-CHAIN tag (compare widtsoe-many-gods-1949).

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1938/1938-04-stephen-l.-richards-intelligence-man-s-chief-investiture.md and re-verified against the archive.org djvu text of conferencereport1938a (the second passage is split across printed p. 24 by a running head in the scan; the vault reading is confirmed on both sides of the break). Conference Report, so hearsay A; the title is supplied by the vault. The frame is worth recording: Richards presents the whole address as “a new interpretation of the Gospel of Christ,” saying he uses “new” rather than “true” for diplomatic reasons, and builds it on the uncreatedness of intelligence from D&C 93:29 — so the family-of-God section quoted in q2 arrives already committed to intelligences that were never made, which is what makes “Creator and veritable Father” a substantive tension rather than loose phrasing.

title: Heber J. Grant reads “O My Father” into the conference record
speaker: Heber J. Grant
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference, opening address, first day morning session (Conference Report, October 1938)

quotes.excerpt: I have a little book in which I have recorded from time to time for many years items that have very profoundly impressed me… I have decided to read here today a part of what was in my Christmas greeting. I wish that all that is in my greeting might be read by all of the Latter-day Saints. As our conference proceedings are to be published, that is my excuse for reading a portion of this book entitled, "Treasures I Would Share," which was distributed by me for Christmas of 1937.
quotes.note: The mechanism of transmission, stated by the transmitter. Grant's reason for reading the hymn aloud is explicitly that the Conference Report will print it — he is using the opening address as a publishing channel. That is why this entry exists: nothing is argued, and the whole text of the hymn enters the official record anyway.

quotes.excerpt: I had learned to call thee Father, Through thy Spirit from on high; But until the Key of Knowledge Was restored, I knew not why. In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason, truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there.
quotes.note: The Mother stanza, read by the President of the Church in the opening address of general conference. Spacing before semicolons normalized from the printed OCR, and the hymn's verse line breaks are rendered as running text; no words changed. See o-my-father.

quotes.excerpt: When I leave this frail existence, When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high? Then, at length, when I've completed All you sent me forth to do, With your mutual approbation, Let me come and dwell with you.
quotes.note: The closing stanza, which is where the hymn does its heaviest devotional work: the Mother is not merely posited, she is addressed, and reunion with her is the thing prayed for. This stanza, not the “parents single” couplet, is what most twentieth-century speakers actually quote — Henry D. Taylor in 1961, Hugh B. Brown in 1968, Neal A. Maxwell in 1978 — which is why phrase searches for “parents single” badly undercount the cluster.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1938/1938-10-heber-j-grant-selections-from-treasures-i-would-share.md, whose Final Review collated the text against the archive.org scan conferencereport1938sa, leaves n2–n16, with reading order rebuilt from the scan's DjVu word coordinates; five running-head bleeds were removed and side-heads converted to headings, no wording changed. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. A pure citation and deliberately so — Grant makes no argument about a Mother in heaven, offers no gloss, and does not pause at the stanza. He is reading ten favorite poems and hymns from a Christmas booklet, and “O My Father” is the fourth of the six he got through before the clock beat him. The entry earns its place on office and date rather than content: this is the President of the Church putting the full text of the doctrine's primary vehicle into the printed proceedings in 1938, in the middle of the stretch where the dataset otherwise goes quiet. Transmission without argument is the characteristic mid-century mode, and this is the cleanest specimen of it.

title: Rudger Clawson: “he as a king and a priest and she as a queen and priestess”
speaker: Rudger Clawson
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1939)

quotes.excerpt: Before we can enter into full and complete exaltation and glory and receive a fulness of joy we must take into account the sublime doctrine of marriage. It is necessary to our final exaltation. … that he as a king and a priest and she as a queen and priestess might rise to exaltation and glory and together receive a fulness of joy.
quotes.note: Exaltation made conditional on marriage and then described entirely in royal-priestly terms — king and priest, queen and priestess — with the pair rising “together.” Increase is never named, nor offspring, nor a mechanism, so this is euphemism at the far end of the scale: the temple's endowment vocabulary standing in for whatever the couple's exaltation consists of. The precedent for tagging godhood-via-temple-marriage without any generative content is eldred-smith-slavery-godhood-1950. The elision covers Clawson's retelling of Eden — that man and woman were made in “one creative act” and that it was not right for Adam to be alone — and also steps over an OCR artifact in the printed text (“for a. companion”) that is present in the Internet Archive text layer for conferencereport1939a.
