venue: General conference, second day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1965)

quotes.excerpt: Someday we will more clearly know who we are. We will understand the great scriptural teaching that God, angels, spirits, and men are all of the same species in different stages of righteousness and development.
quotes.note: Species identity stated as flatly as the corpus has it, and called “the great scriptural teaching” with no scripture named. Left untagged on the reading applied to brown-deify-man-1956-q2, the closest parallel in the corpus (“Father and children, belong to the same society of eternal intelligences … he is the most advanced”): placing God at the top of a developmental scale implies an ascent, but Sill does not state one, and the no-retrojection rule keeps the inference out of the categories. Recorded because the implication is unusually bare here — “different stages of … development” distributes across a list whose first member is God.

quotes.excerpt: God placed the gold and silver in the earth, but he endowed his children with his own attributes and made them heirs to his potentialities. And according to his own immutable laws of heredity, the children may hope sometime to become like the parents.
quotes.note: The heredity argument, printed under the side-head “The Handiwork of God.” It is the same like-begets-like move Romney makes in October 1964 and Hugh B. Brown makes in October 1966, and by itself it asserts likeness, not offspring — untagged for the same reason romney-1964-q1 is. Sill runs it twice: earlier, under “Partake of the Divine Nature,” he asks “why should we call God our Heavenly Father and at the same time fail to believe his promise that the offspring of God may someday become like the parent?”

quotes.excerpt: Then what may not be done in eternity by one of these Godmen? Remove from his path the incident of death; or, better yet, contemplate him as raised from the dead; and give to him in the full splendor of manhood's estate, immortality, endless existence, what may we not hope that he will accomplish? What limits can you venture to fix as marking the boundary of his development, of his progress? … Why should there be any limits thought of?
quotes.note: B. H. Roberts, The Mormon Doctrine of Deity (1903), pp. 33–35, as Sill cites it — read to general conference at extraordinary length, roughly a full printed page of the Report. Not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION: the unbounded progress is predicated of resurrected men, Roberts's “Godmen,” not of God. Contrast roberts-progress-of-god-1911, where the same author does predicate it of God and Joseph Fielding Smith later calls the proposition dangerous. The ellipsis inside the passage is Sill's, as printed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1965/1965-10-sill-my-brothers-and-sisters-i-appreciate-very.md, whose body was collated line by line against the DjVu column-order reconstruction of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1965sa, leaves n55–n60, printed pp. 55–60) in the final-review pass, which fixed three mechanical OCR artifacts and restored the printed side-heads. Conference Report, so A. Every quote here is deliberately untagged: the address is theosis at full volume — a three-act framing of existence, species identity with God, heredity, and a long reading from Roberts on limitless progress — and it never asserts eternal increase, spirit offspring, or a backward claim about the Father. That is exactly why it belongs in a comprehensive corpus: it is the shape of the mid-century deification sermon with the generative and genealogical halves absent, and the untagged rows are the evidence for that absence rather than an oversight. Sill's three-stage framing (premortal, mortal, eternal) is the standard three estates and not the intelligence→spirit→body staging, so no TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK tag.

title: Truman G. Madsen: an imaginary Joseph Smith on how God became God
speaker: Truman G. Madsen
office: Professor of Philosophy, Brigham Young University
venue: Eternal Man (Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 1966), ch. “Evil and Suffering,” pp. 55–57

quotes.excerpt: Now the Creeds say that God has always been God. But this well-motivated expression of reverence is a solemn travesty. The truth is infinitely more inspiring: that God Himself became God (whose power now extends in and through all things) by the mastery of the same ultimate and unchanging conditions to which you and I are subject. So, likewise, did His Firstborn Son, Jesus the Christ.
quotes.note: These words are not Madsen speaking in his own voice. They are assigned to a character labelled “The Prophet” in an invented dialogue between Joseph Smith and the mother of a blind baby — see the next quote. The content itself is past attainment plus subjection to conditions God did not create; Madsen does not say God was mortal, and he asserts no chain of any length. The always-God tag marks a denial: the passage calls the creedal always-God position a travesty while asserting attainment.

quotes.excerpt: The dialogue is imaginary, but the ideas are not. The “Mother” poses questions that have been raised numberless times. For every sentence in the Prophet's “replies” there is a first-hand counterpart in his writings or sermons.
quotes.note: Madsen's own footnote 5 on the device, printed at p. 55, before the dialogue begins. Any citation of the passage above has to carry this sentence. Note also the limit of Madsen's own claim: he asserts that a first-hand counterpart exists for every sentence, but he supplies no such counterpart for the “God Himself became God” line — his note there points instead to the King Follett Discourse with B. H. Roberts's footnotes, and to a list of finite-God philosophers.

quotes.excerpt: The rare notion that God is in a sense finite, limited by the nature of His environment, has been taught in some form by such men as William James, A. N. Whitehead, Charles Hartshorne, E. S. Brightman, and A. C. Garnett.
quotes.note: Madsen's footnote 11, attached to the “became God” line. It fixes the genre: this is a finite-God theodicy in conversation with process and personalist philosophy, not a genealogical claim about heavenly grandfathers.

notes: Verified verbatim against the printed text at pp. 55–57 (the dialogue passage runs from p. 56 onto p. 57; footnote 5 sits at the foot of p. 55, footnote 11 at the foot of p. 57). The scan's OCR is poor and mangles “but” to “hut” and “William” beyond recognition in the notes; those are scanner artifacts of an otherwise clear text and are silently corrected here. The framing caveat is not optional: the speaker is a fictional Joseph Smith, ventriloquized by Madsen for a theodicy, and quoting “God Himself became God” as though Madsen or Joseph Smith said it flatly is the single most common misuse of this book. Never-official: a BYU philosopher's trade book from Deseret Book. Adjacent interest for the Roberts/James strand — Madsen aligns his position with James, Whitehead, Hartshorne and Brightman by name.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith on how a Father of flesh and bone begot spirits: “this question the Lord has not fully explained”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and Church Historian (later President of the Church)
venue: Answers to Gospel Questions, vol. 5 (1966), “Personal Father and Spiritual Offspring” (question 54); originally a “Your Question” column in the Improvement Era

quotes.excerpt: Question: "If God has a body of flesh and bones plus spirit, how is it that his children were spirits, in the pre-existence?"
quotes.note: The spirit-birth mechanism question in its bluntest form: an embodied Father is supposed to have produced non-embodied offspring, and the member wants to know how. The title the volume gives the answer — “Personal Father and Spiritual Offspring” — names the problem exactly.

quotes.excerpt: This is a very proper question, and perhaps we cannot give an answer that will satisfy these people who have been traditioned in the doctrine that God is a Spirit. … This question the Lord has not fully explained, but there are sufficient reasons why we should believe that he does have a tabernacle of flesh and bones.
quotes.note: Concession and pivot in a single sentence. He grants the question is proper, states that the mechanism has not been revealed, and then answers a different question — whether the Father is embodied — for the remainder of the column. The rest of the answer argues from Christ's begetting and resurrected body that the Father must have a body; the spirit-birth mechanism the member asked about is never returned to. Note also the reframing of the questioner: a doctrinal question from within becomes a problem belonging to “these people who have been traditioned” outside.

notes: Verified by reading the complete Q&A in the GSA copy; it is short, running about one page, and the whole of it after the sentence quoted here is an argument from Hebrews 1:3, John 14:9, Zechariah 13:6 and D&C 45:51–54 that the Father has a body of flesh and bones. Dated by publication year of volume 5 (1966) at year precision; this edition prints no individual column dates. Cited by title and volume sequence number (54); the reflowed digital edition carries no printed pagination and page numbers are not asserted. Correlation graded historical-official for the reasons given in jfs-agq-as-man-is-1958. The reason to keep this entry is the contrast with jfs-agq-mother-in-heaven-1960: in 1960 the same author answered a closely related question with a confident mechanism — “how did we become such, if we had no mother to give us spirit birth?” — and here, six years later, tells a member that the Lord has not fully explained it. Whether that is a shift in position or a difference in what each question made convenient to say is not resolvable from the texts, and is not asserted; both are recorded so the pair can be read together.

title: Paul H. Dunn: “His eternal, primal self was born into a spirit body”
speaker: Paul H. Dunn
office: First Council of the Seventy
venue: General conference, first day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1966)

quotes.excerpt: Second, he believes that he has a divine heritage. His eternal, primal self was born into a spirit body of which God is the eternal father. Thus men and women are truly sons and daughters of God.
quotes.note: Real staging, compressed into one sentence: an eternal primal self, then birth into a spirit body, then the mortality the rest of the list assumes — the intelligence→spirit→body model rather than the ordinary three estates. What is born is the body; what inhabits it was never made, which is exactly the distinction bh-roberts-tripartite-q2 spends a printed page establishing. SPIRIT-BIRTH-ADOPTION is hedged, not affirmed: Dunn keeps the birth language and calls God the eternal father of the spirit body, so he is not denying begetting the way abraham-3 and kfd-1844 do — he is relocating it from the self to the body.

quotes.excerpt: First, the Latter-day Saint knows himself to be an eternal being. He is challenged by a divine plan of progression that can make both mortality and the eternities to come an ongoing experience of purpose and meaning.
quotes.note: The immediately preceding item in the same list of five, kept because it establishes the eternity of the self that q1 then has born into a body. Untagged on its own: eternal existence plus a plan of progression, with nothing said about offspring or about the Father's own past.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1966/1966-10-dunn-folks-accept-new-customs-because.md, whose body was collated against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1966sa, leaves n15–n16, similarity 0.9687) and read in full against the reconstructed page order; the final-review pass found no body defects. The heavyweight pass also corrected the speaker attribution, which an earlier ingest had taken from an OCR-garbled running head (“ELDER PAUL H. DUNN” read as a bare “Pal”). Conference Report, so A. The talk is a five-point summary of distinctive Latter-day Saint belief written for a general and partly non-member audience, which is what makes the phrasing notable: the tripartite model is not being argued for, it is being reported as the plain content of point two.

title: Hugh B. Brown: “crowned with immortality, eternal life, and eternal increase”
speaker: Hugh B. Brown
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, third day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1966)

quotes.excerpt: We point out, moreover, that we, as his children, are the only creations of the Father to be blessed with his image. It follows that under the divine law of “like begets like,” our progress through the eternities may be limitless.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head “In His image.” Untagged: “like begets like” is doing work on likeness and human progress, not on offspring, and the inference Brown draws from it is explicitly about our progress rather than about anything we will beget. The same maxim is the hinge of romney-1964-q1, which is untagged for the same reason. Note what precedes it — Brown has just conceded to “orthodox Christianity” every attribute of God it claims, calling him all powerful, all knowing, and perfect, which is the concession his 1956 address made in the opposite direction.

quotes.excerpt: All who are faithful to the teachings of the gospel will continue as a family into the highest degree of the celestial kingdom and will be crowned with immortality, eternal life, and eternal increase.
quotes.note: The bare formula from a member of the First Presidency: increase as the third term of a triad, undefined, in a sentence whose subject is the sealed mortal family continuing. Compare kimball-godhood-1952, the same construction with Godhood as the final term.

quotes.excerpt: President Lorenzo Snow gave an intimation of what eternal marriage meant: “A man and a woman in the other life, having celestial bodies, free from sickness and disease, glorified and beautified beyond description, standing in the midst of their posterity, governing and controlling them, administering life, exaltation and glory, world without end.” And President Joseph F. Smith told us, “The very foundation of the Kingdom of God, of righteousness, of progress, of development, of eternal life, and eternal increase in the Kingdom of God is laid in the divinely ordained home.”
quotes.note: The strongest passage in the address, printed under the side-head “Divinely ordained home,” and still short of explicit. The Snow relay puts a resurrected couple in the other life amid their posterity “administering life … world without end,” which is generative language in everything but name; what it never says is that the posterity are newly begotten spirits, so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than FORWARD-EXPLICIT. Provenance caveat: Brown supplies no citation for either quotation, and the Snow passage as he gives it is an uncited pulpit relay of a nineteenth-century statement — the Conference Report is a faithful record of what Brown said, which is a separate question from whether Snow said it in these words. Neither quoted text corresponds to an existing dataset entry, so no citesId.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1966/1966-10-brown-god-centered-homes-for-children.md, whose body was collated against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1966sa, leaves n103–n107, printed pp. 100–105, similarity 0.9629) with the page images checked directly; the final-review pass restored one dropped line and recovered the address's true closing, which had been misfiled at the head of the following speaker's file. All three excerpts fall in the body, not in the recovered closing. Conference Report, so A. Distinct from brown-deify-man-1956, and the pair is the interesting thing: in 1956, as an Assistant to the Twelve, Brown read Widtsoe aloud on God's own growth and then drew a boundary around it; here, ten years later and in the First Presidency, the God-facing half is gone entirely — the address is about juvenile delinquency and the family, and eternal increase arrives as a crown on the sealed home.

title: William J. Critchlow, Jr.: the seven-act drama ends in “the power of eternal increase”
speaker: William J. Critchlow, Jr.
office: Assistant to the Council of the Twelve
venue: General conference, second day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, October 1967, pp. 87–91)

quotes.excerpt: It is our Father's way of providing his billions of spirit children with mortal, flesh and bone bodies. … It provides his children with powers of procreation for the first time.
quotes.note: Two items from the six-item list of what mortality is for; the elision covers the two intervening items (a fulness of joy, and probationary testing). Untagged, but the second item is the premise the nineteenth-century mechanism arguments are built on — spirits do not have procreative power, embodiment confers it — stated here as a bare fact about the plan. Compare pratt-people-worlds-1871-q1, which runs the identical premise (“Can spirits do this? No, they remain single”) straight through to spirit offspring and worlds. Critchlow does not; he draws no conclusion from it at all, which is why nothing is tagged.

quotes.excerpt: Life is eternal. Faithful members of the cast, after their resurrection, may attain a state of exaltation in God's kingdom in a glory called celestial. That glory holds a promise of eternal life, the power of eternal increase, a continuation of the seeds.
quotes.note: The formula in its most compact form, three terms in apposition, delivered as the answer to the question the address has just posed about what happens to the cast when the drama ends. “A continuation of the seeds” is D&C 132:19 quoted without quotation marks or citation, and Critchlow adds nothing to it — no offspring, no mechanism — so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM. citesId dc-132 records the unmarked borrowing.

notes: Verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1967/1967-10-critchlow-all-the-worlds-a-stage.md. Provenance is worth stating in full: the address had never been ingested into the vault at all, and was transcribed in a heavyweight pass directly from the DjVu word-coordinate reading order of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1967sa, leaves n87–n91, printed pp. 87–91); its closing section — which contains both excerpts here — had additionally been misfiled onto the front of Gordon B. Hinckley's file by a running-head bleed and was split back out in the same pass. A later final-review collation of leaves n87–n91 confirmed the body against the scan, with the only flagged candidates being OCR garbles in the independent scan text rather than vault errors. Conference Report, so A. The address's own staging — “Act 1 I would call the pre-mortal act, involving the cast in their spirit state,” then the mortal act, then the immortal act — is the standard three estates and not intelligence→spirit→body, so no TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK tag despite the three-stage vocabulary.

title: Spencer W. Kimball: knowledge “in order to create worlds and to furnish them”
speaker: Spencer W. Kimball
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, October 1968)

quotes.excerpt: We shall need all of the accumulated secular knowledge in order to create worlds and to furnish them, but only through the “mysteries of God” and these hidden treasures of knowledge may we arrive at the place and condition where we may use that knowledge in creation and exaltation.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head “Secular and spiritual knowledge,” and the world-making is not the sermon's subject — it arrives as the unargued premise of an argument about study. That is what makes it useful: exaltation is given concrete content (the exalted create worlds, plural, and furnish them) in the course of saying something else entirely. MANY-WORLDS alone; the peopling half of the forward chain is absent, so no FORWARD-* tag, and nothing is said about the Father's own past. Compare kimball-godhood-1952, the same speaker sixteen years earlier ending an address on “eternal increase, perfection, and with it all — Godhood,” and kimball-1976, where as President he warns the Church against disseminating doctrines “alleged to have been taught by some of the General Authorities of past generations.”

quotes.excerpt: Spiritual knowledge gives the power to live eternally and to rise and overcome and develop and finally to create.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head “Knowledge not unfindable,” about two-thirds of the way through the address and well before q1. Untagged context, kept because it shows the creation claim is not a slip at the close: creating is named as the terminal item in a progression of powers the first time the subject comes up, and then made specific at the end.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1968/1968-10-kimball-president-alvin-r-dyer-the-tabernacle-choir.md, collated in the final-review pass against the DjVu column-order reconstruction of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1968sa, leaves n129–n133). Provenance caveat a maintainer should know: this file's closing had been missing — the vault text broke off mid-sentence at “since he would not humbly” — and the continuation, which contains q1, had been misfiled as the entire body of the Alma Sonne file for the same session. The final-review pass confirmed the join by direct scan continuity across the leaf 132/133 page break and appended the recovered text here, and the recovered portion carries Kimball's own closing testimony and “Amen.” The reading is sound but q1 sits in recovered text, so it is worth a glance at the page image before publication. Conference Report, so A. The printed Report supplies no title; the vault's placeholder is taken from the opening line.

title: Alma Sonne reads Mormon Doctrine from the pulpit: “Man and God are of the same race”
speaker: Alma Sonne
office: Assistant to the Council of the Twelve
venue: General conference, third day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, October 1968)

quotes.excerpt: “Man and God are of the same race,” said President Bruce R. McConkie. (Mormon Doctrine, pp. 465-66.) Man's destiny is godlike, for he has the opportunity to reach the heights of a glorious exaltation.
quotes.note: Untagged, deliberately. Species identity plus theosis is the whole of the inference Sonne draws — no increase, no offspring, no claim about the Father's past — and per the reading applied to brown-deify-man-1956-q2 that earns no category. Two things are recorded by the row itself rather than by a tag: that Mormon Doctrine is being quoted by name and page from the general-conference pulpit ten years after its contested first edition and two years after the second, by an Assistant to the Twelve expounding the Articles of Faith; and that “President” here is the style for McConkie as one of the seven Presidents of the First Council of the Seventy, not a First Presidency title. The attribution and page reference are reproduced as Sonne gives them; whether the sentence appears in those words at those pages has not been checked against the book for this entry.

notes: Verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1968/1968-10-sonne-bow-in-baptism-the-holy-ghost-is.md. Provenance is unusual and should be read before the entry is relied on: the file under this name previously contained none of Sonne's words at all — its body was the misfiled closing of Spencer W. Kimball's address from the same session (see kimball-create-worlds-1968) — and Sonne's real address was ingested from scratch in the final-review pass from leaves n133–n135 of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1968sa) via the DjVu column-order reconstruction, with the closing boundary confirmed against the narrator's line that follows. The excerpt here is from that fresh ingest of the printed Report, so A, but it has been through one transcription pass rather than a transcription plus an independent collation, and a maintainer should check it against the page image before publication. sourceType citation because the transmission is the entry's whole value: what the row records is Mormon Doctrine reaching a general-conference audience under its own title, not a new doctrinal claim by Sonne.

title: Hugh B. Brown: the spirit “a self-existing entity, uncreated and eternal”
speaker: Hugh B. Brown
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, second day morning meeting (Conference Report, April 1969)

quotes.excerpt: We believe that before the creation of the body, all men existed as intelligences. These intelligences were not created or made, neither indeed can they be; the intelligent entity in man which we call spirit or soul is a self-existing entity, uncreated and eternal. Thus man is crowned with the dignity which belongs to his divine and eternal nature.
quotes.note: Denial, on the abraham-3 and kfd-1844 reading — no beginning means no begetting — and stated by a counselor in the First Presidency in general conference, printed under the side-head “Man's eternal nature.” The middle clause is the sharp one: Brown identifies the uncreated intelligence with “spirit or soul,” which collapses the staging rather than building it. That is why no TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK tag, despite the intelligences vocabulary and despite the source he is working from — the whole point of bh-roberts-tripartite is that the intelligence is a tier prior to the spirit, and here they are the same thing, leaving two stages (uncreated spirit, then body) rather than three. Attribution: Brown introduces the passage as “The late President Brigham H. Roberts, in one of his later writings … I shall quote and paraphrase him,” so the wording is his rendering of Roberts and the boundary between quotation and paraphrase is not marked.

quotes.excerpt: The Church teaches that when God created man in his own image, he did not divest himself of that image. He is still in human form and is possessed of sanctified and perfected human qualities, which we all admire. … In other words, he is an exalted, perfected, and glorified Being.
quotes.note: Marked implied. The work this sentence is doing is anthropomorphism — the surrounding paragraphs are an argument against the creedal God “without body, parts or passions” — and the attainment reading rides on an adjective rather than a verb: an exalted Being, with nothing said about who exalted him, from what, or when. Per the Father-status precedent that is FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone, no mortality claim attached; it is the identical phrase McConkie applies to the Father in Mormon Doctrine (“an exalted, glorified, and perfected Man,” see mcconkie-mormon-doctrine-q1), where the same reading is noted and then left to an explicit quote. Brown has no explicit quote to defer to — the address never returns to the Father's origin — so the tag lands here, marked implied. The elision covers three sentences on the separateness of the Father and the Son and on the scriptural warrant for the image claim.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1969/1969-04-brown-the-apostle-peter-writing-to-the-saints.md, whose body was independently re-collated in the final-review pass against leaves n52–n56 of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1969a) rather than trusting the prior stamps; that pass fixed one accidental mid-name paragraph split and converted twelve printed side-heads, and left two shared OCR artifacts (“Pirst Peter,” “]esus Christ”) untouched because both witnesses agree on them. Neither artifact falls in the excerpts here. Conference Report, so A. This is Brown's Saturday-morning general-session address, distinct from his priesthood-session address later in the same conference and from brown-deify-man-1956 and brown-eternal-increase-1966. The address is an apologia for Latter-day Saint distinctiveness aimed outward (“we are a peculiar people”), which is the frame worth keeping in view: the uncreated-spirit claim and the exalted-Being claim are both offered as selling points to outsiders, not as mysteries. citesId bh-roberts-tripartite for the acknowledged Roberts source; the James E. Talmage passage Brown also reads (“What is man in this boundless setting of sublime splendor?”) is not from The Articles of Faith and has no dataset entry, so it is not linked.

title: S. Dilworth Young: “not just gazers into the wonders of the heavens, but creators of them”
speaker: S. Dilworth Young
office: First Council of the Seventy
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1969; Internet Archive scan conferencereport1969a, leaves n79–n81)

quotes.excerpt: How much greater is the love of the Christ, who becomes our Father by our acceptance of his offer to us not only of earthly development but also of salvation, exaltation, and eternal lives. In the gospel of Christ he offers us the opportunity to become not just gazers into the wonders of the heavens, but creators of them.
quotes.note: Two moves in two sentences. "Eternal lives" is the D&C 132 term of art for eternal increase, used here with no mechanism attached at all — the euphemism in its purest correlated-era form. Then the very next sentence supplies a gloss, and it is not the usual one: what the exalted become is creators of heavens, not parents of spirits. Both tags are carried because both moves are present, and the difference between them is the point of the entry. (The Christology is also unusual and is left untagged: Christ, not the Father, is the one who "becomes our Father" by covenant.)

quotes.excerpt: It is wondrous to know that the most magnificent of God's creations may be duplicated — not by technical knowledge gained here, although this may be of help, but by such simple acts as being kind to and honest with all people. By obeying the first principles and ordinances, one places himself in harmony with eternal teachings that will lead him to the presence of the Creator, and from him he will learn to take part in the acts of creation. We understand that these wondrous accomplishments will not come without work. We know we must learn all we can of the truth of things in this life, and that we shall have to conquer eternal physics, eternal chemistry, eternal biology, and all eternal arts to give eternal science beauty.
quotes.note: The forward claim at full strength: God's creations "may be duplicated," the exalted will "take part in the acts of creation," and the curriculum for it is named — eternal physics, eternal chemistry, eternal biology. Tagged FORWARD-EXPLICIT on the world-making half of the category definition, on the precedent of pratt-key-theology-1855-q3. What is conspicuously absent, and the reason this entry is worth having, is offspring: no spirit children, no heavenly parents, no begetting, no continuation of the seeds anywhere in the address. SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS would be pure retrojection. The address is a standing counterexample to the assumption that a mid-century "we shall become creators" statement is shorthand for eternal increase — here the forward chain runs through creation rather than procreation, and "eternal biology" is as close as it comes to the generative register.

quotes.excerpt: Hear the witness of their Creator, for it is God who speaks: "And by the word of my power, have I created them, which is mine Only Begotten Son, who is full of grace and truth. "And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose; and by the Son I created them, which is mine Only Begotten." (Moses 1:32-33.)
quotes.note: Moses 1:32–33 quoted with no gloss beyond the attribution of creation to the Son, which the surrounding paragraphs develop from Colossians 1 and 3 Nephi 9. Plural worlds under one God; nothing successive is claimed or implied. The astronomical opening of the address — "uncountable island universes" — is the same point made from the telescope rather than the scripture.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1969/1969-04-young-many-years-ago-in-our.md, independently collated at final review against leaves n79–n81 of the Church History Library preservation scan (Internet Archive conferencereport1969a). Conference Report, so A. Speaker disambiguation matters here: this is S. Dilworth Young of the First Council of the Seventy, not Brigham Young and not Levi Edgar Young. The address is filed because of how it distributes the forward axis — "eternal lives" as a bare formula in one paragraph, world-creation as a fully stated destiny in another, and spirit offspring never mentioned at all — which makes it a clean control on the eternal-increase question rather than another witness for it.

title: Harold B. Lee answers a member who cannot believe “God himself was once as we are now”
speaker: Harold B. Lee
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1969; Internet Archive scan conferencereport1969a, leaves n131–n135)

quotes.excerpt: Another man wrote: "If a member cannot believe the concept that God himself was once as we are now, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens," is this justification for excommunication from the Church? … The reasoning of Joseph Smith, in the partial statement from which he has quoted, "that God was once as we are now," is given additional strength if our brother will recall the words of the Master: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do; for what things soever he [the Father] doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise." (John 5:19.) When we consider the fact that our Lord and Master, Jesus of Nazareth, one of the Godhead, came to tabernacle in mortality, then this quoted statement, taken literally, is of great significance.
quotes.note: The occasion is the entry's value: a member has written in to ask whether disbelieving the King Follett statement is grounds for excommunication, and an apostle answers by defending the statement rather than by softening it. Lee's argument is the Christological one — John 5:19, the Son does what he has seen the Father do, plus the fact of Christ's own mortality — which is the same engine that drives kfd-1844-q1 and the Snow couplet. "Taken literally" is Lee's own adverb. FATHER-BECAME-GOD is deliberately not tagged: the member's letter quotes "was once as we are now, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens" but omits the attainment clause "and is an exalted man," and Lee never supplies it. Referent is the Father throughout — Lee's subject is "God, the Eternal Father, also known as the Father of our spirits."

quotes.excerpt: Commenting on this same teaching, President Brigham Young had this to say: ". . . it must be that God knows something about temporal things, and has had a body and been on an earth; were it not so He would not know how to judge men righteously, according to the temptations and sins they have had to contend with." (Journal of Discourses, Vol. 4, p. 271.)
quotes.note: A relay: Young's words reach the 1969 congregation through the Journal of Discourses, so the sentence is Watt-shorthand secondhand inside a first-person Conference Report address. It is quoted here as Lee printed it, ellipsis and all. Journal of Discourses 4:271 has no entry of its own in this dataset, so no citation edge is set for it; if that sermon is ever added, this quote should acquire the edge.

quotes.excerpt: Those who can attain to this highest degree of glory are spoken of in a revelation we know as Doctrine and Covenants 131:1-4: "In the celestial glory there are three heavens or degrees; "And in order to obtain the highest, a man must enter into this order of the priesthood [meaning the new and everlasting covenant of marriage] ; "And if he does not, he cannot obtain it. "He may enter into the other, but that is the end of his kingdom; he cannot have an increase."
quotes.note: D&C 131:1–4 quoted with one interpolation and no gloss on the word that matters. The bracket "[meaning the new and everlasting covenant of marriage]" is Lee's, printed in the Conference Report; "increase" is left standing unexplained, which is the standard correlated-era handling of this passage. What is not standard is what Lee does next — he immediately supplies the explanation from Brigham Young (q4), which is the strongest available one. Tagged euphemism for the scripture itself; the explicit tag belongs to q4. OCR note: the printed spacing "marriage] ;" and the run-in quotation marks are reproduced as the scan has them.

quotes.excerpt: President Young again expands upon the meaning of this quotation: ". . . The kingdoms he possesses and rules over are his own progeny. Every man who is faithful and gets a salvation and glory, and becomes a king of kings and Lord of Lords, or a father of fathers, it will be by the increase of his own progeny. Our Father and God rules over his own children. Wherever there is a God in all the eternities possessing a kingdom and glory and power it is by means of his progeny. . . ." (Journal of Discourses, Vol. 11, p. 262.)
quotes.note: The gloss Lee chooses for D&C 131's "increase": an exalted man's kingdom is literally his own posterity, and — Young generalises — every God's kingdom anywhere is his progeny. That is eternal increase stated as offspring rather than as formula, read into the 1969 Conference Report by an apostle. Two precision points. First, the generalisation is about the class of Gods, not about a line of them: "wherever there is a God in all the eternities" asserts plurality and a shared pattern, not succession, so INFINITE-CHAIN is withheld. Second, the sentence "Our Father and God rules over his own children" applies the pattern to the Father, which is a claim about who populates his kingdom, not about who fathered him. The Conference Report breaks the citation across a column ("Journal of Discourses, Vol. / 11, p. 262."); it is closed up here.

quotes.excerpt: There are those who would think to go beyond that which God has revealed. It was to such as these, who would seek to penetrate that curtain of revealed truth, that inspired writers of our early leaders posed a profound question that was later given a musical setting in one of our most beloved hymns: "If you could hie to Kolob In the twinkling of an eye, And then continue onward With that same speed to fly, D'ye think that you could ever, Through all eternity, Find out the generation Where Gods began to be? … The works of God continue, And worlds and lives abound; Improvement and progression Have one eternal round. There is no end to matter; There is no end to space; There is no end to spirit; There is no end to race." (Hymns, No. 257.)
quotes.note: The clearest statement in the corpus of what the hymn is for when a General Authority reaches for it: it is deployed against "those who would think to go beyond that which God has revealed," as a bar on the question rather than an answer to it. That reading is the hymn's own (see phelps-hie-to-kolob-1856-q1, where the quatrain is tagged BACKWARD-AGNOSTIC for the same reason), and it is worth noting that Lee reaches for it three paragraphs after defending the King Follett statement — the same address holds the claim and the prohibition on pressing it further. MANY-WORLDS for "worlds and lives abound." Deliberately not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION: "Improvement and progression Have one eternal round" is a claim about the universe, not about God, per the note on phelps-hie-to-kolob-1856-q3. Lee prints the older "D'ye think that you could ever" wording and cites the hymn as no. 257; it is no. 284 in the 1985 hymnal.

quotes.excerpt: A prophet-leader of our dispensation then extends this great wisdom to all truth seekers: "Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause of all things; but it would be as easy for an ant to number the grains of sand on the earth. It is not for man, with his limited intelligence, to grasp eternity in his comprehension. . . . What, then, should be the calling and duty of the children of men? Instead of inquiring after the origin of the Gods — instead of trying to explore the depths of eternities that have been, that are, and that will be, — instead of endeavoring to discover the boundaries of boundless space, let them seek to know the object of their present existence, and how to apply, in the most profitable manner for their mutual good and salvation, the intelligence they possess. . . ." (Brigham Young, in Journal of Discourses, Vol. 7, p. 284.)
quotes.note: Young's October 9, 1859 caution (young-origin-caution-1859) reissued from the general conference pulpit 110 years later, and introduced as "this great wisdom." This is the transmission line the 1859 entry's note predicted: the caution survives in usage while the chain language it was delivered alongside does not. Lee's Conference Report prints the Americanised "endeavoring"; the Journal of Discourses reads "endeavouring."

quotes.excerpt: The ancient prophet was not speaking idly when he declared in exaltation, "O how great the holiness of our God! For he knoweth all things, and there is not anything save he knows it." (2 Ne. 9:20.)
quotes.note: Recorded untagged on purpose. This is a full-omniscience assertion, and full omniscience is the premise Joseph Fielding Smith would use two years later to rule out progression in knowledge (jfs-progression-1971), and that the 2002 institute manual uses for the same purpose (dcsm-2002-omniscience). But Lee draws no such inference: he is not addressing whether God progresses, and the next sentence turns to "a state of ultimate perfection to which all might attain" — the subject is man's attainment, not God's stasis. Tagging DIVINE-PROGRESSION here would be reading the later debate back into a doxological line, which is precisely what the no-retrojection rule forbids. The observation belongs in the note, and it is made here so a later reader does not mistake the silence for an oversight.

quotes.excerpt: The wisdom of the teacher's reply to the young men in Chicago is impressed by another statement from a modern prophet: "These are incomprehensible ideas to some, but they are simple. It is the first principle of the gospel to know for a certainty the character of God, and to know that we may converse with Him as one man converses with another. . . ." (DHC, Vol. 6, p. 305.)
quotes.note: A textual datum worth having on the record. Lee's ellipsis falls exactly where the King Follett text continues "and that he was once a man like us; yea, that God himself, the Father of us all, dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ himself did." He stops one clause short of the mortality claim. This is not suppression — Lee has already defended that claim in his own voice earlier in the same address (q1) — but it is the standard mid-century citation habit, and it is worth setting beside cullimore-character-of-god-1970-q1, where the identical sentence is printed eighteen months later with the clause intact. Lee also quotes DHC 6:306–7 elsewhere in the address (the ladder passage on learning "all the principles of exaltation"), naming it "King Follett Discourse"; that is the second of the two explicit citation edges to kfd-1844.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1969/1969-04-lee-in-the-spirit-of-that-beautiful-hymn.md, whose final-review pass independently re-collated leaves n131–n135 of the Church History Library preservation scan (Internet Archive conferencereport1969a) with reading order rebuilt from the scan's DjVu word coordinates and found the body already clean. Conference Report, so hearsay A; the two Journal of Discourses passages and the two Documentary History passages quoted inside it are relays and are graded in their quote notes. Filed sourceType original, not citation: Lee is answering a live question with an argument of his own, and the quoted material is his evidence rather than the entry's whole content. Why this entry matters. It is the fullest single-address demonstration in the dataset that the backward claim and the prohibition on pursuing it were held together rather than in sequence: within about a thousand words Lee defends "God was once as we are now" as literally true, adds Brigham Young's "has had a body and been on an earth," glosses D&C 131's "increase" with Young's "father of fathers … by the increase of his own progeny," and then quotes both "If You Could Hie to Kolob" and Young's "instead of inquiring after the origin of the Gods" to close the question off. Two years before the Ensign reprinted the King Follett Sermon whole (ensign-king-follett-1971), an apostle was defending it from the pulpit against a member who could not accept it — and telling the same congregation not to go further back. Context flag carried from the vault file: President Joseph Fielding Smith's address from the same session was never ingested into the corpus, so no comparison with it is offered here.

title: Relief Society theology lesson: the “eternal round” of spirit children born to exalted beings
speaker: Roy W. Doxey
office: Writer of the Relief Society Magazine theology lessons (styled “Elder Roy W. Doxey” in the lesson heading)
venue: “Lesson 97—Eternal Marriage,” Lesson Department, The Relief Society Magazine 56, no. 7 (July 1969): 540–545

quotes.excerpt: The children born to an exalted man and woman after the resurrection are spirit beings. The parents are tangible, resurrected persons referred to in the scriptures as having spiritual bodies; that is, with spirit element in their veins rather than blood as in mortal bodies. (D&C 88:27; Al. 11:45; Brigham Young, Discourses of Brigham Young, p. 374.)
quotes.note: Printed p. 543, under the heading “Eternal Increase.” Explicit on both axes the taxonomy separates. Forward: exalted couples have children after the resurrection and those children are spirits. Mechanism: the lesson does not leave the physiology alone, but supplies it — the parents are tangible resurrected persons with “spirit element in their veins rather than blood,” the Brigham Young account of how resurrected bodies can beget spirits, cited to Discourses of Brigham Young. That is spirit-matter physiology in the Pratt–Young line, so SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS applies; what it stops short of is gestation or sexual language, which the lesson never uses.

quotes.excerpt: In the premortal world the plan of salvation was formed whereby the spirit sons and daughters of God could receive an earth life necessary for eternal progression. The relationship between God and his children was a parent-child relationship because his spirit children were born of a Heavenly Father and Heavenly Mother. (Harold B. Lee, Youth and the Church, pp. 126-27.) The eternal round of spirit children being born to exalted beings and the opportunity to reach the heights of exaltation by an earth life require marriage for eternity by mortals.
quotes.note: Printed p. 545, under the heading “Implementation.” Heavenly Mother is stated as the reason the divine parent-child relationship is what it is, not offered as a devotional aside, and the authority cited is a sitting apostle's book (Harold B. Lee, Youth and the Church). On the forward chain: the lesson names the round and names the exaltation route, but it does not say in terms that the spirit children born to exalted beings will themselves receive worlds and become gods. The whole weight of that claim rests on the word “round,” and the sentence's grammar leaves “the opportunity to reach the heights of exaltation by an earth life” attached to mortals generally rather than specifically to the newly born spirits. So the closed forward chain is implied by the vocabulary and is not asserted — recorded here, deliberately, as implication rather than as text.

notes: Verified verbatim against the archive.org page images of printed pp. 543 and 545 (item reliefsocietymag56reli, IA leaves 565 and 567), collated against the item's full text. This is the answer to the open question the archival sweep left: the lesson is “Lesson 97—Eternal Marriage” by Roy W. Doxey, in the Lesson Department of the July 1969 issue, printed pp. 540–545, with the reading assignment D&C 131:1–4 and 132, and headed for use in the first meeting of October 1969 (Northern Hemisphere) or March 1970 (Southern). The sweep's provisional B3 upgrade should not be made: the lesson is unambiguous B2 with stated physiology, and the forward chain beyond that is carried only by the phrase “eternal round” — see the note on q2. Two further passages set the register. On p. 543 the lesson glosses D&C 132:24–25 as “eternal lives, the power of eternal increase, which is the opposite of the deaths, or the lack of such power.” And the whole lesson is built on quoted authorities rather than on its own voice — Joseph Smith, Brigham Young, Joseph F. Smith, Widtsoe, McKay, Melvin J. Ballard, and Harold B. Lee — which is what makes it useful evidence about what was safe to teach women in 1969 rather than merely about what one lesson writer thought. Filed historical-official: an official auxiliary magazine's correlated lesson course, no longer published.

title: Sterling W. Sill: “God, angels, spirits, and men are all of the same species”
speaker: Sterling W. Sill
office: Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1969; Internet Archive scan conferencereport1969sa, leaf n18)

quotes.excerpt: It is helpful for us to remember that God, angels, spirits, and men are all of the same species in different stages of development and in various degrees of righteousness.
quotes.note: A species-identity claim, not a bare "we may become like God": God and men are asserted to be one kind, distinguished only by stage of development and degree of righteousness. The tag is a judgment call and is flagged as such. What earns it is that the developmental scale is predicated of a list with God on it, which places God at a stage rather than outside the sequence; what holds the stance at "hedges" is that Sill never says God attained that stage, never says he was once mortal, and is not, in context, discussing God's origin at all — the paragraph is about seeing fellow worshippers in "the light of their real identity as children of God." Referent must stay ambiguous: "God" is unqualified here, and the address nowhere pins the word to the Father as against Christ. Bare theosis carries no tag in this scheme, so a reader should not take the pill as evidence that Sill taught the backward claim; the note is the finding.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1969/1969-10-sill-if-we-were-looking-for-some-program.md, independently collated at final review against leaf n18 of the Church History Library preservation scan (Internet Archive conferencereport1969sa). Conference Report, so A. Deliberately lean: the address is a Sabbath-observance sermon, and the ontology surfaces in a single aside under the printed side-head "Rewarding Associations," alongside the claim that "the most ordinary individual that we know may be the kind of person that we would feel like falling down and worshiping before." The sentence is nonetheless worth a row, because the same-species formulation is the ontological premise the whole dataset turns on, and this is it stated flatly, in general conference, in 1969, with no argument offered and none apparently thought necessary. Note that Sill supplies no source for it; the formulation echoes the nineteenth-century scale-of-intelligence language (compare pratt-heirship-intelligence-1853-q3) rather than any scripture he cites.

title: Victor L. Brown: seminary students “had existed as intelligences and then as spirit children”
speaker: Victor L. Brown
office: Counselor in the Presiding Bishopric
venue: General conference, third day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1969; Internet Archive scan conferencereport1969sa, leaves n134–n135)

quotes.excerpt: It was interesting to note that these young people were thrilled with the knowledge that they had existed as intelligences and then as spirit children of their Heavenly Father before they were born into this life.
quotes.note: Three stages, named in order, in one sentence: intelligences, then spirit children of the Father, then birth into this life. This is what the category actually requires — real intelligence → spirit → body staging rather than the two-stage eternalism that gets retrojected onto Abraham 3 and the King Follett Discourse. Two things make it more than a one-speaker datum. It is reported as what fifteen-year-olds had been taught in a seminary class and could recite back with enthusiasm, so it is evidence about correlated curriculum in 1969, not about Brown's private view; and the tripartite frame is stated with no mechanism whatever for the intelligence-to-spirit-child transition, which is the shape the model usually takes in this period. Because no begetting is described, neither SPIRIT-BIRTH tag applies.

quotes.excerpt: It is my testimony that every person born into this world is a spirit child of God, that we did in very deed live with our Heavenly Father before taking a mortal body.
quotes.note: Brown's own voice, and it is two-stage: spirit child, then mortal body, with the intelligences dropped. Recorded so the entry shows where the three-stage frame actually sits — in the reported seminary lesson of q1, not in the apostolic-office testimony that follows it. No mechanism is offered for how one becomes a spirit child, so nothing on the spirit-birth axis is tagged.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1969/1969-10-brown-my-brethren-and-sisters-i-am-grate.md, whose final-review pass re-collated leaves n134–n135 of the Church History Library preservation scan (Internet Archive conferencereport1969sa), reconstructed a two-column OCR interleave in the opening paragraph, and trimmed a large block of unrelated matter (David O. McKay's closing address and the conference back matter) that had been absorbed into the file's tail; the passages quoted here sit inside Brown's own body text, well before that boundary. Conference Report, so A. This is Bishop Victor L. Brown of the Presiding Bishopric, not President Hugh B. Brown, who also spoke at this conference. A lean entry by design: the address is about eternal life and agency, and the tripartite sentence is an aside — which is exactly why it is useful as a measure of what the model's ordinary, unremarkable statement looked like in 1969.

title: Bruce R. McConkie: “one of our great doctrinal hymns”
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: General conference, second session, Saturday afternoon (Conference Report, April 1970)

quotes.excerpt: In one of our great doctrinal hymns we sing: "In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason, truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there. "When I leave this frail existence, When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high? Then, at length, when I've completed All you sent me forth to do, With your mutual approbation Let me come and dwell with you." —Hymns, No. 138
quotes.note: “One of our great doctrinal hymns” — the classification is the datum. McConkie, who spent a career policing the boundary between doctrine and folklore, files the Heavenly Mother stanzas on the doctrine side without qualification, and opens the talk with them. The hymnal number McConkie gives is 138, from the book then in use; Gordon B. Hinckley will cite the same lines as no. 292 from the 1985 hymnal in 1991 — the numbering is a cheap dating check on any later quotation of the hymn. Verse line breaks rendered as running text; the stray opening quotation mark before “When I leave” is in the printed Report.

quotes.excerpt: Manifestly if we are to become like our Eternal Father, we must become immortal as he is immortal; we must gain the character, perfections, and attributes which he possesses; we must attain the power, glory, and dominion which he enjoys; and we must create for ourselves eternal family units patterned after his eternal family.
quotes.note: The euphemism in its mature form, and it is doing real work: “create for ourselves eternal family units patterned after his eternal family” says everything the older sources said about generative exaltation except the word children. The pattern claim also runs backward by implication — his family is the template — but McConkie asserts nothing about the Father's own origin here, so no backward tag.

quotes.excerpt: Full salvation consists of the continuation of the family unit in celestial glory… heaven itself is but the projection of a Latter-day Saint family into eternity… That power by which salvation comes is so great that it can make of earth a heaven, and of man, a god.
quotes.note: The closing formulation, with two elisions marked. “Continuation of the family unit” is D&C 132's “continuation of the seeds” with the biology removed — compare hunter-beget-spirit-children-1949 twenty-one years earlier, where the same verse is glossed as “the power to beget spirit children.” Same doctrine, same scripture, and in the interval the mechanism has gone silent while the promise (“of man, a god”) has not.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1970/1970-04-mcconkie-salvation-is-a-family-affair.md, whose Final Review collated the full body against the archive.org scan conferencereport1970a, leaves n27–n30, word for word, with no lexical fixes needed; seven bled-in printed side-heads were converted to Markdown headings and trailing material belonging to the following speaker was stripped in an earlier pass. One shared OCR artifact survives elsewhere in the talk (“prepare arid qualify us”), reproduced identically by the independent witness and therefore left alone; it does not touch any quoted excerpt. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. Filed as a citation because the entry's Heavenly Mother content is the hymn — McConkie adds no argument about her, and the talk's own argument is about the family unit — but the two euphemism quotes are carried because this is McConkie establishing the vocabulary he will police for the next two decades. Read against mcconkie-heresies-1980 and mcconkie-mormon-doctrine.

title: James A. Cullimore reads the King Follett material twice: the God who makes a “literal Father in heaven” intelligible
speaker: James A. Cullimore
office: Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1970; Internet Archive scan conferencereport1970sa, leaf n42)

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph Smith taught, "It is the first principle of the Gospel to know for a certainty the Character of God, and to know that we may converse with him as one man converses with another, and that he was once a man like us; yea, that God himself, the Father of us all, dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ himself did." (Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, pp. 345-46.)
quotes.note: The same sentence Harold B. Lee cut short with an ellipsis eighteen months earlier (lee-true-concept-of-god-1969-q8), here printed whole, mortality clause and all, in the Conference Report. The referent is explicit in the text — "God himself, the Father of us all" — which is why this is one of the cleaner Father-referent attestations in the correlated era. Hearsay C for this quote: Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith is a 1938 compilation drawing on the Documentary History amalgam of the four King Follett witnesses, not an independent report of what was said in 1844; see kfd-1844.

quotes.excerpt: The kind of a God as described by the Prophet Joseph Smith makes me understand him as my literal Father in heaven. He said: "God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens! That is the great secret. If the veil were rent today, and the great God, who holds this world in its orbit, and who holds all worlds and all things by His power, was to make himself visible — I say, if you were to see him today, you would see him like a man in form — like yourselves in all the person, image, and very form as a man…" (Documentary History of the Church, vol. 6, p. 305.)
quotes.note: Both halves of the Father-status axis in one sentence — past mortality ("was once as we are now") and attainment ("is an exalted man") — so both tags, per the precedent set on kfd-1844-q1 and ensign-king-follett-1971-q2. The framing clause is the entry's own contribution and is quoted with the passage on purpose: Cullimore offers the King Follett God not as a mystery to be handled carefully but as the thing that makes God pastorally intelligible, "my literal Father in heaven." Hearsay C: the Documentary History reading is the smoothed amalgam, not any of the four contemporaneous witnesses.

quotes.excerpt: It is man's purpose in life to learn to know God, to know the nature and kind of being God is, and then to conform to his laws and ordinances; to progress, to be exalted to that high state wherein man becomes perfect as the Father is perfect.
quotes.note: The forward direction as Cullimore leaves it: bare theosis on the Matthew 5:48 model, with no increase, no offspring, no worlds, and no "eternal lives." Untagged, because plain likeness-to-God carries no tag in this scheme. Recorded because it shows where the address's weight actually falls — everything radical in it is backward-facing, and the forward half is the mildest available formula.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1970/1970-10-cullimore-my-brethren-and-sisters-how-de-esting.md, whose final-review pass collated the body word for word against the Church History Library preservation scan (Internet Archive conferencereport1970sa, reading order reconstructed, leaves 40–43) and re-verified the prior de-interleaving of a two-column OCR garble in the opening sentence. The Conference Report is A; the two Joseph Smith quotations inside it are Documentary History / Teachings amalgams and are downgraded to C per quote. Filed as a citation of kfd-1844, on the abrea-same-as-all-gods-1981 precedent: the address's doctrinal content on this axis is the two quoted passages, and Cullimore's own addition is a frame rather than an argument. What the entry documents. In October 1970 — the last conference before the Ensign began, the year before Joseph Fielding Smith's First Presidency message denying that God progresses (jfs-progression-1971), and in the middle of Correlation — an Assistant to the Twelve built a general conference address on the nature of God around the King Follett statement, quoted it twice from two different compilations, and treated it as the ordinary answer to a schoolchild's question about how to draw God. No hedge, no caveat, no counsel to leave it alone. The rest of the address is about the personality of God as a precondition for revelation, worked out through William E. Berrett's 1941 contrast with Henry Wieman.

title: The Ensign reprints the King Follett Sermon in two parts
speaker: Joseph Smith, reprinted by the Ensign
office: President of the Church (d. 1844); text reprinted under the Ensign's “Classics in Mormon Thought” series
venue: “The King Follett Sermon,” Ensign, April 1971, 13–14, and Ensign, May 1971, 13

witnesses.scribe: Ensign, May 1971 — part two
witnesses.note: The concluding installment, carrying its own headnote and the intelligence/eternalism material.

quotes.excerpt: The King Follett Sermon, one of the classics of Church literature, was given by the Prophet Joseph Smith at the April 7, 1844, conference of the Church in Nauvoo, Illinois. Some twenty thousand Saints were assembled. … Longhand notes of the discourse were made by Willard Richards, Wilford Woodruff, Thomas Bullock, and William Clayton. This reprint was taken from the Documentary History of the Church, vol. 6, pages 302–17. That volume notes: “This was not a stenographic report, but a carefully and skillfully prepared one made by these men who were trained in reporting and taking notes. Evidently, there are some imperfections in the report and some thoughts expressed by the Prophet which were not fully rounded out and made complete. …”
quotes.note: The whole editorial apparatus the Ensign supplies, and the reason this entry is worth having as its own row: the Church, in 1971, names the discourse “one of the classics of Church literature,” prints it under a standing series heading “Classics in Mormon Thought,” and does so with no doctrinal hedge whatsoever. The only caution offered is textual — the DHC's own admission that the report is imperfect — and even that is quoted from the source rather than issued by the Ensign in its own voice. The headnote does name all four longhand reporters, which is more transparency than most reprints of the sermon give. What it does not say is that the DHC text is an editorial amalgam of those four accounts rather than any one of them.

quotes.excerpt: God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens! That is the great secret.
quotes.note: Both halves of the Father-status axis in one sentence, printed under the section heading “God an Exalted Man”: past mortality (“was once as we are now”) and attainment (“is an exalted man”). Per the precedent set on kfd-1844-q1, that pairing takes both tags. Hearsay downgraded to C for this quote: these are not the words of any of the four contemporaneous witnesses but the smoothed 1855 History draft reading, which is exactly the amalgam kfd-1844 flags in its own notes.

quotes.excerpt: In order to understand the subject of the dead, for consolation of those who mourn for the loss of their friends, it is necessary we should understand the character and being of God and how He came to be so; for I am going to tell you how God came to be God. We have imagined and supposed that God was God from all eternity. I will refute that idea, and take away the veil, so that you may see. … It is the first principle of the gospel to know for a certainty the character of God, and to know that we may converse with Him as one man converses with another, and that He was once a man like us; yea, that God himself, the Father of us all, dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ Himself did
quotes.note: Denial — FATHER-ALWAYS-GOD is carried here for the explicit rejection, “We have imagined and supposed that God was God from all eternity. I will refute that idea.” Set this beside lectures-on-faith-decanonized-1921-q3, which is the proposition being refuted, printed in the Church's own canon until 1921 and here refuted in the Church's own magazine in 1971. Hearsay C: same amalgam problem as q2, and note that Bullock at this point actually reads “he was God from the begin of all Eternity,” which is the opposite of what the smoothed text says — see kfd-1844.

quotes.excerpt: and you have got to learn how to be gods yourselves, and to be kings and priests to God, the same as all gods have done before you, namely, by going from one small degree to another, and from a small capacity to a great one; from grace to grace, from exaltation to exaltation, until you attain to the resurrection of the dead, and are able to dwell in everlasting burnings, and to sit in glory, as do those who sit enthroned in everlasting power.
quotes.note: The chain clause, and the single most important thing to know about this entry is that the Ensign prints it in the smoothed form. “The same as all gods have done before you” is the amalgam. Of the four contemporaneous accounts only Clayton attests a comparison class of Gods (“as all Gods has done”); Bullock has the weaker “same as all have done” with no “Gods” at all; Richards and Woodruff record the deification injunction with no comparison clause attached to it. So the reading that reaches 1971 readers — and, through them, most later citation of the sermon — rests on one witness and silently resolves a real divergence. See kfd-1844-q2, where the divergence is laid out. Hearsay C. Referent “father” for consistency with kfd-1844-q2, though strictly the clause is about the class of gods rather than the Father as such.

quotes.excerpt: The mind or the intelligence which man possesses is co-equal [co-eternal] with God himself. … God never had the power to create the spirit of man at all. God himself could not create himself. Intelligence is eternal and exists upon a self-existent principle. It is a spirit from age to age and there is no creation about it.
quotes.note: From the May installment. Organization over begetting, in the Church's own current magazine archive, in direct tension with fp-1909 and with the viviparous statements of the mid-century — which is worth noting given that all of it remains hosted side by side today. The bracket is the apparatus datum: “co-equal [co-eternal]” is an editorial gloss carried over from the Documentary History, and the same silent-correction convention appears throughout the reprint (“I will call [for] the attention,” “I calculate [intend] to edify you”). The Ensign supplies no footnotes of its own and no marginal apparatus; the brackets are the only editorial marks in the text. Hearsay C.

quotes.excerpt: This is the conclusion of the King Follett Sermon, delivered by the Prophet Joseph Smith at the April 7, 1844, conference of the Church in Nauvoo, Illinois. The first part of this classic was reprinted in the April Ensign (page 12). Readers should be reminded that the account of the talk was reconstructed from longhand notes taken by four brethren. It is also important to know that the Prophet's enemies were within just a few months of bringing about his death. This reprint was taken from the Documentary History of the Church, volume 6, pages 302–17.
quotes.note: The May headnote. “Reconstructed from longhand notes taken by four brethren” is a franker description of the text's status than the April headnote gave, and it is the closest the Church came in 1971 to saying that no single witness underwrites the printed wording. Small apparatus discrepancy worth recording: this headnote places the first installment at page 12, while the citation line on the April article reads “Ensign, Apr. 1971, 13–14.”

notes: Both installments were read verbatim from the live churchofjesuschrist.org pages on 2026-08-10; the quotations above are the hosted text exactly, including its bracketed editorial insertions and its section headings (“God an Exalted Man,” “Eternal Life to Know God and Jesus Christ,” “The Immortal Intelligence”). Filed as a citation of kfd-1844 rather than as an original, because the value of the entry is the event, not the text: in April and May 1971 — at the high-water mark of Correlation, in the first months of the newly consolidated Ensign, under a First Presidency headed by Joseph Fielding Smith — the Church reprinted the most theologically radical sermon in its history, in full, over two issues, framed admiringly and without a single doctrinal caveat. The same May 1971 issue carries Smith's own First Presidency message denying that God progresses in knowledge or power (jfs-progression-1971). Those two texts are thirteen pages and one issue apart, which is as concise a demonstration as the dataset contains that the C question and the D question are independent: the Church President could print “God himself was once as we are now” and “his progression consists not in gaining more knowledge or power” in the same magazine without contradiction, because they are not the same claim. Correlation graded current-correlated: both installments remain hosted in the official Gospel Library archive today and are reachable from the Church's own search. Textual caution repeated from kfd-1844 and applied per quote via hearsayByQuote: the reprint is the Documentary History text, an editorial amalgam of the Richards, Woodruff, Bullock, and Clayton accounts, and it is not identical with any of them. Where the amalgam and the witnesses diverge — most consequentially at “the same as all gods have done before you” — the quote notes say so. Do not treat any wording in this entry as a fifth witness to what was said on 7 April 1844.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith: progression “not in gaining more knowledge or power”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: First Presidency message, “The Most Important Knowledge,” Ensign, May 1971

quotes.excerpt: And I am grateful that we know he is an infinite and eternal being who knows all things and has all power and whose progression consists not in gaining more knowledge or power, not in further perfecting his godly attributes, but in the increase and multiplying of his kingdoms.
quotes.note: Denial — the definitive official statement of the only-in-dominions position, from a sitting Church President in a First Presidency message. Note the mechanism: God's progression is relocated into the expansion of kingdoms, i.e. the forward/generative chain.

notes: Smith had argued this position for decades in Doctrines of Salvation (which prints “HOW GOD DOES NOT PROGRESS” roughly a page before “The Prophet taught that our Father had a Father and so on” — denying progression while affirming the regress, proof the two questions are independent). This 1971 First Presidency message is the position's most official form.

title: Eldred G. Smith: “the same type of experiences they had done”
speaker: Eldred G. Smith
office: Patriarch to the Church
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session

quotes.excerpt: In the heavens, before the earth was formed, the plan of this earth life was explained to all of us. We were then but spirit offspring of our Father and Mother in heaven.
quotes.note: The opening sentence of the talk. “Spirit offspring of our Father and Mother in heaven” asserts the Mother and premortal parentage; no mechanism is named, so HEAVENLY-MOTHER alone and no spirit-birth tag.

quotes.excerpt: We all learned then that through this earth life experience we would have the opportunity of going through the same type of experiences they had done and so become as they are.
quotes.note: The sentence that makes this an original rather than another Heavenly Mother mention. “They” is the Father and Mother of the preceding sentence, and what is predicated of them is a completed earth life: mortality is not merely our probation, it is a repetition of theirs. That is FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE, stated obliquely but unmistakably, and delivered in a currently hosted general conference talk. Per the Father-status precedent it takes that tag alone — “become as they are” is what we may attain, and nothing is said here about how the Father attained anything, so no FATHER-BECAME-GOD. The Mother is swept into the same claim, which is rarer still: whatever the Father did, she did. Referent father for the tagged clause even though the pronoun is plural, since the category concerns the Father's status.

quotes.excerpt: The records tell us that we all shouted for joy at this glorious news.
quotes.note: The next sentence, kept so the reader can see there is no retreat, qualification, or scriptural hedge attached — the King Follett claim is stated in two clauses and the talk moves straight on to Adam and Eve. The remainder of the address is about opposition and agency and never returns to the point.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1973/1973-10-smith-opposition-in-order-to-strengthen-us.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the two categorized excerpts were additionally re-fetched from that live page during drafting and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. No hymn quotation, hence no citesId. Distinct speaker-entry from eldred-smith-no-increase-1948, and the pair is worth reading together: the same man who in 1948 was on record against ongoing divine progression here states, twenty-five years later, that the Father and Mother passed through the same type of mortal experience we are passing through — trap #4 in the taxonomy, denying D while C-adjacent mortality sits comfortably in the same career. It also matters that this survives on the Church's own site: the claim is not quarantined in a 19th-century sermon but sits in the searchable modern archive.

title: Spencer W. Kimball: “that doctrinal hymn and anthem of affection”
speaker: Spencer W. Kimball
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session

quotes.excerpt: Finally, when we sing that doctrinal hymn and anthem of affection, “O My Father,” we get a sense of the ultimate in maternal modesty, of the restrained, queenly elegance of our Heavenly Mother, and knowing how profoundly our mortal mothers have shaped us here, do we suppose her influence on us as individuals to be less if we live so as to return there?
quotes.note: A President of the Church calling the hymn doctrinal, in the same clause in which he explains the doctrine's silence as a property of its subject. The Mother's absence from scripture and prayer becomes “maternal modesty” and “restrained, queenly elegance” — the reticence is relocated from the institution to her. That move is what makes this the hinge between the confident early-century usage and hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991, which will convert the same silence into a boundary on practice. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER, not RETREAT-REFRAME: Kimball is enlarging her, not fencing her, and he asserts real influence on individuals.

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph gave us the Relief Society organization to advance these high purposes for Latter-day Saint women. That society today is a worldwide movement holding membership in national and world organizations for the advancement of women.
quotes.note: The immediately preceding paragraph, kept for setting. The Heavenly Mother sentence is the peroration of an address about the advancement of Latter-day Saint women, delivered in the same year Neal A. Maxwell reached for her in the same conference — the doctrine surfaces in 1978 as part of a response to the decade's argument about women, not as part of an argument about cosmology.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-04-kimball-the-true-way-of-life-and-salvation.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-checked during drafting and confirmed to load with this passage present. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated.
