Filed as a citation: the hymn is named and characterized, and Kimball's own contribution is a gloss on it rather than an independent argument. Kimball returns to Heavenly Mother repeatedly in 1977–1978 — the October 1978 sisters' address, for instance, says “He and your mother in heaven value you beyond any measure. They gave your eternal intelligence spirit form,” which is the tripartite intelligence-spirit-body sequence rather than a hymn citation, and his April 1977 “Our Great Potential” simply prints the hymn's stanzas. The October 1978 tripartite passage is now its own entry (kimball-intelligence-spirit-form-1978); the April 1977 bare hymn printing remains undrafted by design.

title: Neal A. Maxwell: “the anticipatory arrangements of a Heavenly Mother”
speaker: Neal A. Maxwell
office: Of the Presidency of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session

quotes.excerpt: Finally, remember: When we return to our real home, it will be with the “mutual approbation” of those who reign in the “royal courts on high.” There we will find beauty such as mortal “eye hath not seen”; we will hear sounds of surpassing music which mortal “ear hath not heard.” Could such a regal homecoming be possible without the anticipatory arrangements of a Heavenly Mother?
quotes.note: Two hymn phrases quoted in quotation marks with no attribution — “mutual approbation” and “royal courts on high” — on the assumption that the congregation will hear the source. That mode of citation is the measure of how thoroughly the hymn had been absorbed by 1978, and it is why phrase searches for “parents single” miss talks like this one. The claim itself goes past anything in the hymn: the hymn's Mother is present and addressed, Maxwell's Mother acts, and heaven is her preparation. It is still a rhetorical question — the strongest Heavenly Mother assertion of the modern corpus, and it is interrogative.

quotes.excerpt: We know so little, brothers and sisters, about the reasons for the division of duties between womanhood and manhood as well as between motherhood and priesthood. These were divinely determined in another time and another place… The story of the women of God, therefore, is, for now, an untold drama within a drama.
quotes.note: The talk's opening, kept because it sets the epistemic frame that the closing question depends on: what is known is little, what is asserted is asserted as inference from the shape of things. Elision marked. Untagged — this makes no claim about a Mother.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-04-maxwell-the-women-of-god.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the closing paragraph was re-fetched from the live page during drafting and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as an original with the citesId edge preserved: the hymn supplies the vocabulary of the last paragraph, but the proposition — that a Heavenly Mother has made arrangements for our return — is Maxwell's and is not in Eliza R. Snow. Delivered in the same session as kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978, which is the fact to notice: April 1978 is the high-water mark of official Heavenly Mother language in the modern era, and both instances arise from the Church's engagement with the decade's arguments about women. Thirteen years later Gordon B. Hinckley will address the same audience on the same subject to draw a line.

title: Spencer W. Kimball: “They gave your eternal intelligence spirit form”
speaker: Spencer W. Kimball
office: President of the Church
venue: General Women's Meeting, general conference, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: This is a partnership. God and his creation. The Primary song says, “I am a child of God.” Born with a noble birthright. God is your father. He loves you. He and your mother in heaven value you beyond any measure. They gave your eternal intelligence spirit form, just as your earthly mother and father have given you a mortal body. You are unique. One of a kind, made of the eternal intelligence which gives you claim upon eternal life.
quotes.note: Both tags are stated, not read in. HEAVENLY-MOTHER: "your mother in heaven" is named as a second agent — "They gave" — not merely acknowledged. TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK: the three tiers and both transitions are all present in one sentence — an eternal intelligence that is not made, given spirit form by heavenly parents, then given a mortal body by earthly parents — and the parallel construction ("just as") makes the premortal transition as real as the mortal one. Compare eom-premortal-life-1992, which states the identical sequence fourteen years later and sources it to Melvin J. Ballard; Kimball sources it to nothing and states it to a worldwide audience of women as catechesis. What he does not say is how, and "gave … spirit form" is compatible with organizing as well as with begetting, so no SPIRIT-BIRTH tag attaches in either direction.

quotes.excerpt: Let there be no question in your mind about your value as an individual. The whole intent of the gospel plan is to provide an opportunity for each of you to reach your fullest potential, which is eternal progression and the possibility of godhood.
quotes.note: The very next paragraph, untagged on purpose. "Eternal progression and the possibility of godhood" is theosis and nothing more — the A-framing trap — and it is recorded here precisely to show that the tripartite sentence above is not doing forward-generative work in this address. Kimball tells the sisters what they came from; he does not tell them they will do it in turn.

quotes.excerpt: Mothers have a sacred role. They are partners with God, as well as with their own husbands, first in giving birth to the Lord’s spirit children and then in rearing those children so they will serve the Lord and keep his commandments.
quotes.note: Kept for the semantic reading it forces. "The Lord's spirit children" here means us — already-existing spirits receiving mortal bodies from mortal mothers. That is the modern sense of the phrase, and it is the exact inverse of the 1949 sense in hunter-beget-spirit-children-1949, where spirit children are what exalted couples will beget. The same three words, twenty-nine years apart, pointing in opposite directions in the same corpus. Untagged: nothing here is a claim about eternal increase.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-10-kimball-privileges-and-responsibilities-of-sisters.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all three excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Delivered at the first worldwide General Women's Meeting — "Nothing like it has ever been held before in the Church," as Kimball says in the third paragraph — which is worth recording alongside the doctrine: the strongest tripartite sentence in the modern conference corpus was spoken at the inaugural session of a new meeting for women. Filed as an original with no citesId: the hymn is not quoted here and the Primary song is named rather than argued from. Two housekeeping notes for whoever maintains the neighbouring entries. First, this address completes the 1978 cluster with kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978 (April, "that doctrinal hymn and anthem of affection") and maxwell-heavenly-mother-1978 (April, "the anticipatory arrangements of a Heavenly Mother") — three official Heavenly Mother statements in one calendar year, the high-water mark of the modern era, all of them arising from the decade's argument about women rather than from any argument about cosmology. Second, kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978's own notes state that this October address was "deliberately not drafted" as the weaker member of the cluster; that judgment is superseded by this entry, on the ground that the two make different claims — April is a gloss on the hymn, October is the intelligence-to-spirit staging, which no other Kimball text in the dataset supplies — and that note should be revised when sources.json is next edited.

title: Bruce R. McConkie, “The Seven Deadly Heresies”
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Brigham Young University fireside address

quotes.excerpt: [On the proposition that God is progressing in knowledge and learning new truths, listed as heresy one:] This is false—utterly, totally, and completely. There is not one sliver of truth in it. It grows out of a wholly twisted and incorrect view of the King Follett Sermon and of what is meant by eternal progression. God progresses in the sense that his kingdoms increase and his dominions multiply—not in the sense that he learns new truths and discovers new laws.
quotes.note: Denial, the sharpest on record. Note the rhetorical mechanism: “God progresses” is affirmed and immediately redefined as expansion of kingdoms — quoting the first clause alone reads as an affirmation of the position being denounced.

notes: Never official — a BYU fireside, not conference. It triggered the McConkie–England correspondence (February 1981), the classic institutional episode of this debate; the denial position entered official channels through Joseph Fielding Smith's writings and the correlated manuals instead. Wording verified against the BYU Speeches text.

title: Angel Abrea reads the King Follett Discourse: “the same as all Gods have done before you”
speaker: Angel Abrea
office: Of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session

quotes.excerpt: “Here, then, is eternal life—to know the only wise and true God; and you have got to learn how to be Gods yourselves, and to be kings and priests to God, the same as all Gods have done before you, namely, by going from one small degree to another, and from a small capacity to a great one; from grace to grace, from exaltation to exaltation, until you attain to the resurrection of the dead, and are able to dwell in everlasting burnings, and to sit in glory, as do those who sit enthroned in everlasting power. … “… [You] shall be heirs of God and joint heirs with Jesus Christ. What is it? To inherit the same power, the same glory and the same exaltation, until you arrive at the station of a God, and ascend the throne of eternal power, the same as those who have gone before.” (Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, sel. Joseph Fielding Smith, Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1938, pp. 346–47.)
quotes.note: The comparison-class clause is what earns the tag, twice over: "the same as all Gods have done before you" and "the same as those who have gone before." A plurality of Gods preceded us on this path — which is the backward claim, made in general conference in 1981. Referent is ambiguous and must stay so: Abrea nowhere applies the clause to the Father, and the deification half of the passage ("learn how to be Gods yourselves," "the station of a God") is theosis, which carries no tag of its own. Provenance caveat carried forward from kfd-1844-q2, and it bears on exactly this sentence: "the same as all Gods have done before you" is the Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith amalgam, and of the four contemporaneous witnesses only Clayton attests "as all Gods has done" at all — Bullock has the weaker "same as all have done" with no "Gods," and Richards and Woodruff record the deification injunction with no comparison clause. Abrea is reading the strongest available reconstruction, at second hand, from a 1938 compilation. The printed ellipses are as published; the bracketed "[You]" is the published text's.

quotes.excerpt: This incident made me think about what often happens in our own lives. I thought about the tremendous potential that exists in each one of us, potential that can direct us to eternal life. … How many times do we allow little “butterflies” to reduce, restrain, or restrict our immense potential from guiding us to exaltation?
quotes.note: The two sentences that bracket the quotation, kept because they are the whole of Abrea's use of it. The King Follett material is not exposited, defended, qualified, or returned to; it is the warrant for a motivational point about Sabbath observance, sacrament meeting attendance, sustaining leaders, and tithing. The rest of the talk is about butterflies on a radiator and a branch member named Jose. That is the finding — the strongest backward-facing text in the tradition passing through a 1981 general conference as an unremarked-upon preamble.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1981/1981-10-abrea-the-little-things-and-eternal-life.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the Joseph Smith block and its source citation were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim, including the parenthetical Teachings citation. Official published text, so A, and still hosted on churchofjesuschrist.org, so current-correlated. Filed as a citation with a citesId edge to kfd-1844, per the rule that Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith is a citation of the four King Follett witnesses rather than an independent original — the entry's value is entirely that the passage is being read aloud, not what Abrea adds to it. Two contextual facts the timeline reader needs. First, the date: this is October 1981, sixteen months after Bruce R. McConkie's "Seven Deadly Heresies" (mcconkie-heresies-1980) and in the middle of the period when the dataset's correlated backward-explicit column is otherwise nearly empty — the material is not being taught, but it is still being quoted, from the published compilations, without comment. Second, the speaker: Abrea was the first Latin American General Authority, called to the First Quorum of the Seventy in 1981, and this is an early conference address; nothing about the setting marks the quotation as controversial or as requiring defense. Compare hunter-exalted-man-1948, where the same body of material is read aloud with full doctrinal intent, and note how much thinner the use has become in thirty-three years.

title: Boyd K. Packer, “The Pattern of Our Parentage” — plurality deflated to the Godhead
speaker: Boyd K. Packer
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: There is *one* God, the Father of all. This we accept as fundamental doctrine. There is only *one* Redeemer, Mediator, Savior. This we know. There is *one* Holy Ghost, a personage of spirit, who completes the Godhead. I have emphasized the word *one,* in each sentence, but I have used it three times. Three is plural.
quotes.note: The deflation, executed in five sentences. “Plurality of Gods” is redefined to mean the arithmetic of the Godhead — three persons — rather than a class of exalted beings or a succession of them. Asterisks are the italics of the published text.

quotes.excerpt: Anyone who believes and teaches of God the Father, and accepts the divinity of Christ, and of the Holy Ghost, teaches a plurality of Gods.
quotes.note: The conclusion the arithmetic was built for, and its rhetorical function: on this definition the distinctively Latter-day Saint plurality claim becomes something every trinitarian Christian already holds, and the doctrine is defended by being made unremarkable. Compare Rev. 1:6, which Packer cites in passing here and which the 2018 New Testament Student Manual will read in the older, stronger sense (see nt-manual-2018).

quotes.excerpt: The acceptance of this truth does not mean accepting the multiple gods of mythology nor the polytheism of the pagans, which was so roundly condemned by Isaiah and the other prophets.
quotes.note: The boundary drawn explicitly: whatever plurality means, it is not many gods. Delivered in a talk that opens by warning against “self-appointed spokesmen who scoff at what we believe and misrepresent what we teach,” which is the apologetic setting the reframe is answering.

quotes.excerpt: This doctrine is not at variance with the scriptures. Nevertheless, it is easy to understand why some Christians reject it, because it introduces the possibility that man may achieve Godhood.
quotes.note: Untagged, and instructive for that reason. Theosis is retained without apology in the same discourse in which plurality is deflated — nothing generative, no offspring, no chain, so no category applies. The pattern the entry documents is precisely this: the promise is kept and the cosmology around it is quietly emptied.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1984/1984-10-packer-the-pattern-of-our-parentage.md, which was diffed paragraph-by-paragraph against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page at a 1.0000 match. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Likely RETREAT-REFRAME and tagged as such, with the qualification that this is a reframe rather than a repudiation: Packer nowhere denies a plurality of exalted beings, he simply supplies a reading of “plurality of Gods” on which the phrase costs nothing. The pulpit sweep that surfaced it makes the surrounding fact available — explicit deification vocabulary (“become gods,” “gods yourselves”) appears in thirty-four talks before 1900 and six after, against a far larger twentieth-century corpus, while “become like God” rises steadily to peak in the 2010s–2020s. This talk is a legible instance of that substitution being performed deliberately in front of a general conference audience. Its structural ancestor is Orson Pratt in 1855, who also defused plurality by redefining what “God” refers to; the difference is that Pratt was constructing a metaphysics and Packer is managing an inheritance.

title: Millet and McConkie: God's development “has brought him to the point at which he now presides”
speaker: Robert L. Millet and Joseph Fielding McConkie
office: Professors of Ancient Scripture, Brigham Young University
venue: The Life Beyond (Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1986), 148–49

witnesses.scribe: David L. Paulsen and R. Dennis Fisher, FARMS Review 15/2 (2003), 429–30 n. 22
witnesses.note: Quotes the passage in full with page citation, and states its function: Millet and McConkie “argue for the same understanding of this attribute as do Bruce R. McConkie and Joseph Fielding Smith.”

witnesses.scribe: Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), n. 42
witnesses.note: Recorded as quoting the same passage to the same effect. The archive's scan of that issue is too badly OCR'd to re-collate, so England is listed as a witness rather than as a second verification. England's reproduction reads “to a point at which he now presides” against Paulsen and Fisher's “to the point”; the excerpt here follows Paulsen and Fisher, and the reading is not independently confirmed.

quotes.excerpt: Our Father's development and progression over an infinitely long period of time has brought him to the point at which he now presides as God Almighty, He who is omnipotent, omniscient, and, by means of his Holy Spirit, omnipresent: he has all power, all knowledge, and is, through the Light of Christ, in and through all things.
quotes.note: Denial, not affirmation. The verb is the tell: development “has brought him to the point at which he now presides,” and the payoff clause is “he has all power, all knowledge.” The progression is finished. Note also that “over an infinitely long period of time” is a claim about duration, not about a line of ancestors — the sentence contains no Father of God and no chain.

notes: The book itself is not in the collated corpus; the text was verified verbatim against Paulsen and Fisher's block quotation with page citation in the FARMS Review 15/2 (2003), 429–30 n. 22, where the note runs across the two printed pages. Recorded here because the sentence circulates as regress evidence when both scholarly sources that quote it read it as the opposite — a divine-progression denial, placing Millet and McConkie with Bruce R. McConkie and Joseph Fielding Smith against the Brigham Young–Woodruff–Roberts–Widtsoe side of the intra-LDS debate. Under this project's taxonomy it belongs outside category C entirely. Never-official: a Bookcraft trade book by two BYU religion faculty.

title: Howard W. Hunter quotes Orson F. Whitney: “more like our Father and Mother in heaven”
speaker: Howard W. Hunter
office: Acting President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session

quotes.excerpt: I share the view expressed by Orson F. Whitney in these words: “No pain that we suffer, no trial that we experience is wasted. It ministers to our education, to the development of such qualities as patience, faith, fortitude, and humility. All that we suffer and all that we endure, especially when we endure it patiently, builds up our characters, purifies our hearts, expands our souls, and makes us more tender and charitable, more worthy to be called the children of God … and it is through sorrow and suffering, toil and tribulation, that we gain the education that we come here to acquire and which will make us more like our Father and Mother in heaven” (as quoted in *Faith Precedes the Miracle,* p. 98).
quotes.note: Graded C rather than A on its own, and the reason is the attribution the talk gives. Hunter's own words are published official text; the Whitney material is not sourced to any Whitney publication but only to page 98 of Spencer W. Kimball's 1972 Faith Precedes the Miracle, which itself prints the passage without a citation. No conference address that uses it — and there are four — supplies a primary source, so the chain is Whitney (d. 1931) → Kimball's uncited book → the pulpit. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER only: "more like our Father and Mother in heaven" is likeness, which is theosis, and asserts nothing generative — the same reading given to whitney-father-and-mother-1907-q1, which is a different Whitney text. The ellipsis is printed in the published talk, not an editorial cut; the asterisks are the italics of the published text.

quotes.excerpt: President Spencer W. Kimball, who knew a good deal about suffering, disappointment, and circumstances beyond his control, once wrote: “Being human, we would expel from our lives physical pain and mental anguish and assure ourselves of continual ease and comfort, but if we were to close the doors upon sorrow and distress, we might be excluding our greatest friends and benefactors. Suffering can make saints of people as they learn patience, long-suffering, and self-mastery” (*Faith Precedes the Miracle,* Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1972, p. 98).
quotes.note: Earlier in the same address, and from the same page of the same book. Kept because it shows the mechanism of transmission exactly: Hunter is working from a single page of a devotional paperback on adversity, and the Heavenly Mother clause arrives as a passenger on a quotation about suffering. Untagged — nothing here concerns a Mother.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1987/1987-10-hunter-the-opening-and-closing-of-doors.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-checked during drafting on 2026-08-10 and confirmed to load with the Whitney paragraph present and with the attribution reading "as quoted in Faith Precedes the Miracle, p. 98." Official published text, so A at entry level, with the Whitney quote graded C — see the quote note. Filed as an original despite being substantively a quotation, because the quoted source is not an entry in this dataset and a citesId edge would dangle: whitney-father-and-mother-1907 is Whitney's October 1907 conference address on Heavenly Mother as philosophy, a different text making a different argument, and it must not be used as the target here. What this entry actually documents is a quotation lineage, and the lineage is larger than it first appears. The identical Whitney passage, always with the "Father and Mother in heaven" clause and always sourced only to Faith Precedes the Miracle p. 98, is read in general conference by Adney Y. Komatsu in October 1979 ("After Much Tribulation Come the Blessings"), by Komatsu again in April 1987 ("Looking to the Savior"), by Hunter here six months later, and by Neill F. Marriott in April 2016 ("What Shall We Do?", footnote 5: "Orson F. Whitney, in Spencer W. Kimball, Faith Precedes the Miracle (1972), 98"). Marriott's version silently trims the passage with four ellipses but keeps the closing clause intact. Four conference appearances across thirty-seven years, none of them arguing for a Heavenly Mother and none of them able to cite Whitney directly — which is how the doctrine kept surfacing in official discourse during the decades when almost no one taught it: not as doctrine but as a fixed phrase inside a quotation about adversity. Per the drafting charter, the Komatsu and Marriott instances are recorded here rather than drafted as entries of their own.

title: Gordon B. Hinckley, “Daughters of God” — the Mother affirmed and fenced
speaker: Gordon B. Hinckley
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General Women's Meeting, general conference, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: I am therefore on this occasion going to take the liberty of rereading that portion of the talk which pertains to a matter over which some few women of the Church appear to be greatly exercised. I give it to all, in this forum, because of the activities of a few who evidently are seeking to lead others in the paths which they are following. I speak of those who advocate the offering of prayers to our Mother in Heaven.
quotes.note: The occasion, stated. Everything that follows is Hinckley rereading his own April 1991 address to the regional representatives, verbatim and in quotation marks, to a general audience of women — so the boundary is being set twice, once in a training meeting and once, deliberately, in public. Provenance is still first-person and A: the inner quotation is the same speaker quoting himself from six months earlier, not a relay.

quotes.excerpt: “It was Eliza R. Snow who wrote the words: ‘Truth is reason; truth eternal / Tells me I’ve a mother there.’ (*Hymns,* 1985, no. 292.) “It has been said that the Prophet Joseph Smith made no correction to what Sister Snow had written. Therefore, we have a Mother in Heaven. Therefore, [some assume] that we may appropriately pray to her.
quotes.note: The hymn cited by author and hymnal number, and the traditional warrant for the doctrine restated in its weakest available form: not that Joseph revealed it, but that he did not correct it. Compare iverson-mother-in-heaven-1908, where the same doctrine is credited to “inspiration flowing first through the mind of the Prophet Joseph Smith.” Eighty-three years have converted a revelation claim into an argument from silence. The bracketed “[some assume]” is Hinckley's own interpolation as printed; asterisks are the italics of the published text.

quotes.excerpt: “Logic and reason would certainly suggest that if we have a Father in Heaven, we have a Mother in Heaven. That doctrine rests well with me.
quotes.note: The affirmation, and the ground it stands on. This is Erastus Snow's inference and Rudger Clawson's rhetorical question arriving intact in 1991 — logic and reason, not revelation and not scripture. “Rests well with me” is a personal endorsement rather than a doctrinal declaration, and the sentence is placed so that the concession precedes the restriction. See snow-heavenly-mother-1885 and clawson-mother-there-1929.

quotes.excerpt: “However, in light of the instruction we have received from the Lord Himself, I regard it as inappropriate for anyone in the Church to pray to our Mother in Heaven.… “I have looked in vain for any instance where any President of the Church, from Joseph Smith to Ezra Taft Benson, has offered a prayer to ‘our Mother in Heaven.’
quotes.note: The restriction, and the two arguments for it: the scriptural pattern of prayer to the Father, and an argument from the absence of precedent among Church presidents. Elision marks the omitted run of scriptural citations from Matthew 6 and 3 Nephi. Note what is not said — the doctrine is nowhere denied, and no claim is made that she does not exist or is not a person. What is fenced is practice.

quotes.excerpt: “I suppose those … who use this expression and who try to further its use are well-meaning, but they are misguided. The fact that we do not pray to our Mother in Heaven in no way belittles or denigrates her.” That is the end of the quotation from the talk I gave earlier, to which I may add that none of us can add to or diminish the glory of her of whom we have no revealed knowledge.
quotes.note: The closing sentence is the most consequential clause in the modern corpus on this subject: “her of whom we have no revealed knowledge.” The Mother is affirmed as real and simultaneously placed outside revelation altogether — which retroactively reclassifies the whole nineteenth- and early twentieth-century tradition, including Iverson's claim that the doctrine came by inspiration through Joseph Smith and Kimball's description of “O My Father” as a doctrinal hymn, as something other than revealed. The ellipsis in the first sentence is printed in the published text, not an editorial cut. Carries both tags: the reframe is executed and the doctrine is affirmed in the same breath, which is precisely the pattern the category exists to capture.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1991/1991-10-hinckley-daughters-of-god.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; three of the five excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as an original with the citesId edge preserved — the hymn is quoted and attributed, but the entry's substance is Hinckley's own ruling on what may be done with it. The pivotal modern boundary text, and its structure is worth stating plainly, because both critics and defenders routinely collapse it: the doctrine is affirmed (q3), the practice is prohibited (q4), the affirmation is then hollowed by the epistemic claim that nothing about her is revealed (q5). Nothing here repudiates Heavenly Mother, and nothing here leaves room for anyone to say much more about her. Read forward to essay-2015, which restates the doctrine while citing this address, and back to maxwell-heavenly-mother-1978, delivered to a comparable audience thirteen years earlier with no fence at all.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “God the Father: Overview”
speaker: Stephen E. Robinson
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 2:548–550

quotes.excerpt: This doctrine is stated concisely in a well-known couplet by President Lorenzo Snow: “As man now is, God once was: as God now is, man may be”… This principle is clearly demonstrated in the person of Jesus Christ, a God who became mortal, and yet a God like whom mortals may become… But the maxim is true of the Father as well. As the Prophet Joseph Smith said, “God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens! That is the great secret”… Thus, the Father became the Father at some time before “the beginning” as humans know it, by experiencing a mortality similar to that experienced on earth.
quotes.note: Both tags earned under the Father-status precedent: past mortality (“was once as we are now,” “by experiencing a mortality similar to that experienced on earth”) *and* attainment (“the Father became the Father at some time before ‘the beginning’”). Note the order of the argument — the couplet is first demonstrated on Christ, then extended to the Father by the word “also.” That is precisely the referent move the 2014 Gospel Topics essay would later exploit in the other direction; here in 1992 the extension to the Father is made explicit and without hedging. Elisions drop parenthetical scripture and TPJS citations only.

quotes.excerpt: There has been speculation among some Latter-day Saints on the implications of this doctrine, but nothing has been revealed to the Church about conditions before the “beginning” as mortals know it. The important points of the doctrine for Latter-day Saints are that Gods and humans are the same species of being, but at different stages of development in a divine continuum, and that the heavenly Father and Mother are the heavenly pattern, model, and example of what mortals can become through obedience to the gospel.
quotes.note: The 1992 snapshot's handling of the regress: it does not deny that the Father has a Father, it declares the prior conditions unrevealed and reclassifies the question as “speculation… on the implications.” Five years ahead of Hinckley's 1997 “I don't know that we teach it,” and the same shape of move — but note the difference: Robinson keeps the mortality claim itself (q1) fully intact and quarantines only what lies behind it.

quotes.excerpt: The Father, Elohim, is called the Father because he is the literal father of the spirits of mortals (Heb. 12:9). This paternity is not allegorical. All individual human spirits were begotten (not created from nothing or made) by the Father in a premortal state, where they lived and were nurtured by Heavenly Parents.
quotes.note: Tagged viviparous on the viviparous-versus-adoption axis: the article insists on literal begetting against creation ex nihilo (“This paternity is not allegorical”). It does not describe physiology — no gestation, no spirit-matter mechanics of the Pratt/Ballard kind — so the grade of explicitness is well below B4 in the working taxonomy.

quotes.excerpt: The Father existed prior to the Son and the Holy Ghost and is the source of their divinity. In classical terms, LDS theology is subordinationist; that is, it views the Son and the Holy Ghost as subordinate to and dependent upon God the Eternal Father. They are his offspring… The Son and the Holy Spirit were “in the beginning, with God,” but the Father alone existed before the beginning of the universe as it is known.
quotes.note: Context, not a category claim — but the tension is worth recording. One page before the article says the Father “became the Father,” it says he “alone existed before the beginning of the universe as it is known” and is “ultimately the source of all things.” Robinson never reconciles the two; the reconciliation is exactly what q2 declares unrevealed.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 2 (PDF pp. 126–128 = printed 2:548–550); the article is signed “Stephen E. Robinson” on p. 550. Small-capital cross-reference styling in the printed text has been normalized to ordinary case; wording is unaltered. On status: the Encyclopedia is the semi-official 1992 snapshot, not an official publication. Its own Preface (1:lxii, signed by editor in chief Daniel H. Ludlow) states that “The Encyclopedia of Mormonism is a joint product of Brigham Young University and Macmillan Publishing Company, and its contents do not necessarily represent the official position of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. In no sense does the Encyclopedia have the force and authority of scripture,” and that contributors' “statements and opinions remain their own.” At the same time the Acknowledgments (1:lxiii) record that the General Authorities designated BYU as the contractual Author, and that the First Presidency appointed Elders Neal A. Maxwell and Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve as advisers to the project — which is why correlationStatus is never-official but the entry should be read as an authorized-adjacent reference work rather than a private book.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Eternal Progression”
speaker: Lisa Ramsey Adams
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 2:465–466

quotes.excerpt: No official Church teaching attempts to specify all the ways in which God progresses in his exalted spheres; “there is no end to [His] works, neither to [His] words” (Moses 1:38). God's glory and power are enhanced as his children progress in glory and power (see Moses 1:39; Young, JD 10:5). Ideas have been advanced to explain how God might progress in knowledge and still be perfect and know all things (see Foreknowledge of God; Omnipotent God).
quotes.note: The agnosticism, verbatim, and it is carefully built. Three moves in three sentences: (1) presuppose that God progresses while declaring the manner unspecified by official teaching; (2) grant the safe, McConkie-compatible version — enlargement of glory and power through the progress of his children, i.e. dominions rather than knowledge; (3) acknowledge progression *in knowledge* as a live question — “Ideas have been advanced to explain how God might progress in knowledge and still be perfect” — and refuse to adjudicate it, routing the reader to two other articles instead. Twelve years after Bruce R. McConkie called progression in knowledge one of the seven deadly heresies (see mcconkie-heresies-1980), the standard reference work declines to follow him and leaves the D question open. The direction here is neither affirmation nor denial; the tag marks the question.

quotes.excerpt: At the Resurrection and Judgment, people will be assigned a degree of glory. Further progress is believed possible within each degree. Marriage and family life, however, continue only in the celestial kingdom, allowing “eternal increase” through having spirit children (see Eternal Lives, Eternal Increase).
quotes.note: Spirit children after this life, printed plainly and without euphemism in a general-audience reference work. Note also the flat statement that further progress is possible “within each degree” — the post-1917 Talmage line (see talmage-af-kingdom-excision-1917), inter-kingdom progression conspicuously not asserted.

quotes.excerpt: The principle of eternal progression cannot be precisely defined or comprehended, yet it is fundamental to the LDS worldview. The phrase “eternal progression” first occurs in the discourses of Brigham Young. It embodies many concepts taught by Joseph Smith, especially in his King Follett Discourse. It is based on the proposition that “there is no such thing as principle, power, wisdom, knowledge, life, position, or anything that can be imagined, that remains stationary—they must increase or decrease” (Young, JD 1:350).
quotes.note: Context for the genealogy the article draws for itself: Brigham Young for the phrase, the King Follett Discourse for the content. Worth recording that the article routes the reader to the King Follett Discourse by cross-reference and quotes none of it — the “God himself was once as we are now” material appears in this Encyclopedia under God the Father, not under Eternal Progression.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 2 (PDF pp. 43–44 = printed 2:465–466); signed “Lisa Ramsey Adams” on p. 466. Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. The article's sole bibliography item is John A. Widtsoe, “Is Progress Eternal or Is There Progress in Heaven?,” Improvement Era 54 (Mar. 1951):142, plus Evidences and Reconciliations — that is, the pro-progression side of the twentieth-century debate is the only authority cited, while the text itself stays neutral. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Mother in Heaven”
speaker: Elaine Anderson Cannon
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 2:961

quotes.excerpt: Latter-day Saints infer from authoritative sources of scripture and modern prophecy that there is a Heavenly Mother as well as a Heavenly Father.
quotes.note: The article's opening sentence, and the verb is doing work: “infer.” Compare Lorenzo Snow in 1885 (snow-heavenly-mother-1885), “it is not said in so many words in the Scriptures… It is left for us to infer this.” A century on, the reference work uses the same epistemic register.

quotes.excerpt: Latter-day Saints believe that all the people of earth who lived or will live are actual spiritual offspring of God the Eternal Father (Num. 16:22; Heb. 12:9). In this perspective, parenthood requires both father and mother, whether for the creation of spirits in the premortal life or of physical tabernacles on earth. A Heavenly Mother shares parenthood with the Heavenly Father. This concept leads Latter-day Saints to believe that she is like him in glory, perfection, compassion, wisdom, and holiness.
quotes.note: The argument for Heavenly Mother here is an argument from the mechanics of spirit birth: “parenthood requires both father and mother, whether for the creation of spirits in the premortal life or of physical tabernacles on earth.” That parity between spirit begetting and mortal begetting is the viviparous model, stated as a premise rather than defended.

quotes.excerpt: As early as 1839 the Prophet Joseph Smith taught the concept of an eternal mother, as reported in several accounts from that period. Out of his teaching came a hymn that Latter-day Saints learn, sing, quote, and cherish, “O My Father,” by Eliza R. Snow. President Wilford Woodruff called it a revelation (Woodruff, p. 62). In the heav'ns are parents single? No, the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there. When I leave this frail existence, When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high? [Hymn no. 292]
quotes.note: The Encyclopedia prints both stanzas in full and grades the hymn's authority twice over — Joseph Smith as origin (“as early as 1839… as reported in several accounts”), Wilford Woodruff calling it a revelation. Line breaks in the printed hymn quotation are run together here; wording is unaltered.

quotes.excerpt: In 1909 the First Presidency, under Joseph F. Smith, issued a statement on the origin of man that teaches that “man, as a spirit, was begotten and born of heavenly parents, and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father,” as an “offspring of celestial parentage,” and further teaches that “all men and women are in the similitude of the universal Father and Mother, and are literally the sons and daughters of Deity”.
quotes.note: The 1909 First Presidency statement (fp-1909) carried into a 1992 reference work with the “begotten and born” language intact. Two of these three phrases are quoted again on the facing page under Motherhood (2:962) — the “begotten and born of heavenly parents” and “similitude of the universal Father and Mother” clauses, though not “offspring of celestial parentage” — so the Encyclopedia reproduces the core of the 1909 language twice.

quotes.excerpt: Belief that there is a Mother in Heaven who is a partner with God in creation and procreation is not the same as the heavy emphasis on Mariology in the Roman tradition.
quotes.note: “Procreation,” unhedged, in a Macmillan reference work aimed partly at non-Mormon readers. The sentence exists to distinguish the doctrine from Marian devotion, and in doing so states the doctrine more baldly than the disclaimer around it.

quotes.excerpt: Today the belief in a living Mother in Heaven is implicit in Latter-day Saint thought. Though the scriptures contain only hints, statements from Presidents of the Church over the years indicate that human beings have a Heavenly Mother as well as a Heavenly Father.
quotes.note: The closing paragraph, and the softest thing in the article: “implicit,” “only hints,” authority relocated from scripture to the accumulated statements of Presidents. Read against q2 and q5 in the same column, this is the article hedging its own confidence at the end rather than a change of doctrine.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 2 (PDF p. 539 = printed 2:961); signed “Elaine Anderson Cannon.” Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. The article's bibliography is two items: Linda P. Wilcox, “The Mormon Concept of a Mother in Heaven,” in Sisters in Spirit (Urbana, 1987), and Durham's Discourses of Wilford Woodruff — notable for citing Wilcox, a Dialogue-lineage feminist historian, in an official-adjacent reference work. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Premortal Life”
speaker: Gayle Oblad Brown
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 3:1123–1125

quotes.excerpt: There is indeed indication that the intelligence dwelling in each person is coeternal with God. It always existed and never was created or made (D&C 93:29). In due time that intelligence was given a spirit body, becoming the spirit child of God the Eternal Father and his beloved companion, the Mother in Heaven. This spirit, inhabited by the eternal intelligence, took the form of its creators and is in their image (Ballard, p. 140).
quotes.note: The cleanest tripartite statement in the 1992 Encyclopedia: uncreated coeternal intelligence → spirit body begotten by Heavenly Parents → mortal body. It is sourced not to scripture but to Melvin J. Ballard's collected sermons (see ballard-increase), which is where the viviparous physiology lives; the Encyclopedia takes the structure and leaves the mechanics behind the citation.

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph Smith taught that “God himself, finding he was in the midst of spirits and glory, because he was more intelligent, saw proper to institute laws whereby the rest [of the intelligences] could have a privilege to advance like himself” (TPJS, p. 354). His plan included sending his sons and daughters to earth (the second estate), to obtain a body of flesh and bones and learn by experience through earthly vicissitudes, with no memory of the first estate and with the agency to fail or succeed.
quotes.note: King Follett material (TPJS p. 354) quoted verbatim, but only the half that runs forward: intelligences advancing to be like God. The neighbouring King Follett claim — that God himself was once as we are — is absent from this article and appears in this Encyclopedia only under God the Father. “Advance like himself” is left unglossed, hence euphemism rather than explicit.

quotes.excerpt: Thus, to Latter-day Saints premortal life is characterized by individuality, agency, intelligence, and opportunity for eternal progression. It is a central doctrine of the theology of the Church and provides understanding to the age-old question “Whence cometh man?”
quotes.note: Context — the article's closing summary. Recorded because the framing question it answers is the backward one (“Whence cometh man?”), answered entirely at the level of human origin and never extended to the origin of the Father.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 3 (PDF pp. 153–155 = printed 3:1123–1125); signed “Gayle Oblad Brown” on p. 1125. Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. Drafted in place of the “Pre-existence” heading named in the charter: the Encyclopedia's PRE-EXISTENCE (PRE-EARTHLY EXISTENCE) heading at 3:1123 is not an article at all but a bracketed index note listing the articles that treat the subject, so it carries no claims of its own; Premortal Life is the substantive article behind it. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Spirit Body”
speaker: Wilson K. Andersen
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 3:1405–1406

quotes.excerpt: Latter-day Saints believe that each person was born in premortal life as a spirit son or daughter of God. The spirit joins with a physical body in the process of birth on the earth. At death the spirit and the body separate until they reunite in the resurrection.
quotes.note: Birth language (“was born in premortal life”) with no parentage beyond “of God” — this short article never mentions a Mother in Heaven, and never says who bore the spirit. Contrast the immediately preceding article, Spirit (Jay E. Jensen, 3:1404): “human spirits are the literal offspring of perfected, exalted parents, a Father and a mother in heaven.” Two adjacent columns of the same reference work, one explicit and one silent.

quotes.excerpt: Latter-day Saints believe that “all spirit is matter,” but this matter is so fine that it cannot be discerned by mortal eyes (D&C 131: 7-8). The Doctrine and Covenants explains that “the spirit of man [is] in the likeness of his person, as also the spirit of the beast; and every other creature which God has created” (D&C 77:2).
quotes.note: Context — the materialist premise the viviparous model rests on. Recorded because the 1992 article keeps spirit-as-refined-matter while dropping every trace of the nineteenth-century physiology built on it.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 3 (PDF pp. 435–436 = printed 3:1405–1406); signed “Wilson K. Andersen” on p. 1406. Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. This is a thin entry by design — the Spirit Body article is roughly one column and makes only the one category claim — but it is worth holding for the contrast with the Spirit and Premortal Life articles noted on q1. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Eternal Lives, Eternal Increase”
speaker: Shirley S. Ricks
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 2:465

quotes.excerpt: “Eternal lives” is a term that refers to the right and power to beget children after the resurrection, granted to those who are exalted in the highest degree of the celestial kingdom. This is an aspect of eternal progression.
quotes.note: The opening definition, and about as explicit as the forward direction ever gets in print: “the right and power to beget children after the resurrection.” No euphemism, no “eternal increase” shorthand — the mechanism is named in the first clause of the article.

quotes.excerpt: Except a man and his wife enter into an everlasting covenant and be married for eternity, while in this probation, by the power and authority of the Holy Priesthood, they will cease to increase when they die; that is, they will not have any children after the resurrection. But those who are married by the power and authority of the priesthood in this life, and continue without committing the sin against the Holy Ghost, will continue to increase and have children in the celestial glory.
quotes.note: Joseph Smith at Ramus, Illinois, 16–17 May 1843, quoted by the Encyclopedia from TPJS, pp. 300–301 — the doctrinal root of D&C 131. Note it is the negative form that carries the force: those not sealed “will not have any children after the resurrection.”

quotes.excerpt: In 1864 he elaborated: “In like manner, every faithful son of God, becomes, as it were, Adam to the race that springs from his loins, when they are embraced in the covenants and blessings of the Holy Priesthood… in the progress of eternal lives.… We have not yet received our kingdoms, neither will we, until we have finished our work on the earth, passed through the ordeals, are brought up by the power of the resurrection, and are crowned with glory and eternal lives” (JD 10:355).
quotes.note: Brigham Young's forward chain quoted at length in 1992: each exalted man becomes “Adam to the race that springs from his loins,” each with his own kingdom. Not tagged MANY-WORLDS: the passage distributes kingdoms across every faithful son, which implies a plurality of peopled dominions, but it never says “worlds” — the inference belongs here rather than in the pills. Read with the Adam-God material (young-adam-god-chain-1854) this is the surviving, sanitized half of that framework.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 2 (PDF p. 43 = printed 2:465); signed “Shirley S. Ricks.” Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. Not among the articles named in the drafting charter, but included because the Encyclopedia gives the timeline's own subject its own signed heading and states the forward claim more explicitly than any of the charter articles do — the maintainer should drop it if the scope was meant to be strictly the four named entries. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Teachings of Presidents of the Church: Brigham Young, ch. 4, “Knowing and Honoring the Godhead”
speaker: Church Curriculum Department, quoting Brigham Young
office: Correlated priesthood/Relief Society manual
venue: Teachings of Presidents of the Church: Brigham Young (1997), 28–35

quotes.excerpt: The doctrine that God was once a man and has progressed to become a God is unique to this Church. How do you feel, knowing that God, through His own experience, “knows all that we know regarding the toils [and] sufferings” of mortality?
quotes.note: The manual's own editorial voice, in the “Suggestions for Study” section — not a Brigham Young quotation. Two things worth separating: it asserts God's past mortality (BACKWARD-MORTALITY under the taxonomy's first conflation trap — this is not a claim that God has a Father, and not a claim of ongoing progression), and it frames that doctrine as a distinctive the reader should feel good about, which is a register the later material abandons.

quotes.excerpt: Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause of all things; but it would be as easy for an ant to number the grains of sand on the earth. It is not for man, with his limited intelligence, to grasp eternity in his comprehension. … What then, should be the calling and duty of the children of men? Instead of inquiring after the origin of Gods—instead of trying to explore the depths of eternities that have been, that are, and that will be, instead of endeavoring to discover the boundaries of boundless space, let them seek to know the object of their present existence, and how to apply, in the most profitable manner for their mutual good and salvation, the intelligence they possess. Let them seek to know and thoroughly understand things within their reach, and to make themselves well acquainted with the object of their being here, by diligently seeking unto a super-power for information and by the careful study of the best books.
quotes.note: Excerpted in the manual and sourced there to DBY, 25 (Widtsoe's Discourses of Brigham Young compilation), not to the Journal of Discourses directly. The manual retains the “Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause” sentences that open the passage in the sermon, printing them in the same paragraph immediately before the quoted material; it was this entry's excerpt that dropped them, and they are restored above. Its wording differs slightly from the JoD text logged at young-origin-caution-1859 — “the origin of Gods” rather than “the origin of the Gods,” and a comma where the sermon has a dash — which is characteristic of the DBY compilation as intermediary.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live chapter; the manual does carry the origin-of-the-Gods caution, so this is filed as a citation of young-origin-caution-1859 as charter'd. The chapter is the pairing itself: within one lesson the manual proudly names God's past mortality as a doctrine unique to the Restoration, and hands the reader Brigham Young telling them not to inquire after where the Gods came from. That is the modern settlement in miniature, printed in 1997 — affirm the past-mortality datum, decline the genealogy — and it is worth noting that the decline is voiced by the same president who elsewhere pressed the chain hardest (see by-chain, delivered the day before the caution in the same 1859 conference). Hearsay A as a correlated manual; the Young material inside it is C-tier at origin (Watt shorthand) and passes through a second compiler before reaching this page.

title: Joseph Fielding McConkie: God obtained his exalted status “by obedience to the laws of his own eternal Father”
speaker: Joseph Fielding McConkie
office: Professor of Ancient Scripture, Brigham Young University
venue: Answers: Straightforward Answers to Tough Gospel Questions (Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 1998), 168

witnesses.scribe: Alonzo L. Gaskill, The Savior, Symbols, and Salvation, ch. note 13
witnesses.note: Quotes the sentence with the page citation “Answers, 168,” in a note gathering statements that God became what He is by obedience to eternal law.

quotes.excerpt: God was once a man obtaining his exalted status by obedience to the laws of his own eternal Father.
quotes.note: One sentence carrying both halves at once: past mortality (“God was once a man”) and explicit divine parentage (“his own eternal Father”). Chain length is unstated and no chain is asserted, so no INFINITE-CHAIN tag — but the parentage is unhedged, which makes this one of the most recent flatly affirmative statements available from a named Latter-day Saint author.

notes: The book is not in the collated corpus; the sentence was verified verbatim against Gaskill's quotation, which supplies the page. The 1998-versus-2002 imprint question that trails this citation is now settled in favour of 1998: Gaskill's short-form note gives no year, but his own bibliography lists “McConkie, Joseph Fielding. 1998. Answers: Straightforward Answers to Tough Gospel Questions. Salt Lake City: Deseret Book,” and at least eight other independent bibliographies in the corpus (Harrell, Bradshaw, Gardner, Harris, Wilcox, Valletta, and two Dialogue articles) give the same 1998 Deseret Book imprint. No 2002 imprint appears anywhere in the corpus, so the entry is dated 1998. Never-official: a Deseret Book trade title in a question-and-answer format by a BYU religion professor, notable mainly for how plainly it states in 1998 what correlated materials had by then stopped saying.

title: Henry B. Eyring, “Do Not Delay”
speaker: Henry B. Eyring
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General Conference, October 1999, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: It is the greatest of all the gifts of God. It is to live in families forever with our Heavenly Father and with Jesus Christ and to have eternal increase.
quotes.note: Defining eternal life. “Eternal increase” is the final term in the definition and receives no explanation; the surrounding argument is about not postponing repentance, so the phrase passes without the audience being asked to unpack it.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live talk. The earliest item in this batch and a useful boundary marker: in 1999 an apostle can still put “eternal increase” in a definition of eternal life as though it needs no gloss, which is a different silence from the later one — assumed shared vocabulary rather than deliberate omission. Nothing in the talk distinguishes the two readings, and the entry does not claim to.

title: Sheri L. Dew, “Are We Not All Mothers?”
speaker: Sheri L. Dew
office: Second Counselor in the Relief Society General Presidency
venue: General Conference, October 2001, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: For mother is the word that will define a righteous woman made perfect in the highest degree of the celestial kingdom, a woman who has qualified for eternal increase in posterity, wisdom, joy, and influence.
quotes.note: “Mother” is italicized in print. Two things make this less veiled than the conference norm: “increase” is given an object (“in posterity”), and the exalted woman is defined by motherhood in the celestial kingdom rather than by motherhood recalled from mortality. Still euphemism — “posterity” does not distinguish new spirit offspring from mortal descendants sealed forward, and the list it heads (wisdom, joy, influence) pulls toward the qualitative reading.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live talk. Useful as a register datum: a general officer addressing women about motherhood is the one modern conference setting where post-mortal maternity can be stated as a defining fact rather than alluded to, and even here the operative noun is “posterity.” The address's larger argument — that every woman is a mother by nature regardless of mortal childbearing — is what the sentence serves, so read it as pastoral before cosmological.

title: Doctrine and Covenants Student Manual rejects “He Himself is still learning”
speaker: Church Educational System
office: Institute curriculum
venue: Doctrine and Covenants Student Manual (2002), Section 38, pp. 75–79

quotes.excerpt: Some have questioned whether God is omniscient, that is, whether He knows all things. They say that He knows all things relative to man but that He Himself is still learning. This scripture shows that God has all knowledge.
quotes.note: Denial in correlated curriculum. The position being corrected — God “is still learning” — is the one Woodruff preached in 1857; the manual frames it as an outsider's question. The proof-text is D&C 38:1–2, where the speaker is the Lord (Jesus Christ), hence the ambiguous referent.

notes: Superseded by the 2017 institute manual but still hosted. A clean example of the denial position operating quietly in curriculum rather than conference.

title: Ensign reprint of “The Origin of Man”
speaker: Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
office: Official magazine
venue: Ensign, February 2002

quotes.excerpt: [Full reprint of the 1909 statement, including “begotten and born of heavenly parents.”]
quotes.note: The act of reprinting is the datum; the text is the 1909 original.

notes: Reprinting the strongest viviparous statement in full, five years after the Hinckley interviews minimized the backward direction, cuts against a simple monotonic-taper narrative. The Ensign reprinted “The Father and the Son” two months later. Both belong in any honest account of the period.

title: First Presidency and the Twelve, “The Father and the Son: A Doctrinal Exposition”
speaker: First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
office: First Presidency and the Twelve
venue: Official doctrinal exposition (Improvement Era, August 1916)

quotes.excerpt: God the Eternal Father, whom we designate by the exalted name-title “Elohim,” is the literal Parent of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of the spirits of the human race.
quotes.note: Marked implied: this asserts literal parentage, not birth mechanics. Strictly it is viviparous-implied, and 1909 remains the statement that actually says “begotten and born.”

notes: Reprinted in the Ensign, April 2002, alongside the February reprint of “The Origin of Man.”

title: First Presidency, “‘Mormon’ View of Evolution”
speaker: Heber J. Grant, Anthony W. Ivins, Charles W. Nibley
office: First Presidency
venue: Improvement Era

quotes.excerpt: [Condensed reissue of the 1909 statement. Check whether “begotten and born of heavenly parents” survives the condensation.]
quotes.note: The categories on this entry are deliberately empty until the wording is checked — the whole point of the entry is which language did or did not survive.

notes: Added in v2. A condensed reissue of 1909, and a clean natural experiment: if the “begotten and born” language was trimmed, that is an early retreat data point three decades before correlation; if retained, it strengthens the continuity case. Either result is worth having, which is why the entry belongs in the set regardless. URL currently points at the 1909 reprint and needs replacing with the 1925 text.

title: Melvin J. Ballard on eternal increase
speaker: Melvin J. Ballard
office: Apostle (d. 1939; compilation published posthumously)
venue: Sermon; quoted in Eternal Marriage Student Manual (2003), 167–83, citing Melvin J. Ballard—Crusader for Righteousness, 211

quotes.excerpt: What do we mean by endless or eternal increase? We mean that through the righteousness and faithfulness of men and women who keep the commandments of God they will come forth with celestial bodies, fitted and prepared to enter into their great, high and eternal glory in the celestial kingdom of God; and unto them through their preparation, there will come spirit children. …The nature of the offspring is determined by the nature of the substance that flows in the veins of the being. When blood flows in the veins of the being the offspring will be what blood produces, which is tangible flesh and bone; but when that which flows in the veins is spirit matter, a substance which is more refined and pure and glorious than blood, the offspring of such beings will be spirit children.
quotes.note: Names both the object (spirit children) and the agents (exalted couples) — genuinely explicit where D&C 132 is not.

notes: Hearsay lowered from A to B in v2. Sermons and Missionary Services was assembled posthumously by Bryant S. Hinckley from sermon reports; Ballard did not publish it under his own direction, so first-person A does not apply. Verify which sermon carries the physiological “spirit matter in their veins” material — “Three Degrees of Glory” (Ogden, 22 September 1922) is the likely origin, and “The Sacramental Covenant” is a different sermon that v1 conflated with it. The 2003 manual entry stays A as a citation: the decision to correlate is first-person Church action even where the underlying sermon text is B.

title: Bruce R. McConkie, Mormon Doctrine — “Eternal Progression,” “Spirit Children”
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Seventy, later Apostle
venue: Mormon Doctrine (Bookcraft)

quotes.excerpt: Spirit Children… 1. All men in pre-existence were the spirit children of God our Father, an exalted, glorified, and perfected Man. “The Father has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's” (D. & C. 130:22); the offspring born to him in that primeval sphere had bodies of spirit element… 2. In a future eternity, spirit children will be born to exalted, perfected, glorified couples for whom the family unit continues. The very glory of exalted beings is to have “a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever.” (D. & C. 132:19-25, 29-32; 131:1-4.) … Spirit Birth… 1. In the literal sense, the expression spirit birth has reference to the birth of the spirit in pre-existence. Spirits are actually born as the offspring of a Heavenly Father, a glorified and exalted Man. They will be born in a future eternity to future exalted beings for whom the family unit continues.
quotes.note: Two adjacent entries, “Spirit Children” and “Spirit Birth,” quoted together because the pair is the claim: the same begetting is predicated of the Father in the past and of exalted couples in the future, in the same words. The vocabulary is deliberately literalist — “in the literal sense,” “actually born,” “born to him,” “birth process” in the companion “Spirit Bodies” entry — which is what earns SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS rather than the adoption tag; contrast Roberts, who reaches the same begetting while holding the intelligence uncreated (bh-roberts-tripartite). INFINITE-CHAIN rests on the forward half specifically — the glory of exalted beings is “a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever,” an unending continuation, not a single further generation — and on the fact that the past and future halves are stated as one repeating pattern rather than two unrelated facts. The Father is described as “an exalted, glorified, and perfected Man,” attainment language without a mortality claim, which per the Father-status precedent would be FATHER-BECAME-GOD; that reading is left to q2, where McConkie makes it explicit rather than adjectival. 2nd ed. (1966) pp. 523; 1st ed. (1958) pp. 678–679.

quotes.excerpt: “Every man who reigns in celestial glory is a god to his dominions,” the Prophet said. Hence, the Father, who shall continue to all eternity as the God of exalted beings, is a God of Gods. Further, as the Prophet also taught, there is “a God above the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. … If Jesus Christ was the Son of God, and John discovered that God the Father of Jesus Christ had a Father, you may suppose that he had a Father also. Where was there ever a son without a father? … Hence if Jesus had a Father, can we not believe that he had a Father also?” In this way both the Father and the Son, as also all exalted beings, are now or in due course will become Gods of Gods.
quotes.note: The “God of Gods” entry, 2nd ed. (1966) p. 230, printing the Sermon in the Grove regress approvingly — from the same author whose 1980 fireside denounced divine progression in knowledge. Affirming the backward chain while denying divine progression: the two questions are independent, demonstrated within one corpus. Pagination now checked in both editions: 2nd ed. p. 230, 1st ed. (1958) p. 296, wording unchanged between them.

quotes.excerpt: Those who gain exaltation, having thus enjoyed the fullness of eternal progression, become like God. It should be realized that God is not progressing in knowledge, truth, virtue, wisdom, or any of the attributes of godliness. He has already gained these things in their fullness. But he is progressing in the sense that his creations increase, his dominions expand, his spirit offspring multiply, and more kingdoms are added to his domains. (Doctrines of Salvation, vol. 1, pp. 5-10.)
quotes.note: The “Eternal Progression” entry, 2nd ed. p. 174 / 1st ed. p. 221. A denial, and the canonical statement of the dominions-not-knowledge move — the same distinction B. H. Roberts had used in 1911 to affirm divine progress (roberts-progress-of-god-1911), here run in reverse to deny it, sourced to Joseph Fielding Smith. Worth reading beside q2 on the same page-range logic: God has a Father and is a God of Gods, but does not learn. Also note the third clause of the concession — “his spirit offspring multiply” — which concedes ongoing generation by the Father in the present tense while denying progression, and so keeps the forward chain of q1 alive inside the denial. One textual difference between editions, non-substantive to the tag: the 1st edition adds “and that even for those who participate in eternal progression in its fullest sense there are limits to the doctrine,” dropped in the 2nd.

notes: Placeholder closed in v2. All three excerpts were read from the Gospel Scholar Archive copies of both printings and their printed folios recorded: Mormon Doctrine, 1st ed. (Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1958; title page and June 1958 preface confirmed in the scan) — “Eternal Progression” p. 221, “God of Gods” p. 296, “Spirit Birth”/“Spirit Children” pp. 678–679; 2nd ed. (© 1966 Deseret Book) — pp. 174, 230, 523. Wording is identical across the two editions for every clause quoted here apart from one dropped subordinate clause in “Eternal Progression,” noted on q3, so the previously flagged first-edition pagination gap is closed and the verification flag is cleared. The url now points at the archive page for “Spirit Children,” since that is where q1 lives; the Internet Archive lending copy (archive.org/details/mormondoctrine0000mcco) remains a second witness but is not page-anchored. Never official — it drew First Presidency concern on publication, and the 1865 rule that a member may not publish doctrine without prior approval of the First Presidency and the Twelve (see fp-repudiation-1865) is precisely what it ignored — yet massively influential on lay understanding for half a century, which is exactly why it needs to be in the dataset with its status labelled honestly. Bookcraft/Deseret Book let it go out of print in 2010; that discontinuation is itself a retreat data point, and the reason its correlation status is discontinued rather than never-official. A further passage the maintainer may want as a fourth quote: the “Eternity to Eternity” entry, 2nd ed. p. 175, which states that spirit children “will have gone on to exaltation, having spirit children of their own” and that exalted beings go on “multiplying their race without end” — the cleanest INFINITE-CHAIN statement in the book.
