title: Dale G. Renlund, “Your Divine Nature and Eternal Destiny” — revealed, and fenced
speaker: Dale G. Renlund
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, women's session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: The second truth is that we have heavenly parents, a father and a mother. The doctrine of a Heavenly Mother comes by revelation and is a distinctive belief among Latter-day Saints. President Dallin H. Oaks explained the importance of this truth: “Our theology begins with heavenly parents. Our highest aspiration is to be like them.”
quotes.note: The affirmation, and it is stronger than Hinckley's on the one axis that matters most. "The doctrine of a Heavenly Mother comes by revelation" is the direct contrary of hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991-q5, "her of whom we have no revealed knowledge," and it restores the epistemic claim that Hinckley's closing sentence had removed — thirty-one years later, to a comparable audience, from the same pulpit. It also restores what iverson-mother-in-heaven-1908 had asserted and 1991 had converted into an argument from silence. Note the ground shifts but the content does not: nothing further about her is stated here than in 1991.

quotes.excerpt: Very little has been revealed about Mother in Heaven, but what we do know is summarized in a gospel topic found in our Gospel Library application. Once you have read what is there, you will know everything that I know about the subject. I wish I knew more. You too may still have questions and want to find more answers. Seeking greater understanding is an important part of our spiritual development, but please be cautious. Reason cannot replace revelation.
quotes.note: The fence, and the pivot of the address. Three moves in six sentences: the content is capped ("very little"), the ceiling is set at a Gospel Library page rather than at an apostle's own knowledge ("you will know everything that I know"), and the traditional warrant for the doctrine is disqualified outright — "Reason cannot replace revelation." That last clause retires the argument that had carried the doctrine for 137 years: Erastus Snow's inference from nature (snow-heavenly-mother-1885), Rudger Clawson's "Who ever heard of a father where there was no mother?" (clawson-mother-there-1929), Orson F. Whitney's dare to prove it unphilosophic (whitney-father-and-mother-1907), and Hinckley's own "Logic and reason would certainly suggest" (hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991-q3). The 1991 affirmation and the 2022 prohibition rest on opposite epistemologies, and the 2022 one forbids the 1991 one. Carries both tags for the same reason the Hinckley entry does: the affirmation and the boundary are the same sentence-cluster.

quotes.excerpt: Speculation will not lead to greater spiritual knowledge, but it can lead us to deception or divert our focus from what has been revealed. For example, the Savior taught His disciples, “Always pray unto the Father in my name.” We follow this pattern and direct our worship to our Heavenly Father in the name of Jesus Christ and do not pray to Heavenly Mother.
quotes.note: The prohibition on prayer, restated for a new generation and — this is the point to record — restated without Hinckley. The published footnote for the sentence cites Russell M. Nelson's "Lessons from the Lord's Prayers" (Ensign or Liahona, May 2009), not the 1991 address that is the modern origin of the rule. The scriptural pattern argument survives from 1991 (hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991-q4); the argument from the absence of precedent among Church presidents does not reappear. Note also the framing: what was in 1991 the correction of a named practice by "some few women of the Church" is here a general caution against "speculation," with no group named and nothing to have been done wrong.

quotes.excerpt: Ever since God appointed prophets, they have been authorized to speak on His behalf. But they do not pronounce doctrines fabricated “of [their] own mind” or teach what has not been revealed. … Latter-day prophets are similarly constrained. Demanding revelation from God is both arrogant and unproductive. Instead, we wait on the Lord and His timetable to reveal His truths through the means that He has established.
quotes.note: The most consequential paragraph in the address and the one least often quoted. The reticence is relocated a third time. Spencer W. Kimball had relocated it to the Mother herself — "maternal modesty," "restrained, queenly elegance" (kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978); Hinckley relocated it to the state of revelation; Renlund relocates it to the office, which is now described as constrained rather than reticent. Prophets do not decline to say more, they are unable to, and asking them to is "arrogant." The Balaam analogy is elided; the bracketed "[their]" is the published text's.

quotes.excerpt: The third truth in the opening paragraph of the Young Women theme is that we have “a divine nature.” This is intrinsic to who we are. It is spiritually “genetic,” inherited from our heavenly parents, and requires no effort on our part.
quotes.note: Inheritance language, scare-quoted. "Spiritually 'genetic'" is a heredity metaphor from a cardiologist and is as close as the address comes to any mechanism — but the quotation marks are doing the fencing, and the claim is about nature rather than about generation. HEAVENLY-MOTHER because the parents are plural and are the source; no SPIRIT-BIRTH tag, in either direction, because none is stated.

quotes.excerpt: Our Heavenly Father wants you to become His heir and receive all that He has. He cannot offer you more. He cannot promise you more.
quotes.note: The peroration, and the forward direction as it now sounds: maximal in scope, empty of content. "All that He has" is the D&C 84:38 formula, and the footnote points there. Compare renlund-2020-q3, where the same author encodes the same thing as "His kind of life" — the two together are the clearest available sample of how the generative claim is carried in current apostolic discourse, which is by inheritance vocabulary that never says what is inherited.

quotes.excerpt: Dallin H. Oaks, “Apostasy and Restoration,” Ensign, May 1995, 87; see also Doctrine and Covenants 131:1–4; 132:19. Women and men cannot be exalted without each other.
quotes.note: Published footnote 8 in full, and the only place in the address where D&C 132 appears. The last sentence is Renlund's own gloss, not part of the Oaks citation: a bare statement that exaltation requires both sexes, appended to the "continuation of the seeds" verse (see dc-132) and to the new-and-everlasting-covenant-of-marriage verses, in a footnote to a talk about a Young Women theme. The whole nineteenth-century argument is present in that adjacency and is nowhere in the body text — which is precisely the pattern this dataset exists to make visible.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2022/2022-04-renlund-your-divine-nature-and-eternal-destiny.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned the byline ("By Elder Dale G. Renlund of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles"), the opening of each excerpted paragraph, and footnote 8 in full, all verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. The direct sequel to hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991 and the entry that should be read immediately after it, but the relationship is not the one usually assumed, and three things should be checked against the text rather than repeated from summaries. First, Renlund does not quote or cite Hinckley anywhere in the address or its forty footnotes — the fence is rebuilt from scratch, citing Oaks (1995) for the affirmation and Nelson (2009) for the prayer restriction. Second, he does not cite "O My Father" or Eliza R. Snow, which is why this entry carries no citesId edge to o-my-father: the hymn that had licensed the doctrine from 1845 through Hinckley's own 1991 address has dropped out entirely, and the authority now runs to a Gospel Library page. That page and the Gospel Topics essay "Mother in Heaven" (essay-2015) are named in footnotes 7, 9 and 16 as the whole of what may be known; no edge is drawn to essay-2015 because it is itself a citation-type entry and the dataset draws citesId edges only to originals, but the delegation is the substantive fact and is recorded here. The only citesId is dc-132, earned by footnote 8. Third, the shape is the inverse of 1991 on the epistemic axis and identical on the practical one: Hinckley affirmed the doctrine on logic and then emptied it by denying revelation; Renlund affirms the revelation and then empties it by capping the content and disqualifying the logic. Both end in the same place — she is real, and there is nothing further to say — by opposite routes. What is genuinely new in 2022 is the handoff: the authority on the subject is no longer a hymn, an apostle, or an inference, but a page in an app, and the address says so twice.

title: Matthew L. Carpenter, “Fruit That Remains”
speaker: Matthew L. Carpenter
office: Of the Seventy
venue: General Conference, April 2024, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: What are the blessings of exaltation? They include dwelling in God's presence for eternity together as husband and wife, inheriting “thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers, … and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever,” receiving all that God the Father has.
quotes.note: The speaker poses the question directly — “What are the blessings of exaltation?” — which is exactly the moment a gloss would belong, and then answers it in the scripture's own vocabulary. The elision inside the quotation is the talk's own, not this dataset's.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live talk; the paragraph ends at “receiving all that God the Father has.” with nothing following. Structurally identical to oaks-2019 five years earlier: the D&C 132 code phrase is deployed in conference and the final noun is never supplied. Carpenter's case is the tighter one, because he is answering an enumerating question of his own asking and still declines the gloss — the omission is not an artifact of the talk drifting past the topic.

title: Doctrine and Covenants Seminary Teacher Manual (2025), Lesson 140 on D&C 131
speaker: Church Educational System
office: Seminary curriculum (correlated)
venue: Doctrine and Covenants Seminary Teacher Manual (2025), “Lesson 140—Doctrine and Covenants 131: The New and Everlasting Covenant of Marriage”

quotes.excerpt: Read Doctrine and Covenants 131:1–4, looking for what the Prophet taught about marriage.
quotes.note: The lesson does not reproduce the verses on the page; students are sent to them. So the word “increase” never appears in the manual's own text at all — the reading assignment carries it and the instruction narrows what to look for to “marriage.”

quotes.excerpt: To become like God and live with Him again in the celestial kingdom, we must enter the new and everlasting covenant of marriage.
quotes.note: The doctrinal statement students are told to write down — the lesson's takeaway, and the replacement for the 2014 manual's spirit-offspring material. Marriage is presented as the requirement; what marriage is a requirement *for* stops at “become like God.”

quotes.excerpt: Those who are exalted will live eternally with Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ and become like Them.
quotes.note: The lesson's only description of what exaltation consists of. Association and likeness, no generative content.

quotes.excerpt: How do you think marriage can prepare us to become more like God?
quotes.note: The discussion question. Opened and left open — the manual supplies teachers no answer that mentions children, posterity, or increase.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live lesson: I checked specifically for the word “increase” and for any gloss of it as spirit children, posterity, or offspring after the resurrection, and found none anywhere on the page. Lesson headings in order are Understanding marriage / Eternal marriage / The importance of marriage in God's plan / Explain the doctrine of marriage / Memorize / Additional Resources / Supplemental Learning Activities. The measurement is the contrast with seminary-2014, which taught the same scripture block to the same age group and gave teachers the First Presidency's “parents of spirit offspring,” McConkie's “spirit progeny,” and Parley Pratt's queen-mother passage; eleven years later the material is simply gone rather than replaced by a denial. Two cautions for the reader: (1) this is a softening in one lesson, not a repudiation — ftsoy-2025 printed “eternal spirit children of their own” the same year; (2) citesId points at dc-132 because that is the dataset's entry for the increase/seeds text, though the lesson itself is on D&C 131, which has no entry yet. Distinct from cfm-2025, which logs the Come, Follow Me treatment of the same block; the two are companion measurements, not duplicates.

title: David A. Edwards, “After This Life: Answers to Some Questions”
speaker: David A. Edwards
office: Church Magazines staff writer
venue: For the Strength of Youth (official magazine for teenagers), July 2025

quotes.excerpt: They participate in His work and glory. They were sealed in marriage for eternity and now live in eternal families, having eternal spirit children of their own.
quotes.note: Under the heading “What goes on in the celestial kingdom?” Both nouns are present and unhedged: “spirit children,” and “of their own” — the offspring belong to the exalted couple, not to God. No euphemism is doing any work here.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page. The most explicit forward-generative statement in current correlated print, and the register is what makes it notable: not an institute manual for adult students of scripture but a staff-written FAQ placed before teenagers in 2025. The author is Church Magazines staff, not a General Authority — worth stating, because the explicitness of the sentence tempts a stronger attribution than the byline supports. Its value is as a correlation datum (an editorial decision to print the sentence), not as an authoritative pronouncement.

title: Camille N. Johnson, “Lessons Learned in Inviting Christ to Author My Story”
speaker: Camille N. Johnson
office: Relief Society General President
venue: Liahona (official magazine)

quotes.excerpt: ...whether we are sealed and bear children in this life or the next, our object is exaltation—which can be ours if we make and keep covenants.
quotes.note: Caveat in the v2 spirit of referent discipline: in context this comforts couples childless in mortality, and the plainest reading is posthumous fulfilment of sealing promises. It entails post-mortal childbearing but does not specify spirit children — the object of “bear children... in the next [life]” is left open, and a millennial or resurrected reading is available. Kept explicit because it does name post-mortal childbearing, which nothing else in current correlated print does.

notes: A rare recent explicit, arriving in a pastoral rather than doctrinal register — which may be precisely why it could be said at all.
